school-c9-maths.title: Class 9 Mathematics
school-c9-maths.description: Every chapter of Class 9 Mathematics (NCERT-based): concepts, proofs, solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes and chapter tests, plus revision and mock papers. Chapter names follow the 2023–24 rationalised NCERT edition; newer editions may differ. Independent material — not affiliated with NCERT, CBSE or any board.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Number Systems
courses.summary: Natural numbers to real numbers: rationals, irrationals, decimal expansions, surds, rationalising and laws of exponents — with every type of exam question solved step by step.
outcomes: Classify any number as natural, whole, integer, rational or irrational
Find rational numbers between two given numbers
Convert recurring decimals to p/q form
Locate √2, √3, √5 and √x on the number line
Rationalise denominators and simplify surds
Apply laws of exponents with rational powers

scenes.text: Riya marks 0, 1, 2 on a ruler and wonders what lives in the gaps.
Her brother says: 'Between any two fractions there are infinitely many more.' She does not believe him — yet.

steps.title: The family of numbers
steps.body:
- **Natural numbers N**: 1, 2, 3, …
- **Whole numbers W**: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
- **Integers Z**: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … (Z comes from the German word *zahlen*, 'to count')
- **Rational numbers Q**: numbers that can be written as p/q where p, q are integers and **q ≠ 0** (Q from 'quotient').

Every natural number is whole, every whole number is an integer, every integer is rational (e.g. −5 = −5/1). The reverse is not true.

steps.title: Equivalent forms
steps.body: A rational number has many equal forms: 1/2 = 2/4 = 10/20. When we say 'p/q form' we usually mean the **simplest form**: p and q have no common factor other than 1 and q > 0.

steps.title: Solved: five rationals between 3/5 and 4/5
steps.body:
Step 1: Multiply top and bottom by 6 (one more than 5): 3/5 = 18/30, 4/5 = 24/30.
Step 2: Pick numerators in between: **19/30, 20/30, 21/30, 22/30, 23/30**.
Any larger multiplier (say 10 → 30/50 and 40/50) gives even more.

steps.title: Solved: rationals between 1 and 2 by averaging
steps.body:
Step 1: (1 + 2)/2 = 3/2.
Step 2: (1 + 3/2)/2 = 5/4; (3/2 + 2)/2 = 7/4.
So 5/4, 3/2, 7/4 lie between 1 and 2. Repeating this never stops — there are **infinitely many** rationals between any two rationals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 0 is a natural number (it is whole, not natural).
- Forgetting q ≠ 0: 5/0 is not a number at all.
- Thinking there is a 'next' rational after 1/2 — there is none, because you can always average again.

steps.title: Exam shortcut
steps.body: To find n rationals between a/b and c/b, multiply numerator and denominator by (n + 1).

activity.prompt: Put each number in the SMALLEST set it belongs to

options: Every whole number is a rational number
Every rational number is an integer
Every integer is a natural number
quiz.why: A whole number w can be written as w/1, so every whole number is rational. 0 is not a natural number, and not every rational number is an integer.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a rational number?
quiz.why: 3/0 is undefined, since division by zero is not allowed; a rational number p/q needs q ≠ 0. The others are rational.

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1/3 and 1/2?
quiz.why: Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more, since we can always take averages again and again. So there are infinitely many between 1/3 and 1/2.

quiz.q: A rational number between 2 and 3 is
quiz.why: 5/2 = 2.5, which lies between 2 and 3. 7/2 = 3.5 and 1/2 = 0.5 are outside, and 2 is not between.
−18/24: the HCF of 18 and 24 is 6, so dividing both gives −3/4. The denominator is kept positive.

lessons.title: Irrational numbers and the real number line

story.title: The square no fraction could measure

scenes.text: A square tile has side 1 m. Arjun measures its diagonal: about 1.414 m.
His teacher says the exact length is √2 — and no fraction p/q equals it. Arjun is amazed that a 'missing' number fills a real length.

steps.title: What is an irrational number?
steps.body:
A number is **irrational** if it **cannot** be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0. Examples: √2, √3, √5, √7, π, 0.1011011101111…

The Pythagoreans (around 400 BCE) discovered that √2 is not rational. Rational and irrational numbers together form the **real numbers R**. Every real number is a unique point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number.

steps.title: Careful with roots
steps.body: √n is irrational whenever the whole number n is **not** a perfect square. √4 = 2, √9 = 3 and √0.25 = 0.5 are rational. π is irrational; 22/7 is only a rational **approximation** of π.

steps.title: Solved: locating √2 on the number line
steps.body:
Step 1: On the line take OA = 1 unit from 0.
Step 2: At A draw AB ⟂ OA with AB = 1 unit.
Step 3: By Pythagoras OB = √(1² + 1²) = √2.
Step 4: With centre O and radius OB draw an arc cutting the line at P. **P represents √2.**

steps.title: Solved: locating √5 and √3
steps.body:
√5: take OA = 2, AB ⟂ OA with AB = 1; OB = √(4 + 1) = √5; swing an arc to the line.
√3: first build √2 as above (OB = √2), draw BD ⟂ OB with BD = 1; OD = √(2 + 1) = √3. Continuing gives the **square-root spiral**: √2, √3, √4, √5, …

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing π = 22/7 exactly (it is only an approximation).
- Calling √9 irrational because it has a root sign — simplify first.
- Forgetting the perpendicular must be 1 unit when building the spiral.

steps.title: Where you meet √2
steps.body: A4 paper has sides in ratio about 1 : √2, so folding it in half keeps the same shape — that is why A3, A4, A5 all look alike.

activity.prompt: Rational or irrational?

quiz.why: √2 cannot be written as p/q with integers, so it is irrational. Its decimal never ends or repeats.
√10 is irrational because 10 is not a perfect square. √25 = 5, √(9/16) = 3/4 and 0.333… = 1/3 are rational.

quiz.q: To locate √5 on the number line you build a right triangle with legs
quiz.why: The hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 2 and 1 is √(2² + 1²) = √5. Using it, we can mark √5 on the number line.
Real numbers are made up of rational and irrational numbers together. They fill the whole number line.
22/7 = 3.142857… is a recurring decimal, so it is rational, while π = 3.14159… does not recur. So 22/7 is only an approximation of π.

lessons.title: Decimal expansions and converting to p/q

scenes.text: Kabir divides 1 by 7 and gets 0.142857142857… — the same six digits forever.
Then he tries √2 on the calculator: digits that never settle into a pattern. Two different kinds of 'never-ending'!

steps.title: Three kinds of decimal expansion
steps.body:
- **Terminating**: ends after finitely many digits, e.g. 7/8 = 0.875.
- **Non-terminating recurring**: a block repeats forever, e.g. 1/3 = 0.333… = 0.3̄, 1/7 = 0.142857 with bar over 142857.
- **Non-terminating non-recurring**: no repeating block, e.g. √2 = 1.41421356…, π.

**Rule:** a number is rational ⇔ its decimal expansion is terminating or non-terminating recurring. It is irrational ⇔ non-terminating non-recurring.

steps.title: Predict without dividing
steps.body: In simplest form p/q, the decimal **terminates** exactly when q has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. 3/40 (40 = 2³·5) terminates; 2/15 (15 = 3·5) recurs. Remainders when dividing by q can only be 0, 1, …, q−1, so a repeat must come within q steps.

steps.title: Solved: 0.6666… as p/q
steps.body:
Let x = 0.666…
Multiply by 10: 10x = 6.666…
Subtract: 10x − x = 6 ⇒ 9x = 6 ⇒ **x = 2/3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying by 10 when two digits repeat (use 10ⁿ where n = length of repeating block).
- Forgetting to subtract the non-repeating part separately (as in 0.23535…).
- Thinking 0.101001000100001… is rational — it never repeats a fixed block, so it is irrational.

activity.prompt: Convert recurring decimals (write fractions in simplest form like 4/9)

quiz.q: 1/8 has a decimal expansion that is
quiz.why: 1/8 has denominator 8 = 2³, so its decimal terminates: 1/8 = 0.125. Denominators with only factors 2 and 5 give terminating decimals.

quiz.q: 0.4̄7 (only 7 repeats, i.e. 0.4777…) in p/q form is
Which has a non-terminating recurring expansion?
quiz.why: A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal only if the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. 12 = 2² × 3 contains 3, so 5/12 = 0.41666… recurs. 20, 25 and 16 only have 2 and 5.

quiz.q: A number whose expansion is 0.12122122212222… is
quiz.why: The block of 2s keeps growing (1, 2, 3 …) so no fixed block repeats. A decimal that neither terminates nor repeats is irrational.
0.3̄ = 3/9 and 0.4̄ = 4/9, so the sum is 3/9 + 4/9 = 7/9. Adding the decimals digit by digit as 0.77 would be wrong, since the digits recur.

quiz.q: Maximum possible length of the repeating block of 1/17 is
quiz.why: When dividing by 17 the remainder can only be 1 to 16, so a remainder must repeat within 16 steps. So the block is at most 16 digits, which is less than 17.

lessons.title: Operations on real numbers and rationalising

scenes.text: Neha's answer is 1/√2 but the answer key shows √2/2.
Her teacher explains they are the same number — the key simply 'rationalised' the denominator so it is easier to compute.

steps.title: Closure facts you must know
steps.body:
- Rational ± rational, ×, ÷ (non-zero) → rational.
- Rational (non-zero) + irrational → **irrational** (e.g. 2 + √3).
- Non-zero rational × irrational → irrational (e.g. 5√2).
- Irrational ± × ÷ irrational can be **either**: √2 × √2 = 2 (rational), √2 + √3 (irrational), (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4 (rational).

steps.title: Identities for square roots (a, b > 0)
steps.body:
- √(ab) = √a·√b
- √(a/b) = √a/√b
- (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b
- (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b
- (√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b

**Rationalising**: to remove a root from a denominator multiply top and bottom by its **conjugate** (a + √b ↔ a − √b).

steps.title: Solved: rationalise 1/(√5 + √2)
steps.body: Multiply by (√5 − √2): denominator 5 − 2 = 3. Answer **(√5 − √2)/3**.

steps.title: Solved: showing √9.3 on the number line
steps.body:
Step 1: Mark AB = 9.3 units and extend BC = 1 unit, so AC = 10.3.
Step 2: Mark O, the midpoint of AC, and draw a semicircle on AC.
Step 3: Draw a perpendicular at B to meet the semicircle at D. Then **BD = √9.3**.
Why: with radius 5.15, OB = 5.15 − 1 = 4.15, BD² = 5.15² − 4.15² = (5.15 − 4.15)(5.15 + 4.15) = 1 × 9.3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing √(a + b) = √a + √b. False: √(9 + 16) = 5, but √9 + √16 = 7.
- Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate.
- Writing (√5)² = 25 (it is 5).

statements.s: The product of two irrationals is always irrational
3 + √5 is irrational

quiz.why: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Here (√5)² = 5, (√2)² = 2 and 2·√5·√2 = 2√10, so the result is 7 + 2√10.
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 2 − √3: the denominator becomes 2² − (√3)² = 4 − 3 = 1. So 1/(2 + √3) = 2 − √3.
(3 + √2)(3 − √2) = 9 − 2 = 7, which is rational. The other products still contain a root or π and stay irrational.
√12 = √(4 × 3) = √4 × √3 = 2√3. We take the perfect-square factor 4 out of the root.
1/x = 1/(2 + √3). Multiply by the conjugate (2 − √3) to get (2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 2 − √3.
The conjugate of a − b is a + b, so only the sign between the terms changes. So the conjugate of √7 − √3 is √7 + √3.

lessons.title: Laws of exponents for real numbers

scenes.text: Isha reads that 64^(1/2) = 8 and thinks it is a typo.
Her sister shows her: a power of 1/2 just means square root, so 64^(1/2) = √64 = 8.

steps.title: The laws (a, b > 0; p, q rational)
steps.body:
- aᵖ · a^q = a^(p+q)
- (aᵖ)^q = a^(pq)
- aᵖ / a^q = a^(p−q)
- aᵖ · bᵖ = (ab)ᵖ
- a⁰ = 1,  a^(−p) = 1/aᵖ
- a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a,  a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m = ⁿ√(a^m)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- aᵖ · a^q = a^(pq) ✗ — you ADD powers when multiplying.
- (−8)^(1/3) style questions: our laws assume a positive base.
- 9^(3/2) = 27, not 13.5 — take the square root first (3), then cube.

steps.title: Order of work
steps.body: For a^(m/n) take the root first, then the power: it keeps numbers small. 81^(3/4) = (⁴√81)³ = 3³ = 27.

activity.prompt: Evaluate 16^(3/4)

quiz.why: A power of 1/2 means the square root, so 64^(1/2) = √64 = 8. Do not halve 64 to get 32.
A power of 1/3 means the cube root. Since 5³ = 125, 125^(1/3) = 5.
9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27. First take the square root, then cube it.
(2^(1/2))⁴ = 2^((1/2)×4) = 2² = 4. When a power is raised to a power, multiply the exponents.
A negative exponent means the reciprocal, so 5^(−2) = 1/5² = 1/25. It does not make the number negative.

questions.q: Every rational number is
questions.why: Every rational number is a real number, as the real numbers include both rationals and irrationals. A rational need not be an integer or natural number, like 1/2.

questions.q: Which of these is irrational?
questions.why: √8 = 2√2, and √2 is irrational, so √8 is irrational. √(4/9) = 2/3, √36 = 6 and 0.5 are rational.

questions.q: Decimal expansion of 17/8 is
questions.why: 17 ÷ 8 = 2.125, which ends after three digits. Since 8 = 2³, the decimal terminates.

questions.q: Value of 81^(1/4) is
questions.why: 81^(1/4) is the fourth root of 81. Since 3⁴ = 81, the value is 3.

questions.q: 0.3̄ (0.333…) in p/q form is
questions.why: Let x = 0.333…; then 10x = 3.333…. Subtracting, 9x = 3, so x = 1/3.

questions.q: Assertion (A): √2 + 3 is irrational. Reason (R): the sum of a rational and an irrational number is irrational.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. √2 is irrational, and adding a rational number 3 to an irrational number gives an irrational number.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 1/7 has a non-terminating recurring expansion. Reason (R): 7 is a prime other than 2 and 5.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The denominator 7 has a prime factor other than 2 or 5, so 1/7 = 0.142857… recurs without ending.

questions.q: A rational number between √2 (≈1.414) and √3 (≈1.732) is
questions.why: 1.5 = 3/2 is rational and lies between 1.414 and 1.732. √2.5 ≈ 1.58 also lies between but is irrational, 1.8 is too big and 1.3 too small.

questions.q: Rationalising 6/(√5 − √3) gives
questions.why: Multiply by (√5 + √3)/(√5 + √3): the denominator becomes 5 − 3 = 2. So 6(√5 + √3)/2 = 3(√5 + √3).
When the bases are the same, add the exponents: 2/3 + 1/3 = 1. So the value is 2¹ = 2.

questions.q: Case: A carpenter's square frame has side 1 m; she adds a diagonal brace. To mark the brace length on a straight scale using compass and ruler, she should mark
options: √2 m by the right-triangle arc method
questions.why: The diagonal of a unit square is √(1² + 1²) = √2. It can be marked using a right-triangle arc construction, which cannot be done with a ruler's markings alone.

questions.q: If x = 3 + 2√2, then x + 1/x equals
If a = 5 + 2√6, then √a equals
Value of (243)^(−2/5) is
questions.why: The fifth root of 243 is 3, since 3⁵ = 243. Then 243^(−2/5) = 3^(−2) = 1/9.
Inside the brackets add the exponents: 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so it is 5^(1/2). Squaring gives 5^(1/2 × 2) = 5.

questions.q: If 1/(√2 + 1) = a√2 + b with a, b rational, then (a, b) =
questions.why: 1/(√2 + 1) = (√2 − 1)/(2 − 1) = √2 − 1. Comparing with a√2 + b gives a = 1 and b = −1.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Polynomials
courses.summary: Polynomials in one variable, degree, zeroes, the Factor Theorem, factorising quadratics and cubics, and the algebraic identities used throughout Classes 9–12.
outcomes: Identify degree, terms and coefficients of a polynomial
Find the value and zeroes of a polynomial
Use the Factor Theorem to test and find factors
Factorise quadratics by splitting the middle term and cubics by trial
Apply the identities for (x + y + z)², (x ± y)³ and x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz

scenes.text: Tanvi's garden is a square of side x m; fencing costs depend on 4x, area on x².
She writes cost = 3x² + 40x + 500 and realises this expression has a name: a polynomial.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **polynomial in one variable x** is an expression aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀ where the powers are **whole numbers** (0, 1, 2, …) and the a's are real constants (coefficients).

- 2x³ − 5x + 7 ✔
- √2·x² + 1 ✔ (a coefficient can be irrational)
- x + 1/x ✗ (it has x⁻¹)
- √x + 3 ✗ (power 1/2)

steps.title: Terms, degree and names
steps.body:
- **Degree**: highest power with a non-zero coefficient. 5x⁴ − x + 2 has degree 4.
- By terms: **monomial** (1 term), **binomial** (2), **trinomial** (3).
- By degree: **constant** (degree 0, e.g. 7), **linear** (1, ax + b), **quadratic** (2, ax² + bx + c), **cubic** (3).
- The **zero polynomial** 0 has no defined degree.

steps.title: Solved: degree and type
steps.body:
p(x) = 4 − y²? Careful: variable y, degree 2, quadratic binomial.
q(x) = 5x³ − 4x² + x − √2: degree 3, cubic, 4 terms.
r(t) = 12: constant polynomial, degree 0.

steps.title: Solved: coefficients
steps.body:
In 2 + x² + x, coefficient of x² is 1 and of x is 1; constant term 2.
In (π/2)x² + x, coefficient of x² is π/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling x² + 1/x a polynomial.
- Giving the degree of the zero polynomial as 0 (it is not defined; 0 is the degree of a non-zero constant).
- Reading degree from the first term when terms are not in order: degree of 3 + x⁵ − x² is 5.

activity.prompt: Polynomial or not?

quiz.why: Degree is the highest power of the variable. In 5t − √7, the highest power of t is 1, so the degree is 1.
A polynomial has only whole-number powers of the variable. x² − √3x has powers 2 and 1, and √3 is just a coefficient. The others have powers −1, −2 or 1/2.
A cubic polynomial has degree 3, the highest power being x³. Linear is 1, quadratic 2 and biquadratic 4.
x¹⁰¹ − 1 has two terms, so it is a binomial. Its degree is 101, but that doesn't change the number of terms.

quiz.q: The degree of the zero polynomial is
quiz.why: The zero polynomial has no term with a non-zero coefficient, so no highest power exists. Its degree is not defined.

lessons.title: Value and zeroes of a polynomial

scenes.text: A stall's profit is p(x) = x² − 5x + 6 (x in hundreds of cups).
The owner asks: for what x is the profit exactly zero? Those x are the zeroes of p.

steps.title: Value and zero
steps.body:
The **value** of p(x) at x = c is p(c), found by substitution.
If p(c) = 0, c is a **zero** of p(x) (also called a *root* of the equation p(x) = 0).

- A non-zero constant polynomial has **no** zero.
- Every real number is a zero of the zero polynomial.
- A linear polynomial ax + b (a ≠ 0) has exactly one zero: **x = −b/a**.
- A polynomial can have more than one zero; a degree-n polynomial has at most n zeroes.

steps.title: Solved: check zeroes
steps.body:
Is 0 a zero of x² − 2x? p(0) = 0 ✔. Is 2? p(2) = 4 − 4 = 0 ✔. So both 0 and 2 are zeroes.
Find the zero of 2x + 1: 2x + 1 = 0 ⇒ **x = −1/2**.

steps.title: Solved: zeroes of p(x) = (x − 2)(x + 3)
steps.body: p(x) = 0 when x − 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0 ⇒ zeroes **2 and −3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Substituting without brackets: p(−2) for x² gives (−2)² = 4, not −4.
- Saying 'zero of a polynomial' means p(0) — it means the input that makes the output 0.
- Forgetting the zero of cx (c ≠ 0) is 0.

activity.prompt: Find p(−1) for p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 4x + 5

quiz.why: A zero makes the polynomial zero. 3x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2/3.

quiz.q: Value of p(x) = x² − 3x + 2 at x = 2 is
quiz.why: Put x = 2: 2² − 3(2) + 2 = 4 − 6 + 2 = 0. So the value is 0, which also means 2 is a zero.

quiz.q: If x = 1 is a zero of x² + kx − 3, k =
quiz.why: Put x = 1 in x² + kx − 3 = 0: 1 + k − 3 = 0, so k = 2.
x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so the zeroes are 3 and −3. Both values make the polynomial zero.

quiz.q: A linear polynomial has how many zeroes?
quiz.why: A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, x = −b/a. So it has one zero.

quiz.q: The zero of p(x) = cx (c ≠ 0) is
quiz.why: cx = 0 with c ≠ 0 gives x = 0. So the zero of cx is 0.

scenes.text: A box has volume x² + 7x + 12 cm³ (base area times height).
Divya wonders: can this split into two neat lengths? Factorising answers it: (x + 3)(x + 4).

steps.title: Factor Theorem
steps.body:
If p(x) has degree ≥ 1 and a is a real number:
- if **p(a) = 0**, then **(x − a)** is a factor of p(x);
- if (x − a) is a factor, then p(a) = 0.

Test a factor (x + k) by checking p(−k) = 0. (Related idea: dividing p(x) by x − a leaves remainder p(a) — the Remainder Theorem.)

steps.title: Solved: find k
steps.body: x − 1 is a factor of 4x³ + 3x² − 4x + k. p(1) = 4 + 3 − 4 + k = 0 ⇒ **k = −3**.

steps.title: Splitting the middle term
steps.body: For ax² + bx + c find two numbers p, q with **p + q = b** and **pq = ac**, then group.

steps.title: Solved: 6x² + 17x + 5
steps.body:
ac = 30; numbers adding to 17 with product 30: 2 and 15.
6x² + 2x + 15x + 5 = 2x(3x + 1) + 5(3x + 1) = **(3x + 1)(2x + 5)**.

steps.title: Solved: y² − 5y + 6 using the Factor Theorem
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using p(1) to test (x + 1) — use p(−1).
- Choosing numbers with product c instead of ac when a ≠ 1.
- Sign errors when grouping: −3x − 6 = −3(x + 2), not −3(x − 2).

activity.prompt: Match each quadratic with its factors

quiz.q: x − 2 is a factor of p(x) if
quiz.why: By the Factor Theorem, x − a is a factor of p(x) if p(a) = 0. For x − 2, we need p(2) = 0.
We need two numbers with sum 9 and product 18. They are 3 and 6, so x² + 9x + 18 = (x + 3)(x + 6).

quiz.q: For 2x² + 7x + 3, the middle term splits as
quiz.why: Multiply a and c: 2 × 3 = 6, and we need two numbers with sum 7 and product 6. They are 6 and 1, so 7x = 6x + x.

quiz.q: If x + 1 is a factor of x² + kx + 1, k =

quiz.why: ac = 6 × (−6) = −36, and we need numbers with sum 5 and product −36: 9 and −4. So 6x² + 9x − 4x − 6 = 3x(2x + 3) − 2(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)(3x − 2).

quiz.q: Remainder when x³ + 1 is divided by x + 1 is
quiz.why: By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder on dividing by x + 1 is p(−1) = (−1)³ + 1 = 0. So x + 1 divides x³ + 1 exactly.

scenes.text: A carton's volume is x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120.
Vikram wants its three dimensions. Trial with the Factor Theorem, then splitting, gives (x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12).

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Step 1: List factors of the constant term (±1, ±2, …).
Step 2: Test them until p(a) = 0; then (x − a) is a factor.
Step 3: Divide (or compare coefficients) to get a quadratic.
Step 4: Factorise the quadratic by splitting the middle term.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing only positive values: if all coefficients are positive no positive number can be a zero.
- Errors in long division — check by expanding back.
- Stopping after one factor: the question wants complete factorisation.

steps.title: Quick checks
steps.body: Sum of all coefficients = 0 ⇒ x = 1 is a zero. Sum of coefficients of even powers = sum of odd powers ⇒ x = −1 is a zero.

quiz.q: Which is a factor of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6?
quiz.why: Check p(2) = 8 − 24 + 22 − 6 = 0, so x − 2 is a factor. The others do not give 0.

quiz.q: Sum of coefficients of 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 4 is 0, so a factor is
quiz.why: The coefficients add to 2 − 3 − 3 + 4 = 0, which means p(1) = 0. So x − 1 is a factor.

quiz.q: For x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6, which value can be a zero?
quiz.why: All the coefficients are positive, so a positive value cannot make the polynomial zero. Checking p(−1) = −1 + 6 − 11 + 6 = 0, so −1 is a zero.
p(−1) = −1 − 3 + 9 − 5 = 0, so x + 1 is a factor. Dividing gives x² − 4x − 5 = (x − 5)(x + 1), so the product is (x + 1)²(x − 5).

scenes.text: At a school fair Zoya computes 104³ in her head in seconds.
Her secret: (a + b)³ with a = 100 and b = 4. Identities turn hard arithmetic into easy steps.

steps.title: The identities
steps.body:
1. (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y²
2. (x − y)² = x² − 2xy + y²
3. x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y)
4. (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab
5. (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx
6. (x + y)³ = x³ + y³ + 3xy(x + y)
7. (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ − 3xy(x − y)
8. x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx)
Special cases: x³ + y³ = (x + y)(x² − xy + y²), x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²).

steps.title: Solved: factorise 4x² + 9y² + 16z² + 12xy − 24yz − 16xz
steps.body:
Look for squares: (2x)², (3y)², (−4z)². Check cross terms: 2(2x)(3y) = 12xy, 2(3y)(−4z) = −24yz, 2(2x)(−4z) = −16xz ✔.
**= (2x + 3y − 4z)²**.

Solved: factorise 27x³ + y³ + z³ − 9xyz
steps.body: = (3x)³ + y³ + z³ − 3(3x)(y)(z) = **(3x + y + z)(9x² + y² + z² − 3xy − yz − 3xz)**.

steps.body:
- (a + b)² = a² + b² ✗ (missing 2ab).
- (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ ✗.
- Sign of cross terms in (x + y + z)² when some terms are negative: write each term with its sign, e.g. (−2x + 3y + 2z)² gives −12xy, +12yz, −8zx.

We need two numbers with sum −7 and product 12. They are −3 and −4, so x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4).

options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. p(x) = x³ − 1 gives p(1) = 0, so by the Factor Theorem, x − 1 is a factor.

options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: x + 1/x contains 1/x = x⁻¹, a negative power, so it is not a polynomial. The reason is true: powers must be whole numbers.

questions.why: Use (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² with a = 2x and b = 3y: 4x² − 12xy + 9y².

questions.why: Square x − 1/x = 4: x² − 2 + 1/x² = 16, so x² + 1/x² = 18.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Coordinate Geometry
courses.summary: The Cartesian plane: axes, origin, quadrants, coordinates of a point, plotting points and reading figures from coordinates.
outcomes: Describe a point's position using an ordered pair (x, y)
Name the axes, origin and four quadrants and the sign pattern in each
Plot points and read coordinates from a graph
Use coordinates to find lengths and areas of axis-parallel figures

scenes.text: Ms Rao says 'Sit at the desk in row 3.' Five students in row 3 stand up!
She corrects: 'Row 3, seat 2.' Two numbers fixed one exact place — the core idea of coordinates.

steps.title: Locating a point in a plane
steps.body: On a line one number fixes a point. In a plane we need **two** reference lines and two distances. French philosopher-mathematician **René Descartes** (1596–1650) developed this idea, so it is called the **Cartesian system**.

steps.title: Axes and origin
steps.body:
- A horizontal number line **XʹX** = the **x-axis**; a vertical one **YʹY** = the **y-axis**.
- They meet at right angles at the **origin O**.
- Right of O and above O are positive; left and below are negative.
- The axes divide the plane into four **quadrants** I, II, III, IV, numbered anticlockwise from the top-right.

steps.title: Coordinates
steps.body:
A point P is written **(x, y)**:
- **x-coordinate (abscissa)** = perpendicular distance from the **y-axis**, measured along the x-axis (with sign).
- **y-coordinate (ordinate)** = perpendicular distance from the **x-axis** (with sign).
Origin = (0, 0).

steps.title: Solved: reading a point
steps.body: P is 4 units right of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis ⇒ x = 4, y = −3 ⇒ **P(4, −3)**, which lies in quadrant IV.

steps.title: Solved: distance from the axes
steps.body: Point (−5, 2): distance from the y-axis = |−5| = 5 units; distance from the x-axis = |2| = 2 units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the meaning: the abscissa is the distance from the **y-axis**, not the x-axis.
- Numbering quadrants clockwise.
- Forgetting that distance is never negative even when the coordinate is.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning

quiz.q: The point where the axes meet is the
quiz.why: The point where the x-axis and y-axis meet is the origin, O(0, 0). The ordinate and abscissa are coordinates.
The abscissa is the first coordinate, the x-value. For (−3, 7) it is −3.
The y-axis is the vertical line, and the x-axis is horizontal. It is straight, not curved.

quiz.q: Distance of (6, −8) from the x-axis is
quiz.why: The distance of a point from the x-axis is the absolute value of its y-coordinate. For (6, −8) it is |−8| = 8.

quiz.q: The Cartesian system is named after
quiz.why: The Cartesian system is named after René Descartes, the French mathematician. Euclid and Pythagoras are known for other work.

lessons.title: Quadrants, signs and points on the axes

scenes.text: A treasure map says: 'Dig at (−2, −3).' Aman walks 2 steps left and 3 steps down from the big tree.
His friend went right and up — and dug in the wrong quadrant!

steps.title: Sign pattern
steps.body:
- Quadrant I: (+, +)
- Quadrant II: (−, +)
- Quadrant III: (−, −)
- Quadrant IV: (+, −)

steps.title: Points on the axes
steps.body: A point on the **x-axis** has y = 0: (a, 0). A point on the **y-axis** has x = 0: (0, b). Points on the axes belong to **no quadrant**.

steps.title: Solved: name the quadrant
steps.body: (−4, 5) → II; (3, −1) → IV; (−2, −2) → III; (0, −6) → on the y-axis (no quadrant); (7, 0) → on the x-axis.

steps.title: Solved: (x, y) ≠ (y, x)
steps.body: (2, 5) is 2 right and 5 up; (5, 2) is 5 right and 2 up — different points. They are equal only if x = y, e.g. (3, 3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying (0, 5) is in quadrant I. It is on the positive y-axis.
- Assuming (a, b) and (b, a) are the same point.
- Mixing up 'left of the y-axis' (x < 0) with 'below the x-axis' (y < 0).

activity.prompt: Where does each point lie?

quiz.why: (−5, −1) has both coordinates negative, so it lies in the third quadrant, III.

quiz.q: A point on the x-axis has
quiz.why: A point on the x-axis is at distance 0 from it, so its y-coordinate is 0. So y = 0.
The origin (0, 0) lies on both the x-axis and the y-axis. It is not in any quadrant.

quiz.q: A point with abscissa positive and ordinate negative is in
quiz.why: A positive abscissa and negative ordinate means (+, −), which is the fourth quadrant, IV.
The order of coordinates matters, so (3, −2) and (−2, 3) are different points. They lie in different quadrants (IV and II).

quiz.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
quiz.why: A point on the y-axis has x = 0. So (0, −9) is on the y-axis.

scenes.text: Sara draws a rangoli on squared paper and labels its corners (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4), (1, 4).
Her mother asks how big it is. Coordinates give the answer without a ruler: 4 by 3, so 12 squares.

steps.title: How to plot (a, b)
steps.body:
Step 1: From O move a units along the x-axis (right if a > 0, left if a < 0).
Step 2: From there move b units parallel to the y-axis (up if b > 0, down if b < 0).
Step 3: Mark the point and label it.

steps.title: Solved: length of an axis-parallel segment
steps.body:
A(−2, 3), B(5, 3) have the same y, so AB is horizontal. Length = 5 − (−2) = **7 units**.
C(4, −1), D(4, 6): same x, vertical, length = 6 − (−1) = **7 units**.

steps.title: Solved: rectangle from coordinates
steps.body: Vertices P(1, 1), Q(5, 1), R(5, 4), S(1, 4). PQ = 5 − 1 = 4, QR = 4 − 1 = 3. Area = 4 × 3 = **12 square units**, perimeter = 2(4 + 3) = **14 units**.

steps.title: Solved: fourth vertex of a square
steps.body: Three vertices of a square: (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 3). The fourth must be **(0, 3)** — same x as (0, 0), same y as (3, 3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plotting y first.
- Counting grid lines instead of gaps when finding lengths.
- Using the 'difference of coordinates' rule for slanted segments — it only works for horizontal/vertical ones (slanted lengths use Pythagoras or the distance formula of Class 10).

steps.title: Coordinates everywhere
steps.body: GPS locations (latitude, longitude), seats in a cinema (row, number), cells in a spreadsheet (B7) and pixels on a phone screen all use the same two-number idea.

activity.prompt: Area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4) in square units

quiz.q: Length of the segment joining (2, −3) and (2, 5)
quiz.why: The points have the same x, so the segment is vertical. Its length is the difference of the y-values: 5 − (−3) = 8.
x = −3 means 3 units to the left, and y = 4 means 4 units up. So go 3 left, then 4 up.
The length is 4 and the breadth is 2, so the area is 4 × 2 = 8.

quiz.q: Mid-way point between (0, 0) and (6, 0) on the x-axis is
quiz.why: The midpoint of the segment from (0, 0) to (6, 0) is at half the distance along the x-axis, i.e. (3, 0). The y-coordinate stays 0.

quiz.q: Perimeter of a square with vertices (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4), (1, 4)
quiz.why: The side of the square is 4 − 1 = 3, so the perimeter is 4 × 3 = 12.

scenes.text: A drone starts at the depot (0, 0), flies to (4, 0), then to (4, −3).
The controller asks: in which quadrant is the parcel and how far did it fly? Coordinates answer both.

steps.title: Key results to remember
steps.body:
- Point on x-axis: (x, 0); on y-axis: (0, y).
- Mirror image of (x, y) in the x-axis: (x, −y); in the y-axis: (−x, y); in the origin: (−x, −y).
- Horizontal distance = difference of x's; vertical distance = difference of y's.

steps.title: Solved: reflections
steps.body: Reflect A(3, −5) in the x-axis → (3, 5) [quadrant I]; in the y-axis → (−3, −5) [quadrant III].

steps.title: Solved: drone path
steps.body: (0, 0) → (4, 0): 4 units. (4, 0) → (4, −3): 3 units. Total **7 units**; parcel at (4, −3) is in **quadrant IV**. (Straight-line distance from depot would be 5 units by Pythagoras, 3-4-5.)

steps.title: Solved: unknown coordinate
steps.body: If (a − 2, 5) lies on the y-axis, then a − 2 = 0 ⇒ **a = 2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing both signs when reflecting in only one axis.
- Writing 'quadrant 0' for points on axes.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Draw a quick sketch for every coordinate question — even a rough one prevents sign errors.

quiz.q: Mirror image of (−2, 6) in the x-axis
quiz.why: The reflection in the x-axis keeps x and changes the sign of y. So (−2, 6) becomes (−2, −6).

quiz.q: If (3, b + 1) lies on the x-axis then b =
quiz.why: A point on the x-axis has y = 0, so b + 1 = 0 and b = −1.

quiz.q: A point 5 units left of the y-axis on the x-axis is
quiz.why: The point is on the x-axis, so y = 0, and 5 units to the left means x = −5. So it is (−5, 0).
The image in the origin changes the signs of both coordinates. So (4, −1) becomes (−4, 1).

quiz.q: Which pair lies on a line parallel to the x-axis?
quiz.why: A line parallel to the x-axis has the same y-coordinate (ordinate) for all points. (3, 4) and (−2, 4) both have y = 4.

questions.q: The x-coordinate is also called the
questions.why: The x-coordinate is called the abscissa. The y-coordinate is the ordinate.

questions.q: Coordinates of the origin are
questions.why: The origin is where both axes cross, with coordinates (0, 0).

questions.q: (−2, −7) lies in quadrant
questions.why: (−2, −7) has both coordinates negative, so it lies in quadrant III.

questions.q: A point on the y-axis at distance 4 below the origin is
questions.why: A point on the y-axis has x = 0, and 4 units below the origin means y = −4. So it is (0, −4).

questions.q: Signs of coordinates in quadrant II are
questions.why: In the second quadrant, x is negative and y is positive, so the signs are (−, +).

questions.q: Distance of (−6, 8) from the y-axis
questions.why: The distance from the y-axis is |x|, the absolute value of the x-coordinate. For (−6, 8) it is 6.

questions.q: Assertion (A): (0, −3) lies in quadrant IV. Reason (R): its ordinate is negative.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: (0, −3) has x = 0, so it lies on the y-axis and in no quadrant. The reason is true, its ordinate is negative, but that does not put it in quadrant IV.

questions.q: Length of segment joining (−3, 2) and (5, 2)
questions.why: The points share the y-value 2, so the segment is horizontal. Its length is 5 − (−3) = 8.

questions.q: If (2a − 4, 7) lies on the y-axis, a =
questions.why: On the y-axis, the x-coordinate is 0. So 2a − 4 = 0 and a = 2.

questions.q: Area of rectangle with vertices (−1, −1), (3, −1), (3, 2), (−1, 2)
questions.why: The length is 3 − (−1) = 4 and the breadth is 2 − (−1) = 3. So the area is 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.q: Reflection of (−3, −8) in the y-axis lies in quadrant
questions.why: The reflection in the y-axis changes the sign of x: (−3, −8) becomes (3, −8), which has (+, −) and lies in quadrant IV.

questions.q: Case: In a park map, the gate is at (0, 0), a fountain at (6, 0) and a bench at (6, 8). The straight path from gate to bench is
questions.why: The gate (0, 0), fountain (6, 0) and bench (6, 8) form a right triangle with legs 6 and 8. The path is √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 units.

questions.q: Three vertices of a rectangle are (2, 1), (7, 1), (7, 4). The fourth vertex and area are
questions.why: The sides are 7 − 2 = 5 and 4 − 1 = 3. The fourth vertex is (2, 4) and the area is 5 × 3 = 15.

questions.q: Points (a, b) with a·b < 0 lie in quadrants
questions.why: a × b < 0 means the signs are opposite. That happens in quadrant II (−, +) and quadrant IV (+, −).

questions.q: Area of triangle with vertices (0, 0), (8, 0), (3, 5)
questions.why: The base on the x-axis is 8 and the height (the y-coordinate of the apex) is 5. Area = ½ × 8 × 5 = 20.

questions.q: The figure with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (6, 3), (2, 3) is a parallelogram. Its area is
questions.why: A parallelogram's area is base × height. The base on the x-axis is 4 and the height is 3, so the area is 12.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Linear Equations in Two Variables
courses.summary: Writing situations as ax + by + c = 0, finding solutions, checking ordered pairs and (as an extension) drawing the straight-line graph.
outcomes: Write a linear equation in two variables in standard form and identify a, b, c
Express one-variable equations like x = 3 as two-variable equations
Find several solutions and check whether a pair is a solution
Translate word problems into linear equations
Draw and read the graph of a linear equation (extension)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; graph sections may be trimmed in rationalised editions

scenes.text: Rohan buys some pencils at ₹5 and some erasers at ₹3 and pays ₹40.
He writes 5x + 3y = 40 — one equation, two unknowns. How many possibilities are there?

steps.title: Definition and standard form
steps.body: An equation that can be written as **ax + by + c = 0**, where a, b, c are real numbers and **a and b are not both zero**, is a linear equation in two variables x and y. 'Linear' because each variable has power 1 (its graph is a straight line).

steps.title: Solved: one-variable equations in two-variable form
Solved: write as an equation
steps.body: 'The cost of a notebook is twice the cost of a pen.' Let notebook = ₹x, pen = ₹y: x = 2y ⇒ **x − 2y = 0**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to move every term to one side before reading c (sign of c changes).
- Calling xy + x = 3 linear — the term xy has degree 2.
- Thinking b = 0 is not allowed: a or b may be zero, just not both.

activity.prompt: Match each equation with (a, b, c) in ax + by + c = 0

quiz.q: Which is a linear equation in two variables?
quiz.why: 3x − 2y = 7 has both variables to the power 1, so it is linear. Terms like xy, x² or 1/y make an equation non-linear.

quiz.q: In 2x − 5y = 10 written as ax + by + c = 0, c =
quiz.why: Move 10 to the left side: 2x − 5y − 10 = 0. So c = −10.

quiz.q: y = 3 written in two variables is
quiz.why: y = 3 can be written as 0·x + 1·y − 3 = 0, with a = 0 and b = 1. It is a linear equation in two variables.
The sum of two numbers x and y is x + y, so the equation is x + y = 27. The difference or product would give other equations.

quiz.q: In ax + by + c = 0 the condition is
options: a and b not both zero
quiz.why: In ax + by + c = 0, a and b must not both be zero. Otherwise there would be no variables in the equation.

scenes.text: Pens cost ₹10 and notebooks ₹20; Meena spends exactly ₹100.
(10, 0), (6, 2), (2, 4), (0, 5)… She finds many correct baskets — every one is a solution.

steps.title: What a solution is
steps.body: A **solution** is a pair (x, y) that makes both sides equal. A linear equation in two variables has **infinitely many** solutions (each one a point on its straight line). To find solutions: choose any x, solve for y.

steps.title: Solved: find k
steps.body: If x = 2, y = 1 is a solution of 2x + 3y = k, then k = 4 + 3 = **7**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing only one solution when 'infinitely many' is the correct description.
- Substituting x and y the wrong way round: (a, b) always means x = a, y = b.
- Arithmetic with fractions — choose x values that make y a whole number.

activity.prompt: Find y if (3, y) is a solution of 2x + 3y = 18

quiz.why: A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions, as each value of x gives a value of y. So 2x + 5y = 10 has infinitely many.

quiz.q: Which is a solution of x + y = 5?
quiz.why: For (3, 2), 3 + 2 = 5, so it satisfies x + y = 5. The other pairs do not add up to 5.
For (1, 3), y = 3 = 3 × 1, so it satisfies y = 3x. The others do not give y = 3x.
Put x = 0 in 2x + y = 7: y = 7.
Put (2, 0): 2 − 2(0) = 2, which is not 4. So (2, 0) is not a solution.

scenes.text: An auto charges ₹15 for the first km and ₹8 for each further km.
Asha writes y = 15 + 8(x − 1) — a linear equation that turns a fare card into maths.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Name the unknowns (x = …, y = …) with units.
2. Translate each phrase: 'twice' → 2×, 'more than' → +, 'is' → =.
3. Simplify to ax + by + c = 0.
4. Find solutions that make sense (often only whole, non-negative values).

steps.title: Solved: taxi fare
steps.body:
Fare: ₹8 for first km and ₹5 per km after. Distance x km, fare ₹y.
y = 8 + 5(x − 1) ⇒ y = 5x + 3 ⇒ **5x − y + 3 = 0**. For 10 km: y = 53.

steps.title: Solved: donations
steps.body: Two students together contribute ₹100 to a relief fund. x + y = 100. Solutions include (50, 50), (60, 40), (100, 0) — many.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging the first km twice in fare problems (use x − 1 for 'each further km').
- Ignoring units or meaning (negative pencils!).

activity.text: 'The cost of a notebook (x) is ₹4 more than twice a pen (y)': x = ___y + ___

quiz.q: 'Ravi's age (x) is 3 years more than Sita's (y)'
quiz.why: Ravi is 3 years older than Sita, so Ravi's age equals Sita's age plus 3: x = y + 3.

quiz.why: The perimeter of a rectangle is 2(length + breadth), so 2x + 2y = 40.

steps.title: Graphing
steps.body:
Make a table of 2–3 solutions, plot them, join with a ruler and extend. The graph of ax + by + c = 0 is always a **straight line**.
- x = a is a line parallel to the y-axis; y = b is parallel to the x-axis.
- y = mx passes through the origin.

steps.body: In recent rationalised NCERT books the graph sections of this chapter may be trimmed; the skill is still essential for Class 10 'Pair of Linear Equations'.

steps.body: x = 0 → y = 6; x = 3 → y = 0; x = 1 → y = 4. Plot (0, 6), (3, 0), (1, 4); join. It cuts the y-axis at (0, 6) and the x-axis at (3, 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Thinking x = 3 is a point — on the plane it is a vertical line.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Introduction to Euclid's Geometry
courses.summary: Where geometry came from, Euclid's definitions, axioms and five postulates, the parallel postulate, and how to prove simple statements from axioms.
outcomes: Trace the history of geometry from Egypt, the Indus Valley and the Sulbasutras to Euclid
Distinguish defined terms, undefined terms, axioms, postulates and theorems
State Euclid's axioms and five postulates
Use axioms to justify simple geometric statements

scenes.text: Every year the Nile flooded and washed away farm boundaries in ancient Egypt.
Surveyors re-measured the land with ropes — 'geo' (earth) + 'metrein' (to measure) = geometry.

steps.title: Early geometry
steps.body:
- **Egypt**: practical rules for areas of fields and volumes of granaries (some only approximate).
- **Indus Valley (Harappa, c. 3000 BCE)**: well-planned towns with parallel streets, and burnt bricks in dimension ratio **length : breadth : thickness = 4 : 2 : 1**.
- **Sulbasutras (c. 800–500 BCE)**: manuals for building fire altars (vedis); squares, circles, rectangles of equal area, Sriyantra with nested triangles.
- **Babylon**: geometry for land and calculation.

steps.title: The Greeks and Euclid
steps.body: **Thales** is credited with the first known proof (that a diameter bisects a circle). **Pythagoras** and his students studied many properties. Around **300 BCE**, **Euclid** of Alexandria collected known results into the **Elements**, in **13 books**, building everything from a few definitions and assumptions. This 'axiomatic method' is still how mathematics is written.

steps.title: Solved: why the brick ratio matters
steps.body: A 4 : 2 : 1 brick (say 24 cm × 12 cm × 6 cm) can be laid lengthwise or crosswise and the layers still line up: two breadths = one length, two thicknesses = one breadth. That makes strong interlocking walls.

steps.title: Solved: identify the source
steps.body: 'Rules to build altars of equal area but different shapes' → Sulbasutras. 'First known proof that a diameter bisects a circle' → Thales. 'Elements in 13 books' → Euclid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Euclid invented all of geometry — he organised and proved results, many known before him.
- Mixing up Thales (proof) and Pythagoras (his school).

activity.prompt: Put these in time order

events.text: Thales gives an early geometric proof

quiz.q: The word geometry comes from words meaning
quiz.why: The word geometry comes from Greek words geo (earth) and metrein (to measure), meaning earth measure. It began with land measurement.
Euclid's Elements is a collection of 13 books. It sets out geometry in a logical order.
The Harappan bricks had the ratio length : width : thickness = 4 : 2 : 1. This shows their early geometry.
The Sulbasutras were manuals with rules for building altars for fire rituals. They contain geometric constructions.
Euclid worked in Alexandria, in Egypt, where he taught mathematics. He was not from Athens or Rome.

scenes.text: Before playing chess, Ishaan and Tara agree on the rules — no proof needed, everyone accepts them.
Euclid did the same for geometry: a few accepted starting truths, then everything else proved.

steps.title: Definitions and undefined terms
steps.body:
Euclid began with 23 definitions, e.g.
- A **point** is that which has no part.
- A **line** is breadthless length.
- The ends of a line are points.
- A **straight line** lies evenly with the points on itself.
- A **surface** has length and breadth only.
These 'define' words with other undefined words, so today **point, line and plane** are treated as **undefined terms**.

steps.title: Axioms (common notions) — used throughout mathematics
steps.body:
1. Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
2. If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
3. If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
4. Things which coincide with one another are equal.
5. The whole is greater than the part.
6. Things which are double of the same things are equal.
7. Things which are halves of the same things are equal.

steps.title: Postulates — specific to geometry
steps.body:
1. A straight line may be drawn from any point to any other point.
2. A terminated line can be produced indefinitely.
3. A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.
4. All right angles are equal to one another.
5. If a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side together **less than two right angles**, the two lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side.

Today 'axiom' and 'postulate' are used for the same idea: a statement accepted without proof. A **theorem** (proposition) is a statement proved from them.

steps.title: Solved: which axiom?
steps.body:
If x + y = 10 and x = z, then z + y = 10. Things equal to the same thing (x = z, substitution) → **Axiom 1**.
AB = CD ⇒ AB + BC = CD + BC → **Axiom 2**.

steps.title: Solved: is the 'whole > part' axiom used?
steps.body: If AB is a line segment and C lies between A and B, then AB > AC — **Axiom 5**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a postulate a theorem.
- Thinking axioms must be 'obvious in the diagram' — they are logical starting points, not measurements.

activity.prompt: Match the statement to its type
pairs: Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
The whole is greater than the part
A circle can be drawn with any centre and radius
A point is that which has no part
Two distinct lines meet in at most one point

quiz.why: Euclid's axioms are assumptions used throughout mathematics, not just geometry. They are accepted without proof.

quiz.q: 'If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal' is axiom
quiz.why: 'If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal' is Euclid's Axiom 3. Axiom 2 is about adding equals.

quiz.q: Which is an undefined term today?
quiz.why: A point is one of the undefined terms in geometry today. Triangle, angle and circle are defined using it.
A theorem is a statement that has been proved using axioms and earlier results. It is not accepted without proof.

quiz.q: Postulate 2 says a terminated line can be
quiz.why: Euclid's Postulate 2 says that a terminated line can be produced indefinitely. This is how a line segment extends.

lessons.title: The fifth postulate and parallel lines

scenes.text: Two railway rails stretch to the horizon without ever meeting.
Mathematicians spent 2000 years asking whether this 'never meeting' could be proved from Euclid's other postulates.

steps.title: Playfair's axiom (an equivalent version)
steps.body: For every line l and every point P not on l, there is **exactly one** line through P parallel to l. (Equivalent: two distinct intersecting lines cannot both be parallel to the same line.)

steps.title: Why it was special
steps.body: The fifth postulate is longer and less 'self-evident' than the others. Attempts to prove it from postulates 1–4 failed. In the 19th century this led to **non-Euclidean geometries** (on a sphere, for example, 'straight lines' are great circles and all of them meet).

steps.title: Solved: does postulate 5 imply parallel lines exist?
steps.body: Yes. If a line meets two lines so that the interior angles on the same side add to exactly two right angles (180°), postulate 5 says they do not meet on either side — so they are parallel.

steps.title: Solved: Theorem — two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common
steps.body: Suppose lines l and m share two points P and Q. Then two lines pass through P and Q. But only **one** line passes through two distinct points (Euclid's axiom: given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them). Contradiction ⇒ they share at most one point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying lines are parallel because 'they look parallel' in the figure.
- Forgetting that the fifth postulate talks about angles summing to *less than* two right angles.

statements.s: Through a point not on a line, exactly one parallel can be drawn (Euclidean plane)
Two distinct lines can meet at two points
Postulate 5 was easily proved from the others
statements.why: It cannot be; it is independent.

statements.s: Two distinct intersecting lines can both be parallel to a third line

quiz.q: Playfair's axiom is equivalent to Euclid's postulate
quiz.why: Playfair's axiom, that through a point outside a line exactly one parallel can be drawn, is equivalent to Euclid's fifth postulate.

quiz.q: Two distinct lines in a plane meet in
quiz.why: Two distinct lines cannot meet in two points, so they meet in at most one point. They may not meet at all, if parallel.

quiz.q: Interior angles on one side sum to 180°. The lines are
quiz.why: If interior angles on one side of a transversal add up to 180°, the lines are parallel. They will not meet on that side.

quiz.q: Geometry where Euclid's 5th postulate fails is called
quiz.why: A geometry in which Euclid's fifth postulate does not hold is called non-Euclidean. Examples are geometry on a sphere.

quiz.q: Through two distinct points, the number of lines is
quiz.why: Through two distinct points there is exactly one line. This is Euclid's first postulate.

scenes.text: In a debate, Anu says: 'If AB = BC and BC = CD, then AB = CD.' Her opponent asks: 'Prove it.'
She cites Euclid's first axiom — and wins the point. Every step needs a reason.

steps.title: Solved: if AC = BD then AB = CD
steps.body:
Points A, B, C, D lie on a line in that order, and AC = BD.
AC = AB + BC and BD = BC + CD (point between).
So AB + BC = BC + CD.
Subtract BC from both sides (**Axiom 3**): **AB = CD**.

steps.title: Solved: Euclid's Proposition 1 — equilateral triangle on a segment
steps.body:
Given AB. Step 1: Circle with centre A, radius AB (Postulate 3). Step 2: Circle with centre B, radius BA. Step 3: Let C be where they meet; join CA, CB (Postulate 1).
AB = AC (radii of first circle), AB = BC (radii of second).
Things equal to the same thing are equal (Axiom 1) ⇒ AB = BC = AC: **ABC is equilateral**. (Euclid quietly assumed the circles meet — a gap noticed later.)

steps.title: Solved: every segment has exactly one midpoint
steps.body: Suppose C and D are both midpoints of AB. Then AC = CB and AD = DB, so AC = ½AB = AD. Things halves of the same thing are equal (Axiom 7) and coincide ⇒ C = D. So the midpoint is unique.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing steps without reasons.
- Using a result you are trying to prove (circular reasoning).

steps.title: Proof layout
steps.body: Given → To prove → Construction (if any) → Proof as numbered statements, each with its reason (axiom, postulate, definition or earlier theorem).

activity.prompt: Order the proof that AB = CD when AC = BD (A, B, C, D in order)

quiz.q: In proving AB = CD from AB + BC = BC + CD, we use axiom
quiz.why: From AB + BC = BC + CD, subtracting the same BC from both sides gives AB = CD. This uses Axiom 3, that equals subtracted from equals are equal.

quiz.q: Proposition 1 uses which postulate to draw circles?
quiz.why: Postulate 3 allows us to draw a circle with any centre and radius. Proposition 1 uses this to draw two circles.

quiz.q: If x = y and y = 7, x = 7 uses axiom
quiz.why: If x = y and y = 7, then x = 7, because things equal to the same thing are equal. This is Axiom 1.

quiz.q: A segment has how many midpoints?
quiz.why: A segment has exactly one midpoint, the point that divides it into two equal parts. This follows from the axiom that halves of equals are equal.

quiz.q: Each statement in a proof needs
quiz.why: Each statement in a proof needs a reason, such as an axiom, definition or earlier theorem. This makes the argument sound.

questions.q: Euclid compiled the Elements around
questions.why: Euclid compiled the Elements around 300 BCE, in Alexandria. It is one of the oldest textbooks.

questions.q: Statements accepted without proof are
questions.why: Statements accepted without proof are axioms and postulates. Theorems and lemmas are proved.

questions.q: Today 'point' is treated as
questions.why: Today a point is treated as an undefined term. We describe it but don't define it.

questions.q: 'The whole is greater than the part' is axiom
questions.why: 'The whole is greater than the part' is Euclid's Axiom 5. Axiom 1 is about things equal to the same thing.

questions.q: Postulate 3 is about
questions.why: Postulate 3 states that a circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius. It is about circles.

questions.q: How many lines pass through one point?
questions.why: Infinitely many lines pass through one point. Only when a second point is fixed is the line unique.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common. Reason (R): Through two distinct points there is a unique line.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Through two distinct points there is exactly one line, so two distinct lines cannot share two points.

questions.q: Which statement is equivalent to the fifth postulate?
options: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to it
The whole is greater than the part
A circle can be drawn with any radius
questions.why: Correct answer: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to it.

questions.q: If AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY by
questions.why: If AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY, since things equal to the same thing are equal. This is Axiom 1.

questions.q: Euclid's Proposition 1 constructs a(n)
questions.why: Euclid's Proposition 1 constructs an equilateral triangle on a given line segment, using two circles. It does not make a square or a right angle.

questions.q: If a + b = 15 and a = c, then c + b = 15 is justified by
questions.why: If a = c, then a + b = c + b, so c + b = 15. We substitute equals in the sum, which is Axiom 1 (and Axiom 2).

questions.q: Case: An Indus Valley wall uses bricks 28 cm long in ratio 4 : 2 : 1. The thickness is
questions.why: The ratio 4 : 2 : 1 gives length : width : thickness. If length is 28 cm, then 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm per part, so thickness is 1 × 7 = 7 cm.

questions.q: A, B, C on a line with B between A and C, AC = 12 and AB = BC. Then AB =
options: 6, using halves of the same thing (Axiom 7)
questions.why: AB + BC = AC = 12 and AB = BC, so 2AB = 12 and AB = 6. This uses the axiom that halves of the same thing are equal.

questions.q: Which assumption did Euclid use without stating in Proposition 1?
questions.why: Euclid assumed without stating that the two circles meet at a point, which is needed to complete the triangle. None of his postulates guarantees this.

questions.q: On the surface of a sphere, 'lines' are great circles. Which Euclidean idea FAILS there?
options: The whole is greater than the part
Things equal to the same thing are equal
Exactly one parallel through an outside point
questions.why: On a sphere, any two great circles (lines) meet, so there is no parallel line through an outside point. So the 'exactly one parallel' idea fails there.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Lines and Angles
courses.summary: Angle vocabulary, linear pairs, vertically opposite angles, parallel lines cut by a transversal, and the angle sum and exterior angle properties of a triangle — with proofs.
outcomes: Use correct terms: ray, segment, collinear, acute, obtuse, reflex, complementary, supplementary
Prove and use the linear pair and vertically opposite angles results
Use corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles to find unknowns and prove lines parallel
Prove the angle sum property and exterior angle theorem of a triangle

scenes.text: At 3 o'clock the clock hands make a right angle; at 6 they make a straight line.
Sana notices: as the minute hand moves on, the two angles on either side always add to 360°.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Line segment** AB has two end points; **ray** AB starts at A and goes on through B; a **line** goes on in both directions.
- **Collinear** points lie on one line.
- Angles: **acute** (0° < x < 90°), **right** (90°), **obtuse** (90° < x < 180°), **straight** (180°), **reflex** (180° < x < 360°).
- **Complementary**: sum 90°. **Supplementary**: sum 180°.
- **Adjacent angles**: common vertex, common arm, non-common arms on opposite sides of the common arm.

steps.title: Solved: angle equal to its complement / supplement
steps.body: x = 90° − x ⇒ **x = 45°**. Supplement of an angle is 4 times its complement: 180 − x = 4(90 − x) ⇒ 180 − x = 360 − 4x ⇒ 3x = 180 ⇒ **x = 60°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing complementary (90°) and supplementary (180°). Memory hook: **C** comes before **S**, 90 before 180.
- Calling any two angles with a common vertex 'adjacent' — they also need a common arm.

activity.prompt: Classify each angle

quiz.why: Complementary angles add to 90°. So the complement of 35° is 90° − 35° = 55°.
Supplementary angles add to 180°. So the supplement of 110° is 180° − 110° = 70°.
An angle between 180° and 360° is a reflex angle, so 225° is reflex. A straight angle is exactly 180°.

quiz.q: Two angles are supplementary and equal. Each is
quiz.why: Two equal supplementary angles each have 180° ÷ 2 = 90°. So each is a right angle.

quiz.q: Points lying on the same line are
quiz.why: Points that lie on the same line are collinear. Concurrent lines pass through one point.

lessons.title: Intersecting lines: linear pair and vertically opposite angles

scenes.text: When Dev opens a pair of scissors, the blades form an X.
The angles opposite each other always look equal — and they are. This lesson proves it.

steps.title: Linear pair axiom
steps.body: If a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles so formed add to **180°** (a linear pair). Conversely, if two adjacent angles sum to 180°, their non-common arms form a line.

steps.title: Theorem: vertically opposite angles are equal
steps.body:
Lines AB and CD intersect at O.
∠AOC + ∠AOD = 180° (linear pair, ray OA on line CD).
∠AOD + ∠BOD = 180° (linear pair, ray OD on line AB).
So ∠AOC + ∠AOD = ∠AOD + ∠BOD ⇒ **∠AOC = ∠BOD**. Similarly ∠AOD = ∠BOC.

steps.title: Solved: angles in a ratio
steps.body: Lines meet at O; ∠AOC : ∠BOC = 2 : 3 and they form a linear pair. 2x + 3x = 180 ⇒ x = 36. So ∠AOC = **72°**, ∠BOC = **108°**; the vertically opposite angles are 72° and 108° too.

steps.title: Solved: rays on a line
steps.body: Rays OP, OQ, OR stand on line XY at O with ∠XOP = 40°, ∠POQ = x, ∠QOR = 2x, ∠ROY = 50° filling the straight angle. 40 + x + 2x + 50 = 180 ⇒ 3x = 90 ⇒ **x = 30°**.

steps.title: Solved: angle bisectors of a linear pair
steps.body: Bisectors of a linear pair meet at 90°: ½∠1 + ½∠2 = ½(180°) = 90°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling adjacent angles 'vertically opposite'.
- Forgetting that all angles around a point total 360°.

activity.prompt: Two lines intersect; one angle is 3x + 10° and its vertically opposite angle is 5x − 30°. Find x.

quiz.q: Angles of a linear pair add to
quiz.why: The angles of a linear pair lie on a straight line, so they add to 180°.

quiz.q: If one angle at an intersection is 50°, its vertically opposite angle is
quiz.why: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angle opposite 50° is also 50°.

quiz.q: Sum of all four angles at an intersection is
quiz.why: The four angles at the point of intersection of two lines together make a full turn, 360°.

quiz.q: If ∠AOC = 4x and ∠BOC = 5x form a linear pair, x =
quiz.why: A linear pair adds to 180°, so 4x + 5x = 9x = 180°, and x = 20°.

quiz.q: Bisectors of a linear pair make an angle of
quiz.why: The bisectors of the two angles of a linear pair make an angle of ½(180°) = 90°. So they are perpendicular.

scenes.text: The rungs of a ladder are parallel; each side rail cuts across them.
Carpenter Gopal checks every rung's angle with the rail — equal corresponding angles mean the rungs are truly parallel.

steps.title: Angle pairs
steps.body:
A **transversal** cuts two lines at two points, making 8 angles.
- **Corresponding** angles: same position at each intersection (∠1 & ∠5, …).
- **Alternate interior** angles: between the lines, opposite sides of the transversal.
- **Alternate exterior** angles: outside the lines, opposite sides.
- **Co-interior** (consecutive interior) angles: between the lines, same side.

steps.title: Axioms and theorems
Solved: find all angles
steps.body: AB ∥ CD, transversal makes ∠1 = 65° at AB (top-left). Corresponding angle at CD = 65°; vertically opposite = 65°; adjacent = 180° − 65° = 115°; co-interior partner of the 65° interior angle = 115°.

steps.title: Solved: the bent-line problem
steps.body: AB ∥ CD, a point E lies between them, ∠ABE = 45° and ∠CDE = 30° (angles at B and D toward E). Draw EF ∥ AB through E (so EF ∥ CD too). ∠BEF = 45° (alternate), ∠FED = 30° (alternate). **∠BED = 75°**.

steps.title: Solved: proving lines parallel
steps.body: If ∠PQR = ∠QRS (alternate interior angles made by transversal QR with lines PQ and RS), then PQ ∥ RS by the converse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'alternate angles are equal' when the lines are not parallel.
- Taking co-interior angles as equal (they are supplementary).
- In bent-line problems, forgetting to draw the helping parallel line.

activity.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Match the pair with its relation

quiz.q: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, co-interior angles are
quiz.why: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, co-interior angles are supplementary, i.e. they add up to 180°.

quiz.q: One of eight angles formed is 72° (lines parallel). The other values present are
quiz.why: With parallel lines, the eight angles take only two values, an angle and its supplement. If one is 72°, the others are 72° and 180° − 72° = 108°.

quiz.q: If alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are
quiz.why: If a transversal makes equal alternate interior angles with two lines, the lines are parallel. This is the converse of the alternate angle property.

quiz.q: Co-interior angles are (2x + 10)° and (3x − 30)° with parallel lines. x =
quiz.why: Co-interior angles add to 180°: (2x + 10) + (3x − 30) = 5x − 20 = 180, so x = 40.
Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other. So l ∥ m and m ∥ n imply l ∥ n.

lessons.title: Angle sum property of a triangle

scenes.text: Pooja tears off the three corners of a paper triangle and places them side by side.
They form a perfect straight line — 180°. Now prove it for every triangle.

steps.title: Theorem: angles of a triangle sum to 180°
steps.body:
Given △PQR. Draw line XPY through P parallel to QR.
∠XPQ = ∠PQR (alternate angles, XY ∥ QR).
∠YPR = ∠PRQ (alternate angles).
∠XPQ + ∠QPR + ∠YPR = 180° (angles on a straight line).
⇒ **∠PQR + ∠QPR + ∠PRQ = 180°**.

steps.title: Exterior angle theorem
steps.body: If a side of a triangle is produced, the **exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles**. (Proof: exterior + adjacent interior = 180° = sum of all three interior angles.) So an exterior angle is greater than each interior opposite angle.

steps.title: Solved: angles in ratio
steps.body: Angles of a triangle are in ratio 2 : 3 : 4. 9x = 180 ⇒ x = 20 ⇒ **40°, 60°, 80°**.

steps.title: Solved: exterior angle
steps.body: Exterior angle 110°, one interior opposite angle 45° ⇒ the other = 110° − 45° = **65°**; the third interior angle = 180° − 110° = 70°.

steps.title: Solved: bisectors
steps.body: In △ABC, bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at O. Then ∠BOC = 90° + ½∠A. If ∠A = 70°, ∠BOC = **125°**. (Because ½(∠B + ∠C) = ½(110°) = 55°, ∠BOC = 180° − 55°.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the exterior angle to all three interior angles.
- Forgetting that a triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle.

activity.prompt: A triangle has angles x, 2x and 3x. Find the largest angle.

quiz.q: Angles of a triangle sum to
quiz.why: The angle sum property says the three angles of a triangle add to 180°.

quiz.q: Two angles are 50° and 60°. The third is

quiz.why: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. It is not equal to 180°.

quiz.q: A triangle can have how many obtuse angles?
quiz.why: A triangle's angles add to 180°, so two obtuse angles (each over 90°) would exceed 180°. So it can have 0 or 1 obtuse angle.

quiz.q: Exterior angle 120°, interior opposite angles equal. Each is
quiz.why: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, which are equal. So each is 120° ÷ 2 = 60°.

questions.q: Supplement of 75° is
questions.why: The supplement of 75° is 180° − 75° = 105°.

questions.q: An angle greater than 180° and less than 360° is
questions.why: An angle greater than 180° and less than 360° is called a reflex angle.

questions.q: Vertically opposite angles are
questions.why: Vertically opposite angles, formed when two lines intersect, are equal.

questions.q: If an angle is 4 times its complement, it is
questions.why: Let the angle be x, so x = 4(90 − x) = 360 − 4x. Then 5x = 360, and x = 72°.

questions.q: Two lines intersect; one angle is 40°. The other three are
questions.why: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the opposite angle is 40°. The other two form linear pairs with 40°, so each is 180° − 40° = 140°.

questions.q: Alternate interior angles of parallel lines are
questions.why: When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, alternate interior angles are equal.

questions.q: Assertion (A): If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, co-interior angles add to 180°. Reason (R): Corresponding angles are equal and form linear pairs with the co-interior partner.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Corresponding angles are equal, and the equal angle forms a linear pair (180°) with the co-interior partner, so co-interior angles add to 180°.

questions.q: Angles of a triangle are in ratio 3 : 5 : 7. The smallest is
questions.why: Let the angles be 3x, 5x and 7x. Then 15x = 180, so x = 12° and the smallest is 3 × 12 = 36°.

questions.q: Angles x, x + 10, x + 20 form a triangle. x =
Co-interior angles are 3x + 20 and 2x − 10 with parallel lines. x =
questions.why: Co-interior angles add to 180°: (3x + 20) + (2x − 10) = 5x + 10 = 180, so x = 34.

questions.q: Exterior angle of a triangle is 105°; interior opposite angles are in ratio 2 : 1. They are
questions.why: The exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles: 2x + x = 3x = 105, so x = 35°. The angles are 70° and 35°.

questions.q: Case: A road AB is parallel to CD. A path from B to D bends at E between them with ∠ABE = 50° and ∠EDC = 40°. ∠BED =
questions.why: Draw a line EF through E parallel to AB (and CD). Then ∠BED = ∠ABE + ∠EDC = 50° + 40° = 90°.

questions.q: In △ABC, bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at O. If ∠A = 80°, ∠BOC =
questions.why: ∠BOC = 90° + ½∠A = 90° + 40° = 130°. This is the angle between the bisectors of ∠B and ∠C.

questions.q: If ray OC stands on line AB with ∠AOC = x and ∠BOC = y, and x − y = 40°, then x =
questions.why: A linear pair: x + y = 180, and x − y = 40. Adding, 2x = 220, so x = 110°.

questions.q: The sides AB and AC of △ABC are produced to P and Q. Bisectors of exterior angles at B and C meet at O. Then ∠BOC equals
questions.why: Each exterior angle bisector makes half of (180° − B) and (180° − C). So ∠BOC = 180° − ½(180° − B) − ½(180° − C) = ½(B + C) = 90° − ½∠A.

questions.q: Lines l ∥ m, transversal t makes interior angles on the same side of (5x − 20)° and (3x + 40)°. The acute angle formed is
questions.why: Co-interior angles are supplementary: (5x − 20) + (3x + 40) = 8x + 20 = 180, so x = 20. The angles are 80° and 100°, so the acute one is 80°.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Triangles
courses.summary: Congruence of triangles and the SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS criteria, CPCT, and the properties of isosceles triangles — with full proofs and exam-style problems.
outcomes: Explain congruence and write correspondences correctly
Apply SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS to prove triangles congruent
Use CPCT to prove equal sides and angles
Prove and use: angles opposite equal sides are equal, and its converse

scenes.text: Farhan cuts two kite halves from paper; one fits exactly on the other when flipped.
Same shape and same size — the halves are congruent. But must he check every side and angle? No: three well-chosen parts are enough.

steps.title: Congruent figures
steps.body:
Two figures are **congruent (≅)** if one can be placed exactly on the other. For triangles △ABC ≅ △PQR means the correspondence **A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R**, so AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP and ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R.
**CPCT**: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are equal.

steps.title: SAS congruence rule (taken as an axiom)
steps.body: Two triangles are congruent if **two sides and the included angle** of one are equal to two sides and the included angle of the other. The angle must be **between** the two sides.

steps.title: Solved: segments bisecting each other
steps.body:
AB and CD bisect each other at O (OA = OB, OC = OD). Prove AC = BD and AC ∥ BD.
In △AOC and △BOD: OA = OB, OC = OD, ∠AOC = ∠BOD (vertically opposite). ⇒ △AOC ≅ △BOD (SAS).
So **AC = BD** (CPCT) and ∠OAC = ∠OBD (CPCT). These are alternate angles for lines AC, BD with transversal AB ⇒ **AC ∥ BD**.

steps.title: Solved: perpendicular bisector property
steps.body:
Line l is the perpendicular bisector of AB, P is any point on l. Prove PA = PB.
Let l meet AB at C. △PCA and △PCB: AC = BC, ∠PCA = ∠PCB = 90°, PC common ⇒ SAS ⇒ **PA = PB**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) — it is **not** a congruence rule.
- Writing △ABC ≅ △QPR when the correspondence is A↔P: order of letters matters.
- Forgetting to name the common side or vertically opposite angle as a reason.

activity.prompt: Match the correspondence △ABC ≅ △PQR with the equal parts

quiz.q: Which is NOT a congruence rule?
quiz.why: SSA is not a congruence rule, since two sides and a non-included angle can give two different triangles. SSS, SAS and ASA are valid.

quiz.q: In SAS the angle must be
quiz.why: In SAS, the equal angle must be the one included between the two equal sides. Otherwise the rule does not hold.
If △DEF ≅ △XYZ, the vertices correspond in order: D↔X, E↔Y, F↔Z. So EF = YZ.
CPCT means Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles, which are equal. It is used after proving congruence.

quiz.q: Any point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is
quiz.why: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equidistant from A and B. This is a key property.

scenes.text: Scouts cannot cross a river to measure its width.
They copy two angles and the side between them on their bank — a congruent triangle gives the width without getting wet.

steps.title: ASA rule (theorem)
steps.body: Two triangles are congruent if **two angles and the included side** are equal. It is proved from SAS by contradiction.

steps.title: AAS rule
steps.body: If two angles and **any** side are equal, the third angles are also equal (angle sum 180°), so ASA applies. Hence **AAS** also proves congruence — but the side must **correspond** (be opposite the same angle).

steps.title: Solved: midpoint and parallel lines
steps.body:
Segments AB ∥ CD; AD and BC meet at O, and O is the midpoint of AD. Show O is also the midpoint of BC.
△AOB and △DOC: ∠ABO = ∠DCO (alternate, AB ∥ CD), ∠AOB = ∠DOC (vertically opposite), OA = OD.
AAS ⇒ △AOB ≅ △DOC ⇒ **OB = OC** (CPCT): O is the midpoint of BC.

steps.title: Solved: equal perpendiculars
steps.body:
AD and BC are equal perpendiculars to segment AB (on opposite sides). Show CD bisects AB.
Let CD meet AB at O. △AOD, △BOC: ∠OAD = ∠OBC = 90°, ∠AOD = ∠BOC (vert. opp.), AD = BC ⇒ AAS ⇒ **OA = OB**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using AAS with non-corresponding sides (a side opposite a different angle).
- AAA is not a congruence rule — equal angles only give the same shape (similar), not the same size.

statements.s: AAA proves triangles congruent
ASA needs the side between the two angles
AAS works because the third angles must also be equal
SSA always proves congruence
statements.why: Two different triangles can share SSA.

options: two angles and the included side
quiz.why: ASA means two angles and the side included between them are equal. It is not any two angles and any side.
∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and BC = QR: BC is not between ∠A and ∠B. Two angles and a non-included side give AAS.

quiz.q: Two triangles with all angles equal are
quiz.why: Triangles with all angles equal have the same shape but may differ in size, so they need not be congruent. They are similar.

quiz.q: To prove ASA, you need equal
quiz.why: For ASA, the side must lie between the two angles. AB lies between ∠A and ∠B, so we need ∠A, AB and ∠B.

quiz.q: If ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and AC = DF, then △ABC ≅ △DEF by
quiz.why: ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and AC = DF involve two angles and a side not between them, so it is AAS. Since the third angles are also equal, this is also ASA.

scenes.text: Kavya's tent has two equal slanting poles.
She notices the two base angles look equal. Is that always true? Yes — and the converse holds too.

steps.title: Theorem 1
steps.body:
**Angles opposite to equal sides of a triangle are equal.**
Proof: In △ABC with AB = AC, draw bisector AD of ∠A meeting BC at D. △BAD, △CAD: AB = AC, ∠BAD = ∠CAD, AD common ⇒ SAS ⇒ **∠B = ∠C** (CPCT).

steps.title: Theorem 2 (converse)
steps.body: **Sides opposite to equal angles of a triangle are equal.** (Proved using ASA.) Consequences: every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°; a triangle with all angles equal is equilateral.

steps.title: Solved: find the angles
steps.body: In △ABC, AB = AC and ∠A = 40°. Then ∠B = ∠C = (180° − 40°)/2 = **70°** each.

steps.title: Solved: ∠BCD = 90°
steps.body:
△ABC is isosceles with AB = AC; BA is produced to D so that AD = AB. Show ∠BCD = 90°.
AB = AC ⇒ ∠ABC = ∠ACB. AD = AB = AC ⇒ ∠ACD = ∠ADC.
Angle sum of △BCD: ∠ABC + ∠ADC + (∠ACB + ∠ACD) = 180° ⇒ 2(∠ACB + ∠ACD) = 180° ⇒ **∠BCD = 90°**.

steps.title: Solved: altitudes
steps.body: In △ABC, AB = AC; altitudes BE (on AC) and CF (on AB). △BEC, △CFB: ∠BEC = ∠CFB = 90°, ∠ECB = ∠FBC, BC common ⇒ AAS ⇒ **BE = CF**: the two altitudes to the equal sides are equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the equal angles at the wrong vertices: the equal angles are **opposite** the equal sides (the base angles).
- Assuming a triangle is isosceles because it looks so.

activity.prompt: In an isosceles triangle the vertex angle is 50°. Find a base angle.

quiz.why: If AB = AC, the angles opposite those sides are equal, so ∠B = ∠C. This is the isosceles triangle theorem.

quiz.q: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is
quiz.why: In an equilateral triangle all three angles are equal and add to 180°, so each is 60°.

quiz.q: Base angles are 35° each. The vertex angle is
quiz.why: The vertex angle = 180° − (35° + 35°) = 110°.

quiz.q: A right isosceles triangle has acute angles of
quiz.why: In a right isosceles triangle, the two acute angles are equal and add to 90°, so each is 45°.
Sides opposite equal angles are equal. If ∠B = ∠C, the opposite sides AC and AB are equal, so AB = AC.

scenes.text: A rectangular shelf frame wobbles, but adding a diagonal brace makes it rigid.
A triangle with fixed sides cannot change shape — that is the SSS rule at work in engineering.

steps.title: SSS rule
steps.body: If **three sides** of one triangle are equal to three sides of another, the triangles are congruent. (Triangular frames are rigid for this reason — used in bridges, cranes and roof trusses.)

steps.title: RHS rule
steps.body: In two **right triangles**, if the **hypotenuse and one side** are equal, the triangles are congruent. (A special case where SSA does work, because the angle is 90°.)

steps.title: Solved: SSS with a common side
steps.body:
△ABC and △DBC on the same base BC with AB = AC and DB = DC; A, D on the same side of BC. Show ∠BAD = ∠CAD.
△ABD, △ACD: AB = AC, BD = CD, AD common ⇒ SSS ⇒ **∠BAD = ∠CAD** (CPCT). So AD bisects ∠A (and, extended, is the perpendicular bisector of BC).

steps.title: Solved: RHS
steps.body: AD is an altitude of isosceles △ABC (AB = AC). △ABD, △ACD: ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, hypotenuse AB = AC, AD common ⇒ RHS ⇒ **BD = CD** (AD bisects BC) and ∠BAD = ∠CAD.

steps.title: Solved: equal altitudes ⇒ isosceles
steps.body: If altitudes BE and CF of △ABC are equal, △BEC ≅ △CFB by RHS (hypotenuse BC common, BE = CF) ⇒ ∠C = ∠B ⇒ AB = AC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
