- Using RHS without checking the right angle.
- Using the leg as the 'hypotenuse' — the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

activity.prompt: Which rule proves congruence?

items.text: Right angle, hypotenuse and one side
Two sides and a non-included angle (not right)

quiz.why: SSS needs all three pairs of sides to be equal. Then the triangles are congruent.
RHS applies only to right-angled triangles, where the hypotenuse and one side are equal. It is not for all triangles.
In RHS, R stands for right angle, H for hypotenuse and S for side. So H means hypotenuse.

quiz.q: A triangular truss is rigid because of
quiz.why: A triangle with fixed sides cannot change shape, so it is rigid. This is because of SSS.

quiz.q: △PQR with ∠Q = 90°, PR = 10, PQ = 6 and △XYZ with ∠Y = 90°, XZ = 10, XY = 6 are congruent by
quiz.why: Both are right triangles with equal hypotenuses (10) and one equal side (6), so they are congruent by RHS.

questions.q: △ABC ≅ △PQR implies ∠C equals
questions.why: If △ABC ≅ △PQR, vertices correspond in order: A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. So ∠C = ∠R.

questions.q: Which criterion is not valid?
questions.why: AAA is not a congruence criterion, as equal angles only give similar triangles. RHS, SSS and ASA are valid.

questions.q: In an equilateral triangle each angle is
questions.why: The three angles of an equilateral triangle are equal and add to 180°, so each is 60°.

questions.q: AB = AC and ∠B = 50°. ∠A =
Two sides and the included angle equal ⇒ congruent by
questions.why: Two sides and the included angle equal give congruence by SAS. SSA does not guarantee congruence.

questions.q: If △ABC ≅ △DEF, AB = 5 cm, ∠B = 40°, then
questions.why: In congruent triangles, corresponding parts are equal. AB corresponds to DE and ∠B corresponds to ∠E, so DE = 5 cm and ∠E = 40°.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Two triangles with three equal angles must be congruent. Reason (R): AAA is a congruence rule.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false. Triangles with equal angles need not be congruent, and AAA is not a congruence rule. It only shows similarity.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In △ABC, if ∠B = ∠C then AB = AC. Reason (R): Sides opposite equal angles are equal.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. If ∠B = ∠C then the sides opposite them, AC and AB, are equal, by the theorem that sides opposite equal angles are equal.

questions.q: In △ABC, AB = AC and the exterior angle at C is 115°. ∠A =
questions.why: The exterior angle at C is 115°, so ∠C = 180° − 115° = 65°. Since AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C = 65°, so ∠A = 180° − 130° = 50°.

questions.q: The altitude AD of isosceles △ABC (AB = AC) with BC = 12 cm meets BC at D. BD =
questions.why: The altitude AD ⟂ BC, and AB = AC, so by RHS the triangles ABD and ACD are congruent. So BD = DC = 12/2 = 6 cm.

questions.q: O is the midpoint of AB and CD (they bisect each other). Which is true?
questions.why: O is the midpoint of both AB and CD, so AO = OB and CO = OD, and the vertically opposite angles at O are equal. So △AOC ≅ △BOD by SAS, and AC = BD by CPCT.

questions.q: Case: A roof truss is an isosceles triangle with equal rafters and the ridge angle 100°. The angle each rafter makes with the horizontal beam is
questions.why: The two equal rafters make an isosceles triangle with ridge angle 100°. The base angles are equal: (180° − 100°) ÷ 2 = 40°.

questions.q: In △ABC, AB = AC; D on BC such that AD bisects ∠A. If BC = 10 cm and ∠B = 55°, then BD and ∠ADB are
questions.why: AD bisects ∠A in an isosceles triangle, so △ABD ≅ △ACD by SAS. Hence BD = DC = 5 cm and ∠ADB = ∠ADC, each 90° as they form a linear pair.

questions.q: ABC is isosceles with AB = AC; BA produced to D with AD = AB. ∠BCD equals
questions.why: AB = AC = AD, so A is the centre of a circle through B, C, D, with BD as a diameter. So ∠BCD is an angle in a semicircle, i.e. 90°. (In the angle form: ∠ACB + ∠ACD = ∠B + ∠D, and with BCD angle sum 180°, this gives 90°.)

questions.q: In right △ABC, ∠C = 90°, M is the midpoint of hypotenuse AB. C is joined to M and extended to D with DM = CM. Then CM equals
questions.why: △AMC ≅ △BMD by SAS (AM = BM, CM = DM, vertically opposite angles). So ACBD is a rectangle, as it has a right angle at C, whose diagonals CD and AB are equal. So CD = AB and CM = ½CD = ½AB.

questions.q: △ABC with AB = AC; points D, E on BC with BD = CE. Then
questions.why: Since AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C. With BD = CE, △ABD ≅ △ACE by SAS, so AD = AE by CPCT.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Quadrilaterals
courses.summary: Angle sum of a quadrilateral, properties of parallelograms and special parallelograms, tests for a parallelogram, and the Mid-point Theorem with its converse.
outcomes: Use the angle sum property of a quadrilateral
Prove and apply the properties of a parallelogram (sides, angles, diagonals)
Decide when a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus or square
Prove and apply the Mid-point Theorem and its converse

scenes.text: Tiles, kites, doors, ramps — Rahul spots four-sided shapes everywhere on his walk.
His sister challenges him to name each one properly and find a missing angle on a kite.

steps.title: The family
steps.body:
- **Trapezium**: one pair of opposite sides parallel.
- **Parallelogram**: both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
- **Rectangle**: parallelogram with a right angle.
- **Rhombus**: parallelogram with all sides equal.
- **Square**: rectangle with all sides equal (also a rhombus with a right angle).
- **Kite**: two pairs of equal adjacent sides (not a parallelogram in general).

steps.title: Angle sum property
steps.body: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles, so **sum of angles = 2 × 180° = 360°**.

steps.title: Solved: missing angle
steps.body: Three angles are 80°, 95°, 110°. Fourth = 360 − 285 = **75°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 180° as the angle sum of a quadrilateral.
- Thinking every square is not a rectangle — every square IS a rectangle and a rhombus.

activity.prompt: Is this always true?

quiz.q: Sum of angles of a quadrilateral
quiz.why: The four angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°. A diagonal splits it into two triangles of 180° each.

quiz.q: A parallelogram with all sides equal is a
quiz.why: A parallelogram with all four sides equal is a rhombus. A rectangle has all angles 90°, and a kite has only two pairs of adjacent equal sides.

quiz.q: Three angles are 90°, 90°, 70°. The fourth is
quiz.why: The angles add up to 360°: 90° + 90° + 70° = 250°, so the fourth is 360° − 250° = 110°.

quiz.q: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is a
quiz.why: A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides. A rectangle and rhombus have two pairs.

quiz.q: Angles in ratio 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 — the largest is
quiz.why: Let the angles be x, 2x, 3x, 4x. Then 10x = 360°, so x = 36° and the largest is 4x = 144°.

scenes.text: The shop's folding gate opens and closes but its slats always stay in parallelograms.
The shopkeeper notices opposite rods are always equal — the shape changes, the properties don't.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
In a parallelogram ABCD:
1. A diagonal divides it into **two congruent triangles** (△ABC ≅ △CDA by ASA).
2. **Opposite sides are equal.**
3. **Opposite angles are equal.**
4. **Diagonals bisect each other.**
5. Adjacent angles are supplementary (co-interior angles).
Special: rectangle — diagonals equal; rhombus — diagonals perpendicular; square — diagonals equal and perpendicular, each bisecting the other.

steps.title: Solved: proof that diagonal makes congruent triangles
steps.body: In △ABC and △CDA: ∠BCA = ∠DAC (alternate, BC ∥ AD), ∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate, AB ∥ DC), AC common ⇒ ASA ⇒ **△ABC ≅ △CDA**. Then AB = CD and BC = DA (CPCT).

steps.title: Solved: find the angles
steps.body: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 3x + 10 and ∠B = 2x + 20. Adjacent angles: 5x + 30 = 180 ⇒ x = 30 ⇒ ∠A = **100°**, ∠B = **80°**, ∠C = 100°, ∠D = 80°.

steps.title: Solved: rectangle from parallelogram
steps.body: If the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal it is a rectangle: △ABC ≅ △DCB (SSS, AC = DB) ⇒ ∠B = ∠C, and ∠B + ∠C = 180° ⇒ each 90°.

steps.title: Solved: angle bisectors
steps.body: In parallelogram ABCD, bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at P. ∠PAB + ∠PBA = ½(∠A + ∠B) = 90° ⇒ **∠APB = 90°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming diagonals of a parallelogram are equal (only for rectangles/squares).
- Assuming diagonals bisect the angles (only for rhombus/square).

activity.prompt: Match the special parallelogram with its diagonal property

quiz.q: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are
quiz.why: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. Adjacent angles are supplementary.

quiz.q: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°; the others are
quiz.why: The opposite angle is also 70°. Each adjacent angle is 180° − 70° = 110°, so the angles are 70°, 110° and 110°.

quiz.q: Diagonals of a rhombus intersect at
quiz.why: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so they meet at 90°.

quiz.q: Diagonals of a parallelogram are 10 cm and 16 cm; they cut each other into
quiz.why: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so 10 cm is cut into 5 and 5, and 16 cm into 8 and 8. Each half is 5 and 8.

quiz.q: A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a
quiz.why: A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle. In a rhombus the diagonals are unequal in general.

lessons.title: When is a quadrilateral a parallelogram?

scenes.text: A carpenter cannot easily check parallel sides, but she can measure lengths.
If both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or the diagonals bisect each other, the frame must be a parallelogram.

steps.title: Tests (converses)
steps.body:
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if:
- each pair of opposite sides is equal; or
- each pair of opposite angles is equal; or
- the diagonals bisect each other; or
- **one pair** of opposite sides is **equal and parallel**.

steps.title: Solved: one pair equal and parallel
steps.body: In ABCD, AB = CD and AB ∥ CD. △ABC, △CDA: AB = CD, ∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate), AC common ⇒ SAS ⇒ ∠BCA = ∠DAC ⇒ BC ∥ AD. Both pairs parallel ⇒ parallelogram.

steps.title: Solved: midpoints of opposite sides
steps.body: ABCD is a parallelogram; E, F are midpoints of AB and CD. AE = ½AB = ½CD = CF and AE ∥ CF ⇒ **AECF is a parallelogram** ⇒ AF ∥ EC.

steps.title: Solved: rhombus from perpendicular bisecting diagonals
steps.body: If diagonals bisect each other at right angles, each of the four triangles is congruent (SAS) ⇒ all sides equal ⇒ **rhombus**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'one pair of opposite sides equal' alone (needs also parallel).
- Using 'one pair parallel' alone (that is a trapezium).

statements.s: If both pairs of opposite sides are equal, it is a parallelogram
If one pair is parallel and the other pair equal, it must be a parallelogram
statements.why: An isosceles trapezium is a counter-example.

statements.s: If diagonals bisect each other, it is a parallelogram
If diagonals are perpendicular and bisect each other, it is a rhombus
If diagonals are equal, it is a rectangle
statements.why: Only if they also bisect each other (isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals).

quiz.q: Diagonals bisect each other ⇒ the quadrilateral is a
quiz.why: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram. This is the converse of the diagonal property.

quiz.q: Diagonals equal and bisect each other ⇒
quiz.why: Diagonals that are equal and bisect each other make a rectangle. A square also has this, but additionally perpendicular diagonals.

quiz.q: Diagonals equal, perpendicular and bisecting each other ⇒
quiz.why: Equal diagonals that bisect each other at right angles make a square. A rhombus has only perpendicular ones and a rectangle only equal ones.

quiz.q: One pair of opposite sides equal and parallel ⇒
quiz.why: If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is both equal and parallel, it is a parallelogram. This is a standard test.

quiz.q: ABCD has ∠A = ∠C and ∠B = ∠D. It is a
quiz.why: If both pairs of opposite angles are equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. This is the converse of the opposite angles property.

scenes.text: A triangular plot has a footbridge joining the midpoints of two sides.
The engineer says it is exactly half as long as the third side and parallel to it — the Mid-point Theorem.

steps.title: Theorem and converse
steps.body:
**Mid-point Theorem**: the line segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is **parallel to the third side** and **half of it**.
Proof idea: E, F midpoints of AB, AC. Draw CD ∥ BA meeting EF produced at D. △AEF ≅ △CDF (ASA) ⇒ EF = FD, AE = CD = BE. BCDE is a parallelogram (BE = CD, BE ∥ CD) ⇒ ED ∥ BC and ED = BC ⇒ EF = ½BC.
**Converse**: a line through the midpoint of one side parallel to another side **bisects the third side**.

steps.title: Solved: perimeter of the midpoint triangle
steps.body: Sides of △ABC are 8, 10, 12 cm. The triangle formed by joining midpoints has sides 4, 5, 6 ⇒ perimeter **15 cm** (half of 30).

steps.title: Solved: midpoints of a quadrilateral
steps.body: P, Q, R, S are midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA of any quadrilateral ABCD. In △ABC, PQ ∥ AC, PQ = ½AC. In △ADC, SR ∥ AC, SR = ½AC. ⇒ PQ = SR, PQ ∥ SR ⇒ **PQRS is a parallelogram**. If ABCD is a rhombus, PQRS is a rectangle; if a rectangle, PQRS is a rhombus.

steps.title: Solved: trapezium median
steps.body: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC; E is midpoint of AD; a line through E parallel to AB meets BC at F. By the converse (in △ABD then △DBC), **F is the midpoint of BC**, and EF = ½(AB + DC).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Joining a midpoint to a vertex and calling it a mid-segment.
- Forgetting the 'half' part when finding lengths.

activity.prompt: In △ABC, D and E are midpoints of AB and AC and DE = 4.5 cm. Find BC.

quiz.q: The segment joining midpoints of two sides is
options: parallel and half the third side
quiz.why: The midpoint theorem says that the line joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.

quiz.q: Midpoint triangle of a triangle with perimeter 24 cm has perimeter
quiz.why: Each side of the midpoint triangle is half the corresponding side of the original. So its perimeter is half of 24 = 12 cm.

quiz.q: Joining midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral gives a
quiz.why: Joining the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram, as each side is parallel to a diagonal and half its length.

quiz.q: Joining midpoints of a rhombus gives a
quiz.why: In a rhombus the diagonals are perpendicular, and the midpoint figure's sides are parallel to them. So it has right angles, and is a rectangle.

quiz.q: A line through the midpoint of AB parallel to BC in △ABC meets AC at its
quiz.why: A line drawn through the midpoint of one side parallel to another meets the third side at its midpoint. This is the converse of the midpoint theorem.

questions.q: Angle sum of a quadrilateral
questions.why: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°, as it can be split into two triangles.

questions.q: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are
questions.why: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are both equal and parallel. This is its basic property.

questions.q: Diagonals of a rectangle are
questions.why: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other. They are not perpendicular unless it is a square.

questions.q: Angles of a quadrilateral are x, 2x, 3x, 4x. x =
In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 65°. ∠B =
questions.why: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, so ∠B = 180° − 65° = 115°.

questions.q: Midpoint triangle side lengths for a triangle 6, 8, 10:
questions.why: By the midpoint theorem, each side of the midpoint triangle is half the matching side: 3, 4 and 5.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every rhombus is a parallelogram. Reason (R): A rhombus has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. A rhombus has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, which is the definition of a parallelogram.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Diagonals of every parallelogram are equal. Reason (R): Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false, as only rectangles have equal diagonals among parallelograms. The reason is true: the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

questions.q: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = (4x − 10)°, ∠R = (2x + 30)°. ∠P =
questions.why: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: 4x − 10 = 2x + 30, so x = 20. Then ∠P = 4(20) − 10 = 70°.

questions.q: A diagonal of a rhombus is equal to a side. The angles of the rhombus are
questions.why: If a diagonal equals the side, the diagonal and two sides form an equilateral triangle. So an angle is 60° and the adjacent angle is 120°.

questions.q: Diagonals of a square are 8 cm each. Its side is
questions.why: Half-diagonals are 4 and 4, meeting at right angles, so the side = √(4² + 4²) = 4√2 cm.

questions.q: Case: A garden is a quadrilateral; paths join midpoints of adjacent sides. Its diagonals are 20 m and 30 m. The perimeter of the inner path-figure is
questions.why: The inner figure's sides are half the diagonals, 10 m and 15 m, in two pairs. So its perimeter is 2(10 + 15) = 50 m.

questions.q: In △ABC, D, E, F are midpoints of AB, BC, CA. If the area of △ABC is 48 cm², area of △DEF is
questions.why: The midpoints divide △ABC into four congruent triangles, so △DEF has area 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².

questions.q: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC, AB = 14 cm, DC = 8 cm. The segment joining midpoints of AD and BC has length
questions.why: The segment joining the midpoints of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium is half the sum of the parallel sides: ½(14 + 8) = 11 cm.

questions.q: Bisectors of the angles of a parallelogram enclose a
questions.why: The bisectors of adjacent angles of a parallelogram meet at 90°, since the adjacent angles add to 180°. All four corners are right angles, so the figure is a rectangle.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Circles
courses.summary: Chords and the angles they subtend, the perpendicular from the centre, equal chords and their distances, angles subtended by arcs, and cyclic quadrilaterals — with proofs.
outcomes: Use circle vocabulary precisely (chord, arc, segment, sector)
Prove that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre and its converse
Use the perpendicular-from-centre theorem with Pythagoras to find chord lengths
Use: angle at centre = twice angle at circumference; angles in the same segment are equal; angle in a semicircle = 90°
Use the opposite-angle property of cyclic quadrilaterals

scenes.text: Leela slips a bangle on and notices every point of its edge is the same distance from its centre.
She stretches two equal threads across it as chords — and finds they make equal angles at the centre.

steps.title: Vocabulary recap
steps.body:
- **Circle**: all points in a plane at a fixed distance (**radius**) from a fixed point (**centre**).
- **Chord**: segment joining two points of the circle; the longest chord is a **diameter** (= 2r).
- **Arc**: part of the circle; minor and major arcs. **Semicircle**: arc cut off by a diameter.
- **Segment**: region between a chord and an arc. **Sector**: region between two radii and an arc.
- Circles with the same radius are **congruent**.

steps.title: Theorem: equal chords ⇒ equal central angles
steps.body:
If AB = CD in a circle with centre O, then ∠AOB = ∠COD. Proof: △AOB, △COD have OA = OC, OB = OD (radii), AB = CD ⇒ SSS ⇒ ∠AOB = ∠COD.
**Converse**: if two chords subtend equal angles at the centre, the chords are equal (SAS).

steps.title: Solved: angle at centre
steps.body: A chord equal to the radius subtends an angle at the centre of **60°**: △OAB has OA = OB = AB (equilateral).

steps.title: Solved: using the converse
steps.body: ∠POQ = ∠ROS = 50° in a circle of radius 5 cm; PQ = 4.2 cm ⇒ **RS = 4.2 cm** (equal angles at centre ⇒ equal chords).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing segment (chord + arc) with sector (two radii + arc).
- Thinking a chord passes through the centre — only a diameter does.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Region between two radii and arc

quiz.q: The longest chord of a circle is the
quiz.why: The diameter passes through the centre, and is the longest chord. All other chords are shorter.

quiz.q: A chord equal to the radius subtends at the centre
quiz.why: A chord equal to the radius forms an equilateral triangle with the two radii. So it subtends 60° at the centre.

quiz.q: Equal chords of a circle subtend at the centre
quiz.why: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. This is a standard theorem.

quiz.q: A diameter divides a circle into two
quiz.why: A diameter divides the circle into two equal parts, called semicircles.

quiz.q: Two chords subtend 70° each at the centre. They are
quiz.why: Chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. This is the converse of the equal-chord theorem.

lessons.title: Perpendicular from the centre to a chord

scenes.text: A carpenter needs to find the centre of a round table-top with no mark.
She draws two chords and their perpendicular bisectors — they cross at the centre.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
1. The **perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord** (RHS on the two right triangles).
2. The **line from the centre through the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular** to it (SSS).
3. There is **one and only one circle** through three non-collinear points (its centre is where the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet).

steps.title: Solved: chord length
steps.body: Radius 13 cm, distance of chord from centre 5 cm. Half-chord = √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 ⇒ chord = **24 cm**.

steps.title: Solved: distance from centre
steps.body: Chord 16 cm in a circle of radius 10 cm. Half = 8; distance = √(100 − 64) = **6 cm**.

steps.title: Solved: two parallel chords
steps.body: Radius 5 cm, parallel chords AB = 6 cm and CD = 8 cm on opposite sides of the centre. Distances: √(25 − 9) = 4 and √(25 − 16) = 3 ⇒ gap = **7 cm**. (Same side: 4 − 3 = 1 cm.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full chord instead of half in Pythagoras.
- Forgetting that parallel chords may lie on the same side or opposite sides — check both cases.

activity.prompt: Radius 17 cm, chord at distance 8 cm from the centre. Length of chord?

quiz.q: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord
quiz.why: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. This is a key theorem.

quiz.q: Radius 5 cm, chord 8 cm. Distance from centre:
quiz.why: Half the chord is 4 cm, so the distance from the centre is √(5² − 4²) = √9 = 3 cm.

quiz.q: Through three non-collinear points, how many circles pass?
quiz.why: Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points. Its centre is where the perpendicular bisectors meet.

quiz.q: Through two points, how many circles pass?
quiz.why: Infinitely many circles can pass through two points, since their centres can lie anywhere on the perpendicular bisector.

quiz.q: Radius 10 cm, distance 6 cm. Chord length:
quiz.why: Half-chord = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8, so the chord is 2 × 8 = 16 cm.

scenes.text: On a giant wheel, every spoke-to-spoke bar of the same length sits at the same distance from the hub.
Equal chords, equal distances — the engineer relies on this symmetry.

steps.title: Theorem and converse
steps.body: **Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equidistant from the centre.** Conversely, **chords equidistant from the centre are equal.** Also: the nearer a chord is to the centre, the longer it is.

steps.title: Solved: equal chords that intersect
steps.body: Two equal chords AB and CD intersect at E. Draw OM ⟂ AB, ON ⟂ CD. OM = ON (equal chords). △OME ≅ △ONE (RHS, OE common) ⇒ EM = EN. Since AM = CN (halves of equal chords), **AE = CE and BE = DE** (corresponding segments are equal).

steps.title: Solved: comparing chords
steps.body: Chords at distances 3 cm and 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 7 cm: lengths 2√40 ≈ 12.6 cm and 2√24 ≈ 9.8 cm — the nearer one is longer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Measuring 'distance' along a slanted line — distance of a chord from the centre is always the **perpendicular** distance.

statements.s: Chords equidistant from the centre are equal
A chord nearer the centre is shorter
The diameter is at distance 0 from the centre
Equal chords of two different-size circles are equidistant from their centres

quiz.q: Two equal chords are 4 cm and x cm from the centre. x =
quiz.why: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, so the other distance is also 4 cm.

quiz.q: Distance of a chord from the centre is measured
options: along a radius to an endpoint
quiz.why: The distance of a chord from the centre is the perpendicular distance. Other distances will be longer.

quiz.q: Which chord is longest in a circle?
quiz.why: The closer a chord is to the centre, the longer it is. So the chord at 1 cm is the longest.

quiz.q: Chords AB and CD are equidistant from the centre and AB = 7 cm. CD =
quiz.why: Chords equidistant from the centre are equal, so CD = AB = 7 cm.

quiz.q: Radius 13, two equal chords each 24 cm. Their distance from the centre is
quiz.why: Half the chord is 12, so the distance from the centre is √(13² − 12²) = √25 = 5 cm.

scenes.text: From any seat on the circular stand, the goal posts (a chord) seem to subtend the same angle.
Ali discovers: angles in the same segment are equal — and the angle at the centre is twice as big.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
1. **The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double** the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle: ∠POQ = 2∠PAQ.
2. **Angles in the same segment are equal.**
3. **Angle in a semicircle is a right angle** (since the centre angle is 180°).
4. If a segment joining two points subtends equal angles at two other points on the same side, the four points are **concyclic**.

steps.title: Solved: centre angle
steps.body: ∠AOB = 100° at the centre. Angle at C on the major arc: ∠ACB = **50°**. At D on the minor arc: ∠ADB = ½(360° − 100°) = **130°**.

steps.title: Solved: angle in a semicircle
steps.body: AB is a diameter, C on the circle, ∠CAB = 35°. ∠ACB = 90° ⇒ ∠CBA = 180 − 90 − 35 = **55°**.

steps.title: Solved: same segment
steps.body: A, B, C, D on a circle; ∠BAC = 30° and ∠BDC is in the same segment ⇒ ∠BDC = **30°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Halving the wrong way: the CENTRE angle is the bigger one.
- Using the minor-arc rule for a point on the minor arc (use the reflex central angle).

activity.prompt: ∠AOB = 140° at the centre. Find the angle subtended at a point on the major arc.

quiz.why: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle, 90°. It is half of the 180° angle the diameter subtends at the centre.

quiz.q: Angle at centre = 80°; angle at circumference on the same arc =
quiz.why: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so the angle at the circumference is 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.

quiz.q: Angles in the same segment are
quiz.why: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. This is another standard theorem.
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so ∠AOB = 2 × 35° = 70°.
AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90°. In △ABC, ∠BAC = 180° − 90° − 40° = 50°.

story.title: Four friends on a round track

scenes.text: Four friends stand on a circular track and stretch ropes between them, making a quadrilateral.
Their coach says: opposite corners always add to 180°. They check with a protractor — it works!

steps.title: Theorem and converse
steps.body:
A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on a circle.
- **Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.** (∠A = ½ reflex-arc angle, ∠C = ½ other arc; the two central angles total 360°.)
- **Converse**: if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral sums to 180°, it is cyclic.
- Consequence: the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.

steps.title: Solved: find the angles
steps.body: ABCD is cyclic with ∠A = 3x + 5 and ∠C = 2x + 25. Opposite angles: 5x + 30 = 180 ⇒ x = 30 ⇒ ∠A = **95°**, ∠C = **85°**.

steps.title: Solved: ∠BCD from ∠DBC and ∠BAC
steps.body: ABCD cyclic, ∠DBC = 70° and ∠BAC = 30°. ∠BDC = ∠BAC = 30° (same segment). In △BCD: ∠BCD = 180 − 70 − 30 = **80°**.

steps.title: Solved: isosceles trapezium is cyclic
steps.body: In trapezium ABCD (AB ∥ DC) with AD = BC, base angles are equal: ∠A = ∠B. Co-interior: ∠A + ∠D = 180° ⇒ ∠B + ∠D = 180° ⇒ **cyclic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding adjacent angles instead of opposite ones.
- Assuming every parallelogram is cyclic — only a rectangle is (a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle).

statements.s: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary
Every rhombus is cyclic
statements.why: Only if it is a square.

statements.s: A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle
If ∠A + ∠C = 180° in ABCD, ABCD is cyclic

quiz.why: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°, so ∠C = 180° − 110° = 70°.
∠B and ∠D are opposite angles, so they add to 180°: 3∠D + ∠D = 4∠D = 180°, so ∠D = 45°.

quiz.q: Exterior angle at C of cyclic ABCD equals
quiz.why: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle. At C, it is equal to ∠A.
A rectangle has opposite angles of 90° + 90° = 180°, so it is always cyclic. A rhombus or general parallelogram is not.

quiz.q: Angles of cyclic ABCD: ∠A = 2x, ∠C = x. x =
quiz.why: Opposite angles add up to 180°: 2x + x = 180°, so x = 60°.

questions.q: A segment of a circle is bounded by
questions.why: A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc.

questions.q: Angle in a semicircle
questions.why: The angle in a semicircle is 90°, a right angle. It is not acute or obtuse.

questions.q: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to
questions.why: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so they add to 180°.

questions.q: Radius 5 cm, chord 6 cm. Distance from centre
questions.why: Half the chord is 3, so the distance from the centre is √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.

questions.q: ∠AOB = 120° at the centre. Angle on the major arc
questions.why: The angle at the circumference on the major arc is half the angle at the centre: 120° ÷ 2 = 60°.

questions.q: Equal chords are
questions.why: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre. This is the converse of the closeness theorem.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is 90°. Reason (R): The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The diameter subtends 180° at the centre, and the angle at the circumference is half of that, 90°.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every parallelogram is cyclic. Reason (R): Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false, since a parallelogram is cyclic only if it is a rectangle. The reason is true: opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, but that does not make them add to 180°.

questions.q: Chord of length 24 cm is 5 cm from the centre. Radius
questions.why: Half the chord is 12 and the distance is 5, so r = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 cm.

questions.q: ABCD cyclic, ∠ABC = 92°, ∠BAD = 75°. ∠BCD and ∠ADC are
questions.why: In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add to 180°. So ∠BCD = 180° − 75° = 105° and ∠ADC = 180° − 92° = 88°.

questions.q: ∠AOB = 100° at centre O. Angle at point C on the minor arc
questions.why: The angle on the minor arc is half the reflex angle at the centre: ½(360° − 100°) = 130°.

questions.q: Case: Two parallel chords of a circle of radius 13 cm are 10 cm and 24 cm long, on opposite sides of the centre. Distance between them
questions.why: The distance from the centre to the 10 cm chord is √(13² − 5²) = 12, and to the 24 cm chord is √(13² − 12²) = 5. They lie on opposite sides, so the distance between them is 12 + 5 = 17 cm.

questions.q: Same data as a circle of radius 13 with chords 10 and 24 on the SAME side: distance
questions.why: The distances from the centre are 12 and 5. On the same side the distance between the chords is 12 − 5 = 7 cm.

questions.q: A, B, C on a circle centre O; ∠OAB = 25°. ∠ACB (C on the major arc) =
questions.why: OA = OB, so ∠OBA = 25° and ∠AOB = 180° − 50° = 130°. The angle on the major arc is half: ∠ACB = 65°.

questions.q: ABCD cyclic; AB is a diameter and ∠ADC = 120°. ∠BAC =
questions.why: ABCD is cyclic, so ∠ABC = 180° − 120° = 60°. AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90°, and ∠BAC = 180° − 90° − 60° = 30°.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Heron's Formula
courses.summary: Area of any triangle from its three sides using Heron's formula, with special cases and real-life applications such as plots, signboards and quadrilaterals split into triangles.
outcomes: Compute the semi-perimeter and use Heron's formula
Find areas of scalene, isosceles and equilateral triangles from sides
Find a side or height given the area
Find areas of quadrilaterals by splitting along a diagonal
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; quadrilateral applications may be trimmed in rationalised editions

scenes.text: The municipality knows the three fence lengths of a triangular park: 40 m, 24 m, 32 m.
Nobody knows its height. Can its area still be found? Yes — Heron of Alexandria showed how.

steps.title: Area when the height is known
steps.body: Area = ½ × base × height. Right triangle with legs a, b: area = ½ab. Equilateral triangle of side a: height = (√3/2)a, area = **(√3/4)a²**.

steps.title: Heron's formula
steps.body:
For sides a, b, c, the **semi-perimeter** s = (a + b + c)/2 and
**Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]**.
Heron (Hero) of Alexandria (c. 10–75 CE) gave this result.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the perimeter instead of the semi-perimeter.
- Multiplying before factorising: factor numbers to pull out squares easily.

steps.title: Smart factorising
steps.body: Write each factor as primes: 48·8·24·16 = (2⁴·3)(2³)(2³·3)(2⁴) = 2¹⁴·3² ⇒ √ = 2⁷·3 = 384.

activity.prompt: Fill in for a triangle with sides 13, 14, 15

quiz.q: Semi-perimeter of a triangle with sides 7, 8, 9
quiz.why: The semi-perimeter is half the perimeter: (7 + 8 + 9) ÷ 2 = 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

quiz.q: Area of an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm
quiz.why: The area of an equilateral triangle is (√3/4)a². For a = 4, it is (√3/4) × 16 = 4√3 cm².
Heron's formula needs the lengths of the three sides. It does not need the height or any angle.

quiz.q: s − a for sides a = 10, b = 8, c = 6

scenes.text: A road sign is an equilateral triangle with side 'a' and perimeter 180 cm.
The painter needs its area to buy paint: a = 60 cm, area = 900√3 cm² ≈ 1558.8 cm².

steps.title: Solved: isosceles with given perimeter
steps.body: Perimeter 30 cm, equal sides 12 cm each ⇒ base 6. s = 15. Area = √(15 × 3 × 3 × 9) = √1215 = 9√15 ≈ **34.86 cm²**.

steps.title: Solved: height from area
steps.body: Triangle 13, 14, 15 has area 84. Height on side 14: ½ × 14 × h = 84 ⇒ **h = 12**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding too early — keep the square root exact until the last step.
- Forgetting units are square units (cm², m²).

activity.prompt: Equilateral triangle with perimeter 36 cm: area to 1 decimal (√3 ≈ 1.732)

quiz.q: If area is 24 cm² and base 8 cm, height
quiz.why: Area = ½ × base × height, so 24 = ½ × 8 × h, giving h = 6 cm.
The sides are 3x + 4x + 5x = 12x = 36, so x = 3 and the sides are 9, 12, 15. It's a right triangle, so area = ½ × 9 × 12 = 54.
The area of an equilateral triangle with side a is (√3/4)a². The other forms are not correct.

quiz.q: An isosceles right triangle with legs 6 cm has area
quiz.why: The legs are the base and height, so the area is ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 cm².

scenes.text: Kisan Raju's field is a quadrilateral. He knows its four sides and one diagonal.
The diagonal cuts it into two triangles — Heron's formula twice gives the whole area.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Split the quadrilateral by a diagonal into two triangles whose three sides are known, apply Heron's formula to each and add.

steps.title: Solved: rhombus floor
steps.body: Rhombus with side 5 m and one diagonal 8 m. Split into two triangles 5, 5, 8: each area 12 ⇒ **24 m²** (check: other diagonal 6, area = ½ × 8 × 6 = 24 ✔).

steps.title: Solved: cost
steps.body: A triangular wall-panel 15 m, 11 m, 6 m is rented for ads at ₹2000 per m² per year for 3 months. s = 16; area = √(16 × 1 × 5 × 10) = √800 = 20√2 m². Rent = 20√2 × 2000 × 3/12 = **₹10000√2** ≈ ₹14142.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a diagonal whose length you don't know.
- Forgetting to convert months/years when costs are per year.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the area of a quadrilateral field
items: Draw a diagonal splitting it into two triangles
Find the semi-perimeter of each triangle
Apply Heron's formula to each triangle
Write the answer with square units

quiz.q: To use Heron for a quadrilateral, you need
quiz.why: To find a quadrilateral's area with Heron's formula, you need four sides and a diagonal, which splits it into two triangles.

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 and 24. Its area
quiz.why: The area of a rhombus is ½ × product of the diagonals = ½ × 10 × 24 = 120.
The half-diagonals are 5 and 12, meeting at right angles, so the side = √(25 + 144) = 13.

quiz.q: Triangle 6, 8, 10 plus triangle 6, 8, 10 forming a rectangle: area
quiz.why: Two 6-8-10 right triangles put together along the hypotenuse form a rectangle of 6 × 8 = 48.

quiz.q: Cost to level a 120 m² field at ₹5 per m²
quiz.why: Cost = area × rate = 120 × 5 = ₹600.

scenes.text: For Makar Sankranti, Jaya builds a kite from two triangles of coloured paper.
She must know each triangle's area to buy enough paper without waste.

steps.title: Solved: kite made of two triangles
steps.body: A kite is made of two triangles with sides 20 cm, 20 cm, 24 cm sharing the 24 cm side. Each: s = 32; area = √(32 × 12 × 12 × 8) = √36864 = 192 ⇒ kite = **384 cm²**.

steps.title: Solved: umbrella cloth
steps.body: An umbrella has 10 identical triangular panels, each 20 cm, 50 cm, 50 cm. s = 60; area = √(60 × 40 × 10 × 10) = √240000 = 200√6 ≈ 489.9 cm². Ten panels ≈ **4899 cm²**.

steps.title: Solved: area in two ways
steps.body: Triangle 6, 8, 10: Heron s = 12: √(12·6·4·2) = √576 = 24. Right-triangle formula ½·6·8 = 24 ✔. Always cross-check when you can.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a side that doesn't belong to the triangle you are computing.
- Leaving answers like √576 unsimplified.

activity.prompt: Area of a triangle with sides 8 cm, 15 cm, 17 cm

quiz.why: 7, 24, 25 is a right triangle, as 7² + 24² = 25². So the area is ½ × 7 × 24 = 84.
The area of the 10-10-12 triangle is 48, so two such triangles have 2 × 48 = 96.
Heron of Alexandria lived in the 1st century CE. His formula is named after him.

questions.q: Semi-perimeter of a triangle 10, 12, 14
Heron's formula area =
questions.why: Heron's formula is area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)], where s is the semi-perimeter.

questions.q: Area of right triangle with legs 6 and 8
questions.why: A right triangle's area is ½ × 6 × 8 = 24.

questions.q: Area of triangle 13, 14, 15
Equilateral triangle side 6 cm: area
Isosceles triangle 5, 5, 6: area
Assertion (A): The area of a triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is 6. Reason (R): Heron's formula uses the full perimeter p: area = √[p(p−a)(p−b)(p−c)].
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is true: the 3-4-5 triangle has area ½ × 3 × 4 = 6. The reason is false, as Heron's formula uses the semi-perimeter s, not the full perimeter.

questions.q: Sides in ratio 3 : 4 : 5, perimeter 144 cm. Area
questions.why: The sides are in ratio 3 : 4 : 5 with sum 144, so they are 36, 48, 60. It is a right triangle, so the area is ½ × 36 × 48 = 864 cm².

questions.q: Area 84 cm² for the 13–14–15 triangle; altitude on side 13 is
questions.why: Area = ½ × base × height, so 84 = ½ × 13 × h, giving h = 168/13 cm.

questions.q: Rhombus with side 13 cm and one diagonal 24 cm. Area
questions.why: The half-diagonal is 12 and the side is 13, so the other half-diagonal is √(169 − 144) = 5, making the diagonal 10. Area = ½ × 24 × 10 = 120.

questions.q: Perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 32 cm; base 12 cm. Area
questions.why: The equal sides are (32 − 12) ÷ 2 = 10 each, so the sides are 10, 10, 12. s = 16, and area = √(16 × 6 × 6 × 4) = 48.

questions.q: Case: A triangular park 50 m, 120 m, 130 m is to be grassed at ₹4 per m². Cost
questions.why: 50² + 120² = 130², so it is a right triangle with area ½ × 50 × 120 = 3000 m². Cost = 3000 × 4 = ₹12000.

questions.q: Quadrilateral ABCD: AB = 3, BC = 4, CD = 4, DA = 5, AC = 5 (cm). Area
questions.why: △ABC has sides 3, 4, 5 (right-angled), area 6. △ACD has sides 5, 4, 5: s = 7, area = √(7 × 2 × 3 × 2) = √84 = 2√21. Total = 6 + 2√21 cm².

questions.q: An equilateral triangle has area 16√3 cm². Its perimeter
questions.why: (√3/4)a² = 16√3 gives a² = 64, so a = 8. The perimeter is 3 × 8 = 24 cm.

questions.q: Triangle with sides 25, 17, 12 cm: area

courses.title: Ch 11 · Surface Areas and Volumes
courses.summary: Surface areas and volumes of right circular cones, spheres and hemispheres (with a quick recap of cuboids and cylinders), with many real-life solved problems.
outcomes: Find slant height, curved and total surface area of a cone
Find surface areas of spheres and hemispheres
Find volumes of cones, spheres and hemispheres
Solve real-life problems on cost, capacity and melting/recasting
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; rationalised editions focus on cones, spheres and hemispheres

scenes.text: Before the monsoon, the society checks its cylindrical tank and a cuboid sump.
How much paint for the outside? How many litres inside? Two different questions: surface area and volume.

steps.title: Formulas you already know
steps.body:
- Cuboid l × b × h: TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), volume = lbh.
- Cube side a: TSA = 6a², volume = a³.
- Cylinder radius r, height h: CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h), volume = πr²h.
- 1 m³ = 1000 litres; 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

steps.title: Solved: painting a box
steps.body: Box 1.5 m × 1 m × 0.8 m, open at the top, painted inside: area = lb + 2(bh + hl) = 1.5 + 2(0.8 + 1.2) = **5.5 m²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up CSA (no ends) and TSA (with ends).
- Using diameter instead of radius.
- Forgetting 1 m³ = 1000 L.

activity.prompt: Match shape and volume

quiz.why: The curved surface area of a cylinder is 2πrh. The total surface area also includes the two circular ends.
1 m³ = 1000 litres, since 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ and 1 L = 1000 cm³.

quiz.q: Volume of a cube of side 5 cm
quiz.why: Volume of a cube = side³ = 5³ = 125 cm³.
TSA of a cube = 6 × side² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm².

quiz.q: Cylinder r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm, CSA (π = 22/7)

lessons.title: Surface area of a right circular cone

scenes.text: Nisha makes 20 conical party caps from chart paper.
Each cap is a cone with no base: she needs the curved surface area, πrl, for each.

steps.title: Cone formulas
steps.body:
A right circular cone has radius r, height h and **slant height l = √(r² + h²)**.
Cutting the curved surface open gives a sector of a circle of radius l whose arc = 2πr.
- **CSA = πrl**
- **TSA = πr(l + r)** (adds the base πr²).

steps.title: Solved: tent cloth
steps.body: A conical tent 10 m high with base radius 24 m: l = 26 m. Canvas = πrl = (22/7)(24)(26) = 13728/7 ≈ **1961.14 m²**. At ₹70 per m²: ≈ ₹137280.

steps.title: Solved: corn cob
steps.body: A corn cob shaped like a cone, r = 2.1 cm, l = 20 cm: CSA = (22/7)(2.1)(20) = **132 cm²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using h instead of l in πrl.
- Including the base for caps/tents (no base).
- Using diameter as radius.

activity.prompt: Cone with r = 6 cm and h = 8 cm. Slant height?

quiz.why: In a cone, the slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs r and h. So l = √(r² + h²).
The total surface area of a cone = curved surface πrl plus the base πr², so πr(l + r).
A joker's cap is an open cone, so only its curved surface area is needed, as it has no base.

lessons.title: Surface area of a sphere and hemisphere

scenes.text: Class 9B volunteers to repaint the school's large globe and a dome-shaped bird bath.
The globe is a sphere (4πr²); the dome is a hemisphere — curved part only, 2πr².

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Sphere**: SA = 4πr² (Archimedes showed it equals the CSA of the cylinder that just encloses it).
- **Hemisphere**: CSA = 2πr²; TSA = 3πr² (curved + flat circle).

steps.title: Solved: hemisphere bowl
steps.body: A hemispherical bowl of radius 21 cm (solid): TSA = 3π(21)² = 3 × 22/7 × 441 = **4158 cm²**. Painting only the inside: CSA = 2πr² = 2772 cm².

steps.title: Solved: balloon
steps.body: Radius increases from 7 cm to 14 cm. Ratio of surface areas = (7/14)² = **1 : 4**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 3πr² for an open bowl (should be 2πr²).
- Forgetting that SA scales with r² (double radius ⇒ 4 times area).

activity.prompt: Surface area of a sphere of radius 10.5 cm (π = 22/7)

quiz.why: The surface area of a sphere is 4πr². (4/3)πr³ is its volume.
A solid hemisphere has a curved surface 2πr² and a flat base πr², so TSA = 3πr².
SA is proportional to r². If r becomes 3r, SA becomes (3)² = 9 times.
Diameter 14 means r = 7, so SA = 4 × 22/7 × 49 = 616 cm².

quiz.q: Inner CSA of a hemispherical bowl r = 7 cm
quiz.why: The inner curved surface of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × 22/7 × 49 = 308 cm².

scenes.text: Ankit fills a cone with water and pours it into a cylinder of the same radius and height.
It takes exactly three cones to fill the cylinder — so a cone holds one-third.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: **Volume of a cone = ⅓πr²h**, one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

steps.title: Solved: heap of wheat
steps.body: A conical heap: diameter 10.5 m, height 3 m. r = 5.25. V = ⅓ × 22/7 × 5.25² × 3 = **86.625 m³**. Canvas to cover it: l = √(5.25² + 9) ≈ 6.05 m; CSA ≈ 22/7 × 5.25 × 6.05 ≈ 99.825 m².

steps.title: Solved: capacity in litres
steps.body: A conical pit, diameter 3.5 m, depth 12 m: V = ⅓ × 22/7 × 1.75² × 12 = 38.5 m³ = **38.5 kilolitres**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ⅓.
- Using slant height l in the volume formula (use vertical height h).

activity.prompt: Volume of a cone with r = 3 cm and h = 7 cm (π = 22/7)

quiz.why: The volume of a cone is ⅓πr²h, one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

quiz.q: Cylinder and cone with same r, h: volume ratio
quiz.why: The cylinder's volume is πr²h and the cone's is ⅓πr²h, so the ratio is 3 : 1.

quiz.q: Cone r = 7 cm, h = 3 cm: volume
If the height of a cone is doubled (r same), volume
quiz.why: Volume is proportional to h, so if h doubles, the volume doubles.

quiz.q: If the radius is doubled (h same), volume
quiz.why: Volume is proportional to r², so doubling r makes the volume 2² = 4 times.

lessons.title: Volume of a sphere and hemisphere

scenes.text: A metal workshop melts a solid sphere to make small ball-bearings.
The total volume stays the same — so the number of bearings is big volume ÷ small volume.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Sphere**: V = (4/3)πr³
- **Hemisphere**: V = (2/3)πr³
Volume scales with r³: double the radius ⇒ 8 times the volume.

steps.title: Solved: recasting
steps.body: A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into small spheres of radius 2 cm. Number = (6/2)³ = **27**.

steps.title: Solved: shot-putt mass
steps.body: A metal shot-putt of radius 4.9 cm, density 7.8 g/cm³: V = 4/3 × 22/7 × 4.9³ ≈ 493 cm³; mass ≈ 493 × 7.8 ≈ **3.85 kg**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r² instead of r³.
- In recasting, comparing surface areas instead of volumes.

activity.prompt: Volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm (π = 22/7)

quiz.why: The volume of a sphere is (4/3)πr³. 4πr² is its surface area.
A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is ½ × (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)πr³.
Volume is proportional to r³, so doubling r makes it 2³ = 8 times.

quiz.q: How many balls of radius 1 cm from a ball of radius 4 cm?
quiz.why: Volume ratio = (4/1)³ = 64, so 64 balls of radius 1 cm can be made.

quiz.q: Ratio of volumes of spheres with radii 2 : 3
quiz.why: Volumes of spheres are in the ratio of the cubes of their radii: 2³ : 3³ = 8 : 27.

questions.q: CSA of a cone
questions.why: The curved surface area of a cone is πrl, where l is the slant height. πr² is just the base area.

questions.q: Volume of a sphere radius r
questions.why: The volume of a sphere is (4/3)πr³. 4πr² is its surface area.

questions.q: TSA of a hemisphere
questions.why: A hemisphere has a curved surface of 2πr² and a flat base of πr², so its total surface area is 3πr².

questions.q: Cone r = 5, h = 12: slant height
Sphere r = 7 cm: SA (π = 22/7)
Cone r = 7, h = 24 (cm): volume
Assertion (A): A cone holds one-third as much as a cylinder of the same base and height. Reason (R): V(cone) = ⅓πr²h.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. V(cone) = ⅓πr²h, so it holds one-third of a cylinder's volume πr²h.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Doubling the radius of a sphere doubles its surface area. Reason (R): SA = 4πr².
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: SA = 4πr², so doubling r makes it 4 times, not 2. The reason is true.

questions.q: A conical tent with r = 7 m and l = 15 m needs canvas
questions.why: The canvas needed is the curved surface area πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 15 = 330 m².

questions.q: Volume of a hemisphere of radius 21 cm
Ratio of SA of two spheres is 9 : 25. Ratio of volumes
questions.why: Surface area ∝ r², so r₁ : r₂ = √9 : √25 = 3 : 5. Volume ∝ r³, so the volumes are in the ratio 27 : 125.

questions.q: Case: A sweet shop's laddoos are spheres of radius 2.1 cm. A tray of laddoo mix has volume 3880.8 cm³. Number of laddoos
questions.why: One laddoo's volume = (4/3) × 22/7 × 2.1³ = 38.808 cm³. So 3880.8 ÷ 38.808 = 100 laddoos.

questions.q: A solid cone of r = 3 cm, h = 4 cm. Its TSA (π = 3.14)
A metallic sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and recast into a cone of radius 3 cm. Height of cone
questions.why: The volume is unchanged: (4/3)π(27) = 36π = ⅓π(9)h = 3πh, so h = 12 cm.

questions.q: A hemispherical tank of inner radius 1.05 m is full of water. In litres it holds about
The radius of a cone is reduced to half and height doubled. Volume becomes
questions.why: Volume is proportional to r²h. With r halved and h doubled, it becomes (½)² × 2 = ½ of the original.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Statistics
courses.summary: Collecting and organising data, frequency distributions, bar graphs, histograms (equal and unequal widths), frequency polygons, plus mean, median and mode as useful extensions.
outcomes: Distinguish primary/secondary and raw/grouped data
Build ungrouped and grouped frequency distribution tables with class limits, marks and widths
Draw and read bar graphs, histograms (including unequal class widths) and frequency polygons
Compute mean, median and mode of ungrouped data (extension)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; mean/median/mode included as an extension

scenes.text: Meghna asks all 30 classmates how many hours they slept last night.
A list of 30 numbers is hard to read. A frequency table turns it into a clear picture.

steps.title: Words to know
steps.body:
- **Data**: facts or figures collected for a purpose. **Primary** data you collect yourself; **secondary** data comes from an existing source.
- **Raw data**: as collected, unorganised. **Range** = highest − lowest.
- **Frequency**: how many times a value occurs. A **frequency distribution table** lists values (or classes) with frequencies; **tally marks** help count.

steps.title: Grouped data
steps.body:
For many values, use **class intervals** like 0–10, 10–20, … (exclusive form: the upper limit is not included, so 10 goes in 10–20).
- Lower/upper **class limits**; **class size (width)** = upper − lower.
- **Class mark** = (lower + upper)/2.
- Inclusive form (0–9, 10–19, …) can be converted to exclusive by subtracting/adding 0.5 (−0.5–9.5, 9.5–19.5).

steps.title: Solved: class mark and size
steps.body: Class 25–35: class mark = 30, class size = 10. Class marks 47, 52, 57 ⇒ class size = **5**, so classes are 44.5–49.5, 49.5–54.5, 54.5–59.5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting a boundary value (like 20) in both classes 10–20 and 20–30.
- Total of frequencies not equal to the number of observations — always check.

activity.prompt: For the class 40–50
activity.text: class mark = ___ ; class size = ___ ; upper class limit = ___

quiz.why: Data collected by oneself is primary data. Data taken from existing sources is secondary data.

quiz.q: In exclusive classes 10–20 and 20–30, 20 goes into
quiz.why: In exclusive classes, the upper limit is not included, so 20 belongs to the class 20-30.
The class mark is the midpoint: (60 + 70) ÷ 2 = 65.
Range = highest − lowest = 15 − 2 = 13.
The class marks differ by 5, so the class size is 5.

scenes.text: The canteen wants to know which snack sells most each week.
A bar graph makes the answer jump out — the tallest bar wins.

steps.title: Bar graph
steps.body: A **bar graph** shows data with bars of **equal width** and **equal gaps**; the height (or length) is proportional to the value. Variables are often categories (months, subjects, snacks). Choose a scale, e.g. 1 cm = 10 students, and label both axes.

steps.title: Solved: reading
steps.body: Bars show students born in each month: July 8, Aug 6, Sep 4. Most births: **July**. Total for these months: 18.

steps.title: Solved: choosing a scale
steps.body: Values 150, 230, 410, 380. Scale 1 unit = 50 ⇒ heights 3, 4.6, 8.2, 7.6 units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Unequal bar widths or gaps.
- Starting the axis at a non-zero value without showing a break — it exaggerates differences.

statements.s: In a bar graph all bars have the same width
The gaps between bars must be equal
Bar heights depend on the scale chosen
Bar graphs can only show numbers, not categories

quiz.q: In a bar graph, the value is shown by
quiz.why: In a bar graph, the value is shown by the height (length) of the bar. All bars have the same width.

quiz.q: Scale 1 cm = 20 units; bar height 3.5 cm shows
quiz.why: The bar height 3.5 cm × 20 units per cm = 70 units.
Bar graphs are best for comparing categories, like subjects or cities. Histograms are used for continuous classes.

quiz.q: Which is wrong in a bar graph?
quiz.why: Bars in a bar graph must be of equal width, so unequal widths are wrong. Labelled axes and equal gaps are correct.

quiz.q: Bars: Maths 40, Science 30, English 20. Science is what fraction of the total?
quiz.why: The total is 40 + 30 + 20 = 90, so Science is 30/90 = 1/3.

scenes.text: Coach measures the heights of 40 players in classes 140–145, 145–150, …
He draws touching rectangles — a histogram — because height is continuous, with no gaps.

steps.title: Histogram
steps.body:
For **continuous grouped data**: class intervals on the x-axis, rectangles with **no gaps**. Width = class size; for **equal** widths height = frequency.
If the first class does not start at 0, show a **kink (zig-zag)** on the x-axis.

steps.title: Unequal class widths
steps.body: Area must be proportional to frequency. Choose a standard (usually the minimum) class size and plot **adjusted frequency = (minimum class size ÷ class size) × frequency**.

steps.title: Solved: reading a histogram
steps.body: Bars for weights 30–35: 8, 35–40: 12, 40–45: 5. Students 35 kg or more but under 45: 12 + 5 = **17**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving gaps between rectangles.
- Plotting raw frequencies when class widths differ (misleading areas).
- Forgetting the kink when the axis does not start at 0.

activity.prompt: Class 50–75 has frequency 15; the minimum class size is 5. Adjusted frequency (rectangle height)?

quiz.why: A histogram's rectangles stand side by side with no gaps, since the classes are continuous.

quiz.q: For unequal widths, what is proportional to frequency?
quiz.why: When class widths are unequal, the area of each rectangle (not the height) is proportional to the frequency. So heights must be adjusted.
The class width is 20 and the minimum is 10, so the adjusted height = (10/20) × 8 = 4.

quiz.q: A kink on the x-axis shows
quiz.why: A kink (zigzag) on the x-axis shows that the axis does not start at 0. It marks the skipped part.
Histograms are used for continuous grouped data, like marks in class intervals. Bar graphs are for categories.

scenes.text: Ms Kaur wants to compare marks of Section A and Section B on one graph.
Two histograms would overlap messily — two frequency polygons are clear.

steps.title: Frequency polygon
steps.body:
Join the **midpoints of the tops** of histogram rectangles with line segments. To close it, add an imagined class of frequency 0 before the first and after the last class, and join to their class marks on the x-axis.
Without a histogram: plot (class mark, frequency) and join. Area under the polygon = area of the histogram (equal widths).

steps.title: Solved: comparison
steps.body: Polygon for Section A peaks at class mark 65, Section B at 55 ⇒ Section A had more students in the higher range.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not closing the polygon at both ends.
- Plotting at class limits instead of class marks.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to draw a frequency polygon without a histogram
items: Add zero-frequency class marks before the first and after the last class
Join the points with straight segments

quiz.why: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining the midpoints of the tops of the histogram's rectangles.
Points of a frequency polygon are plotted at class marks, the midpoints of the classes.

quiz.q: For classes 10–20, 20–30, …, the extra point before the first is at x =
quiz.why: The extra class before 10-20 is 0-10, with class mark 5. It is used to close the polygon at the start.
Frequency polygons are good for comparing two distributions on one graph. A histogram would overlap.

quiz.q: A frequency polygon is closed using classes of frequency
quiz.why: The polygon is closed with classes of frequency 0, one before the first class and one after the last. This makes it meet the axis.

scenes.text: Cricketer scores: 12, 45, 8, 45, 90, 30, 45.
Is the typical score 39.3 (mean), 45 (median) or 45 (mode)? Each average tells a different story.

steps.title: Three averages
steps.body:
- **Mean** x̄ = sum ÷ number. For a frequency table x̄ = Σfx / Σf.
- **Median**: middle value after arranging in order. n odd → the ((n + 1)/2)th; n even → mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th.
- **Mode**: most frequent value.
(Grouped-data versions come in Class 10.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Finding the median without sorting.
- Dividing Σfx by the number of rows instead of Σf.
- An extreme value (90) pulls the mean; the median is more robust.

activity.prompt: Find the mean of 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42

quiz.why: Sort the data: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle (third) value is 5, so the median is 5.
The mode is the most frequent value. 5 occurs three times, 3 twice and 7 once, so the mode is 5.

quiz.q: Mean of first five natural numbers

quiz.why: With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values: (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25.

quiz.q: If each value is increased by 3, the mean
quiz.why: Adding 3 to every value raises the total by 3n, so the mean also rises by 3.

questions.q: Data collected by the investigator herself is
questions.why: Data collected by the investigator herself is primary data. Data taken from other sources is secondary.

questions.q: Class mark of 20–30
questions.why: The class mark of 20-30 is (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25.

questions.q: In a histogram the bars are
questions.why: In a histogram the bars are adjacent, with no gaps, since the classes are continuous.

questions.q: Class size of 15–25
questions.why: Class size = upper limit − lower limit = 25 − 15 = 10.
Range = highest − lowest = 40 − 3 = 37.

questions.q: A frequency polygon plots frequency against
questions.why: A frequency polygon plots frequency against the class marks. The points are then joined.

options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. When classes have unequal widths, the area of each rectangle should be proportional to frequency, so the heights must be adjusted.

options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is true, as bar graphs have equal gaps between bars. The reason is false, since bar graphs represent categories, not continuous classes.

questions.q: Case: The mean of 10 observations is 20. One value 30 was wrongly read as 50. Correct mean
questions.why: The wrong total = 10 × 20 = 200. Correct total = 200 − 50 + 30 = 180, so the correct mean = 180 ÷ 10 = 18.

Mean of 6 numbers is 8; one number is removed and the mean of the rest is 7. Removed number
questions.why: The total of the six numbers is 6 × 8 = 48. The remaining five total 5 × 7 = 35, so the removed number is 48 − 35 = 13.

questions.q: For data 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, which is true?
questions.why: The mean is 34 ÷ 8 = 4.25, the median is (4 + 5) ÷ 2 = 4.5, and the mode is 5. So mean < median < mode.

courses.title: Class 9 Maths · Revision & Practice

outcomes: Recall every key formula and theorem of Class 9 Mathematics

scenes.text: It is 9 pm and Aarav has one hour left for maths revision.
He uses a single formula sheet instead of flipping through twelve chapters.

steps.title: Number systems
steps.body:
- Rational ⇔ terminating or non-terminating recurring decimal.
- p/q (lowest terms) terminates ⇔ q = 2ᵐ5ⁿ.
- Recurring to fraction: multiply by 10ⁿ (n = repeating digits) and subtract.
- (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b; rationalise with the conjugate.
- a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m; aᵖa^q = a^(p+q); (aᵖ)^q = a^(pq); a^(−p) = 1/aᵖ.

steps.title: Polynomials
steps.body:
- Degree = highest power; zero polynomial has no degree.
- Zero of ax + b: −b/a.
- Factor theorem: p(a) = 0 ⇔ (x − a) is a factor.
- Split middle term: p + q = b, pq = ac.
- (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx
- (x ± y)³ = x³ ± y³ ± 3xy(x ± y)
- x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx); if x + y + z = 0, x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz.

steps.title: Coordinates & linear equations
steps.body:
- Quadrant signs: I (+,+), II (−,+), III (−,−), IV (+,−); on x-axis y = 0, on y-axis x = 0.
- ax + by + c = 0 (a, b not both 0) has infinitely many solutions; its graph is a straight line; x = a ∥ y-axis, y = b ∥ x-axis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- (a + b)² ≠ a² + b²; √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.
- Test (x + k) with p(−k).
- Always state the reason in proofs.

quiz.why: The identity is x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²). The plus sign in the middle term is for the difference of cubes.
4x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3/4. This is the zero.
(2, −5) has x positive and y negative, so it lies in the fourth quadrant, IV.
3x − y = 2 is a linear equation in two variables, which has infinitely many solutions. Each x gives one y.

scenes.text: Ira knows the answers but loses marks for missing reasons in proofs.
A list of named theorems lets her quote a reason for every line.

steps.title: Lines, angles & Euclid
steps.body:
- Linear pair = 180°; vertically opposite angles equal.
- Parallel lines + transversal: corresponding = , alternate = , co-interior sum 180° (and converses).
- Triangle angle sum 180°; exterior angle = sum of interior opposite angles.
- Euclid: 7 axioms, 5 postulates; Playfair's axiom ≡ 5th postulate.

steps.title: Triangles & quadrilaterals
steps.body:
- Congruence: SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS (not SSA, not AAA); CPCT.
- Angles opposite equal sides are equal, and conversely.
- Quadrilateral angle sum 360°. Parallelogram: opposite sides & angles equal, diagonals bisect each other, diagonal makes two congruent triangles. Tests: both pairs of opposite sides equal; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect; one pair equal & parallel.
- Mid-point theorem: segment joining midpoints is ∥ third side and half of it; converse bisects the third side.

steps.title: Circles
steps.body:
- Equal chords ⇔ equal central angles ⇔ equidistant from centre.
- Perpendicular from centre bisects the chord; one circle through three non-collinear points.
- Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference; angles in same segment equal; angle in semicircle 90°.
- Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum 180° (and converse); exterior angle = interior opposite angle.

steps.title: Quick drill
steps.body: 1) Angles 2x, 3x, 4x of a triangle → 40°, 60°, 80°. 2) Chord 8 cm, radius 5 cm → 3 cm from centre. 3) Cyclic ABCD, ∠A = 75° → ∠C = 105°. 4) Midpoint triangle of 10, 12, 14 → perimeter 18.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 'by figure' as a reason.
- Using alternate-angle equality without parallel lines.
- Assuming diagonals of any parallelogram are equal.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a congruence rule?
quiz.why: SSA is not a congruence rule, as it can give two different triangles. ASA, RHS and SSS are valid.

quiz.q: Exterior angle 130°, one interior opposite angle 60°; other
quiz.why: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. So the other angle is 130° − 60° = 70°.
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. They are equal only in a square.

quiz.q: Angle at centre 110°; at major-arc point
quiz.why: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre: 110° ÷ 2 = 55°.
A cyclic parallelogram has opposite angles that are equal and add to 180°, so each is 90°. So it is a rectangle.

steps.title: Heron's formula & areas
steps.body:
- s = (a + b + c)/2; Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
- Equilateral: (√3/4)a²; right triangle: ½ × legs.

steps.title: Surface areas & volumes
steps.body:
- Cone: l = √(r² + h²), CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l + r), V = ⅓πr²h.
- Sphere: SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³.
- Hemisphere: CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², V = (2/3)πr³.
- Cylinder: CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h), V = πr²h.
- 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 L = 1000 cm³.

steps.title: Statistics
steps.body:
- Class mark = (lower + upper)/2; class size = upper − lower.
- Histogram: no gaps; unequal widths → adjusted frequency = (min width ÷ width) × f.
- Frequency polygon: join (class mark, frequency); close with zero classes.
- Mean = Σfx/Σf; median = middle value; mode = most frequent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- l vs h in cones.
- 3πr² for an open bowl.
- Raw frequencies for unequal-width histograms.

steps.title: Passage

- **शीर्षकम्:** 'एकतायाः बलम्' / 'संहतिः कार्यसाधिका'।

scenes.text: जगत् + ईशः = जगदीशः
जगत् + नाथः = जगन्नाथः

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- **जश्त्व:** a hard consonant at the end before a vowel/soft consonant becomes soft: वाक् + ईशः = वागीशः, जगत् + ईशः = जगदीशः, अच् + अन्तः = अजन्तः
- **अनुनासिक:** before a nasal it becomes the nasal of its class: जगत् + नाथः = जगन्नाथः, वाक् + मयम् = वाङ्मयम्
- **श्चुत्व:** स्/त-वर्ग + श्/च-वर्ग → श्/च-वर्ग: सत् + चित् = सच्चित्, रामस् + शेते = रामश्शेते
- **ष्टुत्व:** स्/त-वर्ग + ष्/ट-वर्ग → ष्/ट-वर्ग: तत् + टीका = तट्टीका
- **मोऽनुस्वारः:** final म् before a consonant → ं: हरिम् + वन्दे = हरिं वन्दे

steps.title: Solved examples

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- **सत्व:** ः + च/छ → श्; ः + त/थ → स्: नमः + ते = नमस्ते, निः + चलः = निश्चलः
- **उत्व:** अः + soft consonant (or अ) → ओ: मनः + रथः = मनोरथः, यशः + दा = यशोदा, सः + अपि = सोऽपि
- **रुत्व:** इः/उः + soft sound → र्: निः + धनः = निर्धनः, निः + आशा = निराशा, दुः + जनः = दुर्जनः

courses.title: Ch 1 · Matter in Our Surroundings
courses.summary: What matter is made of, the particle nature of matter, the three states, changes of state with temperature and pressure, latent heat, and evaporation with its cooling effect.
outcomes: Describe the characteristics of particles of matter with evidence
Compare solids, liquids and gases
Explain melting, boiling, sublimation and deposition using particles and latent heat
Convert between Celsius and kelvin
Explain the factors affecting evaporation and why evaporation causes cooling

scenes.text: Asha stirs a spoon of salt into water. The salt disappears but the water tastes salty everywhere.
Where did the salt go? Into the spaces between water particles — matter is made of tiny particles.

steps.title: What is matter?
steps.body: Anything that has **mass** and occupies **space (volume)** is matter: air, water, wood, you. Ancient Indian thinkers grouped matter into five elements (*panch tatva*: air, earth, fire, sky, water); modern science classifies matter by **physical properties** (states) and **chemical nature** (elements, compounds, mixtures).

steps.title: Characteristics of particles
steps.body:
1. **Particles are very small** — a crystal of potassium permanganate can colour litres of water after repeated dilution.
2. **There are spaces between particles** — salt/sugar dissolve in water without raising its level much.
3. **Particles are continuously moving** — they have kinetic energy, which **rises with temperature**.
4. **Particles attract each other** — the force of attraction holds them together; it varies from substance to substance.

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.body: **Diffusion** is the intermixing of particles of two substances on their own. It is fastest in gases, slower in liquids, very slow in solids, and **faster at higher temperature**. Examples: smell of hot food reaches you from far; a drop of ink spreads in water; hot water dissolves tea colour faster.

steps.title: Solved: explain with particles
steps.body:
Q: Why does the smell of an incense stick spread through a room?
A: Gas particles of the fragrance move fast and randomly, and there are large spaces between air particles, so they **diffuse** quickly into the air.

steps.title: Solved: the dilution experiment
steps.body: 2–3 crystals of KMnO₄ in 100 mL water, then 10 mL into 90 mL clear water, repeated 5–8 times — the colour remains visible. One crystal must therefore contain **millions** of tiny particles that keep dividing among the water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking particles 'disappear' when something dissolves.
- Saying heat makes particles bigger — it makes them move **faster**.
- Saying diffusion needs stirring — it happens on its own.

statements.s: Air is matter
statements.why: It has mass and occupies space.

statements.s: Particles of matter are stationary in a solid
Diffusion is faster in hot water than cold
Light and heat are matter
statements.why: They are forms of energy, not matter.

statements.s: Sugar dissolving shows there are spaces between water particles

quiz.why: Heat is a form of energy and has no mass or volume, so it is not matter. Air and dust are matter, and the smell of perfume is made of gas particles.
In gases the particles are far apart and move fast, with weak attraction. So they mix (diffuse) fastest. Solids diffuse the slowest.

quiz.q: On heating, the kinetic energy of particles
quiz.why: Heating gives energy to the particles, so they move faster. This means their kinetic energy increases.

quiz.q: A drop of ink spreads in water due to
quiz.why: Ink particles spread among the water particles on their own, which is diffusion. It happens because particles are always moving.

quiz.q: The KMnO₄ dilution experiment shows that particles are
quiz.why: A tiny amount of KMnO₄ colours a large volume of water, even after repeated dilution. This shows that particles of matter are very small.

lessons.title: States of matter: solid, liquid and gas

scenes.text: A small cylinder of LPG cooks food for a whole month.
How does so much gas fit? Gases are highly compressible — their particles can be squeezed close together.

steps.title: Comparing the states
steps.body:
**Solids**: definite shape, distinct boundaries, fixed volume, negligible compressibility, rigid; particles closely packed, strongest attraction.
**Liquids**: no fixed shape (take the container's shape) but fixed volume; flow (fluid); low compressibility; particles move freely; diffusion of solids, liquids and gases into liquids is possible (aquatic life depends on dissolved oxygen).
**Gases**: no fixed shape or volume; highly compressible; particles move randomly at high speed and exert **pressure** on container walls by colliding with them.

steps.title: Tricky cases
steps.body:
- A **rubber band** changes shape under force but regains it — still a solid (it breaks under excessive force).
- **Sugar and salt** take the jar's shape but each crystal keeps its own shape — solids.
- A **sponge** is a solid with tiny holes containing air; pressing pushes air out.
- Ice floats on water — an exception (ice is less dense than water).

steps.title: Solved: arrange by force of attraction
steps.body: Water, sugar, oxygen → increasing attraction: **oxygen < water < sugar** (gas < liquid < solid).

steps.title: Solved: why gases exert pressure
steps.body: Gas particles move very fast in all directions and keep hitting the walls of the container. The force of these collisions per unit area is **gas pressure** — that is how a balloon stays inflated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a sponge or rubber band a liquid because it changes shape.
- Saying liquids have no fixed volume (they do; only shape changes).
- Saying gas particles have strong attraction.

activity.prompt: Sort the property to its state

items.text: Flows but cannot be compressed much

quiz.q: Which has the strongest interparticle attraction?
quiz.why: Iron is a solid, so its particles are packed tightly with the strongest attraction. Water is a liquid and oxygen and steam are gases, with weaker attraction.

quiz.q: LPG and CNG are stored compressed because gases are
quiz.why: Gas particles are far apart, so the gas can be squeezed into a small volume. This is why LPG and CNG are stored under pressure.
A sponge is a solid, as it keeps its shape. It can be compressed because it has tiny holes with air in them, but its material is solid.
Fish breathe the oxygen dissolved in water. Gases can dissolve in water, which is why aquatic animals can live in it.
Gas pressure is caused by the particles continually colliding with the walls of the container. It is not caused by weight or attraction.

lessons.title: Changing state: temperature, pressure and latent heat

scenes.text: Rohit heats ice and records the temperature every minute.
The thermometer stays at 0 °C while ice melts, even though the burner is on. Where is the heat going?

steps.title: Melting and boiling
steps.body:
- **Melting point**: the temperature at which a solid melts to a liquid at atmospheric pressure. For ice: **273.15 K (0 °C)**. It indicates the strength of attraction.
- **Boiling point**: the temperature at which a liquid starts boiling at atmospheric pressure. For water: **373 K (100 °C)**. Boiling is a **bulk** phenomenon (whole liquid).
- **Fusion** = melting.

steps.title: Latent heat
steps.body:
During a change of state the temperature stays constant: the heat supplied is used to **overcome the forces of attraction** between particles. This hidden heat is **latent heat**.
- **Latent heat of fusion**: heat needed to change 1 kg of solid into liquid at its melting point (atmospheric pressure).
- **Latent heat of vaporisation**: heat needed to change 1 kg of liquid into gas at its boiling point.
So steam at 100 °C has **more energy** than water at 100 °C — steam burns are more severe.

steps.title: Kelvin scale and sublimation
steps.body:
**T(K) = t(°C) + 273** (more precisely 273.15). SI unit of temperature is kelvin; 0 K = −273 °C.
**Sublimation**: solid → gas directly (camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride, iodine). **Deposition**: gas → solid directly.
**Pressure** also changes states: compressing and cooling a gas can liquefy it. Solid CO₂ (**dry ice**) changes directly to gas when pressure drops to 1 atm.

steps.title: Solved: which feels colder?
steps.body: Ice at 273 K feels colder than water at 273 K because ice absorbs extra heat (latent heat of fusion) from the hand while melting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying temperature rises during melting.
- Subtracting 273 when converting °C to K (you add).
- Saying boiling and evaporation are the same (boiling is bulk at a fixed point; evaporation is surface, at any temperature).

activity.prompt: Convert 47 °C to kelvin (use +273)

quiz.q: Melting point of ice in kelvin
quiz.why: Ice melts at 0 °C, which is 273.15 K, using K = °C + 273.15. 0 K is absolute zero and 373 K is the boiling point of water.

quiz.q: During boiling, the temperature of water
quiz.why: While water boils, the heat supplied is used as latent heat to change the state, so the temperature stays at 100 °C until all of it is steam.

quiz.q: Naphthalene balls disappear over time by
quiz.why: Naphthalene changes directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid, which is sublimation. That is why the balls shrink and vanish.

quiz.q: Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water because steam has
quiz.why: Steam at 100 °C holds extra energy, the latent heat of vaporisation, which is released when it condenses on the skin. So it burns more than water at the same temperature.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. It sublimes straight into gas without leaving liquid.

scenes.text: In summer, water in Nani's matka stays cool without a fridge.
Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates from the surface, taking heat from the pot.

steps.title: Evaporation
steps.body: Changing a liquid into vapour at **any temperature below its boiling point** is evaporation. Surface particles with enough kinetic energy break away. It is a **surface phenomenon**.

steps.title: Factors affecting the rate
steps.body:
- **Surface area ↑** → faster (clothes are spread out to dry).
- **Temperature ↑** → faster.
- **Humidity ↑** → slower (air already holds a lot of water vapour).
- **Wind speed ↑** → faster (vapour is carried away).

steps.title: Evaporation causes cooling
steps.body:
Particles that evaporate take energy (latent heat of vaporisation) from the remaining liquid and the surroundings, so the surroundings cool.
Examples: acetone/nail-polish remover feels cold on the palm; sweating cools the body; people sprinkle water on the roof on hot days; cotton clothes absorb sweat and expose it to air in summer.

steps.title: Solved: drying clothes
steps.body: Clothes dry faster on a sunny, windy day: high temperature and wind speed increase evaporation; low humidity helps too. On a humid rainy day they dry slowly.

steps.title: Solved: the cold glass
steps.body: Water droplets on the outside of a glass of ice water: water vapour in the air **condenses** on the cold surface — the reverse of evaporation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying evaporation happens only at 100 °C.
- Saying more humidity speeds drying.
- Thinking the droplets on a cold glass leak through it.

bands.text: Dry air — wet clothes dry very fast; sweat evaporates quickly and you feel cool.
Humid — clothes dry slowly; you feel sticky because sweat evaporates poorly.
Saturated air — evaporation nearly stops; fog and dew form easily.

quiz.why: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature. Boiling is the bulk phenomenon.
