High humidity means the air already has much water vapour, so less can evaporate. A higher temperature, wind and a larger surface speed up evaporation.

quiz.q: We wear cotton in summer because cotton
options: absorbs sweat and lets it evaporate
quiz.why: Cotton absorbs sweat and exposes it to the air so it can evaporate. Evaporation takes heat from the body and cools us.

quiz.q: Water drops on a cold glass come from
quiz.why: The water vapour in the air touches the cold glass and condenses into drops. The water does not come from inside the glass.

quiz.q: Acetone on the palm feels cold because
options: it evaporates taking heat from the hand
quiz.why: Acetone evaporates quickly, taking the heat it needs from the palm. This makes the hand feel cold.

questions.q: Matter is anything that has
questions.why: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Energy and colour are not matter.

questions.q: Kelvin = Celsius +
questions.why: To convert Celsius to kelvin, add 273 (more exactly 273.15). So K = °C + 273.

questions.q: Which shows sublimation?
questions.why: Camphor changes directly from solid to vapour, so it shows sublimation. Wax and ice melt, and salt does not sublime.

questions.q: Boiling point of water
questions.why: Water boils at 100 °C, which is 100 + 273 = 373 K.

questions.q: Rate of diffusion increases with
questions.why: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they mix faster. So the rate of diffusion increases with temperature.

questions.q: Which is the most compressible?
questions.why: Air is a gas, and its particles are far apart, so it is the most compressible. Iron and wood are solids, and water is a liquid.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Temperature remains constant while ice melts. Reason (R): Heat supplied is used to overcome the attraction between particles.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. During melting, the heat supplied goes into overcoming the attraction between particles, not into raising temperature (latent heat of fusion).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Evaporation causes cooling. Reason (R): Particles that evaporate absorb energy from the surroundings.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The particles that evaporate take their energy from the surroundings, which lowers the temperature, so evaporation causes cooling.

questions.q: Convert 470 K to °C
Arrange in increasing interparticle attraction: water, sugar, oxygen
questions.why: Oxygen is a gas with the weakest attraction, water is a liquid with a medium attraction and sugar is a solid with the strongest. So the order is oxygen, water, sugar.

questions.q: Physical state of water (at 1 atm) at 25 °C, 250 °C and −10 °C respectively
questions.why: Water is liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C, gas above 100 °C and solid below 0 °C. So 25 °C is liquid, 250 °C is gas and −10 °C is solid.

questions.q: Case: On a humid day in Mumbai, clothes take longer to dry than on a dry windy day in Jaipur at the same temperature. The main reason is
questions.why: On a humid day the air already holds a lot of water vapour, so evaporation from the clothes is slower. This is why they dry slowly in Mumbai.

questions.q: Steam at 100 °C vs water at 100 °C: per kg, steam has extra energy equal to
questions.why: Steam has extra energy equal to the latent heat of vaporisation, which water at the same temperature lacks. This is the energy absorbed when water turns to steam.

questions.q: A gas can be liquefied most easily by
questions.why: Lowering the temperature slows the particles and raising the pressure pushes them together. Together these make a gas turn into a liquid.

questions.q: Case: A matka cools water best in
options: a closed room with high humidity
questions.why: A matka cools water best in hot, dry, windy weather, as water seeping through the pores evaporates fast and takes heat away. In humid air, evaporation is slow.

questions.q: Why does a desert cooler cool better on a hot dry day than a humid day?
options: Dry air allows faster evaporation of water from the pads
The fan works faster in dry air
Water is colder on dry days
questions.why: In dry air, water evaporates faster from the cooler pads and takes more heat from the air. In humid air, evaporation is slow, so cooling is poor.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Is Matter Around Us Pure?
courses.summary: Pure substances vs mixtures, solutions and concentration, suspensions and colloids (Tyndall effect), physical and chemical changes, elements and compounds, and how mixtures are separated.
outcomes: Define a pure substance and classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous
Calculate concentration of a solution (mass by mass, mass by volume percent)
Compare true solutions, suspensions and colloids, including the Tyndall effect
Distinguish physical and chemical changes and compounds from mixtures
Choose a separation method for a given mixture
courses.note: separation techniques may be trimmed in rationalised editions; kept as an extension

scenes.text: The milk packet says 'pure'. Riya's chemistry teacher says milk is actually a mixture.
To a scientist, 'pure' means made of only one kind of particle — milk has water, fats, proteins and more.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A **pure substance** has particles of only one kind and a fixed composition: elements (e.g. gold, oxygen) and compounds (e.g. water, salt).
- A **mixture** has two or more substances **not chemically combined**, in any proportion. Each component keeps its own properties and can be separated by **physical methods**.

steps.title: Types of mixture
steps.body:
- **Homogeneous**: uniform composition throughout, no visible boundaries (salt in water, sugar in water, air, brass).
- **Heterogeneous**: non-uniform, visible separate parts (sand + iron filings, oil + water, sulphur + iron filings).

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body: Soda water — homogeneous mixture. Wood — heterogeneous. Air — homogeneous mixture of gases. Distilled water — pure substance (compound). Soil — heterogeneous mixture.

steps.title: Solved: same solute, different colour
steps.body: Two solutions of copper sulphate of different concentrations are both homogeneous but have different shades — mixtures have **variable composition**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every homogeneous thing 'pure' (salt water is homogeneous but a mixture).
- Calling air a compound.

activity.prompt: Pure substance or mixture?

quiz.why: A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle, so it has a fixed composition. Mixtures have more than one kind of particle.
Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases, with a uniform composition throughout. It is not a compound or an element.
Soil has visibly different parts like sand, clay and humus, so it is heterogeneous. Brass, vinegar and salt solution are uniform throughout.

quiz.q: Components of a mixture can be separated by
quiz.why: The components of a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated by simple physical methods such as filtration or distillation. Chemical methods are needed only for compounds.

quiz.q: Milk, by the scientist's definition, is
quiz.why: Milk is made of water, fat, proteins and other substances, so it is a mixture, not a pure substance. In everyday talk 'pure' means unadulterated.

scenes.text: Two friends make lemonade: one adds 20 g sugar to 200 mL water, the other 40 g.
Both are solutions, but one is twice as concentrated. Chemists measure this precisely.

steps.title: Solutions
steps.body: A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The component in larger amount is the **solvent**; the dissolved one is the **solute**. Examples: sugar in water (solid in liquid), tincture of iodine (iodine in alcohol), soda water (CO₂ gas in water), air (gases in gases), alloys like brass (zinc in copper) — solid solutions.

steps.title: Properties of a true solution
steps.body:
- Homogeneous; particles smaller than 1 nm — not visible even under a microscope.
- Do not scatter light (path of light not visible).
- Solute does not settle and cannot be separated by filtration.
- **Saturated** solution: no more solute can dissolve at that temperature; **solubility** = amount in a saturated solution; solubility of most solids rises with temperature. Unsaturated: can dissolve more.

steps.title: Concentration formulas
steps.body:
- **Mass by mass %** = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
- **Mass by volume %** = (mass of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100
- Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.

steps.title: Solved: mass percent
steps.body: 40 g common salt in 320 g water. Solution = 360 g. Concentration = 40/360 × 100 = **11.1%**.

steps.title: Solved: required solute
steps.body: To make 500 g of a 5% (mass by mass) glucose solution: solute = 5/100 × 500 = **25 g** glucose in 475 g water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by the mass of the solvent instead of the solution.
- Thinking alloys are compounds (they are mixtures — solid solutions).

activity.prompt: 10 g sugar dissolved in 90 g water. Mass percent of sugar?

quiz.q: In tincture of iodine, the solvent is
quiz.why: Tincture of iodine is a solution of iodine in alcohol, so alcohol is the solvent and iodine is the solute.

options: cannot dissolve more at that temperature
quiz.why: A saturated solution holds as much solute as it can at that temperature. It cannot dissolve any more.
Brass is a uniform mixture of copper and zinc, a solid solution called an alloy. It is not a compound, as its composition is variable.

quiz.q: 20 g salt in 180 g water: mass %
Particle size in a true solution
quiz.why: The particles of a true solution are smaller than 1 nm, which is too small to be seen or to scatter light.

quiz.q: Solubility of most solids in water on heating
quiz.why: For most solids, solubility in water increases as the temperature rises. More solute can dissolve on heating.

lessons.title: Suspensions, colloids and the Tyndall effect

scenes.text: Walking through a misty forest, Kunal sees bright beams of sunlight between the trees.
Tiny water droplets in the mist scatter light — the Tyndall effect of a colloid.

steps.title: Suspension
steps.body: A **heterogeneous** mixture where solid particles are spread through a liquid without dissolving and are **visible** to the naked eye (e.g. chalk in water, muddy water). Particles scatter light; they **settle** on standing and can be **filtered**. Unstable.

steps.title: Colloid
steps.body:
Particles are intermediate in size (about 1–1000 nm), spread uniformly so the mixture *looks* homogeneous but is actually **heterogeneous**. Particles cannot be seen with the naked eye, do not settle, cannot be filtered with ordinary filter paper, but **scatter light** — the **Tyndall effect**. Separated by **centrifugation**.
Components: **dispersed phase** (the particles) and **dispersion medium**.

steps.title: Common colloids
steps.body:
- Aerosol (liquid in gas): fog, clouds, mist; (solid in gas): smoke, automobile exhaust.
- Foam (gas in liquid): shaving cream; (gas in solid): foam rubber, sponge, pumice.
- Emulsion (liquid in liquid): milk, face cream.
- Gel (liquid in solid): jelly, cheese, butter.
- Sol (solid in liquid): milk of magnesia, mud; solid sol (solid in solid): coloured gemstone, milky glass.

steps.title: Solved: identify the type
steps.body: Milk: emulsion (fat droplets in water). Smoke: aerosol (solid in gas). Shaving cream: foam (gas in liquid). Butter: gel. Fog: aerosol (liquid in gas).

steps.title: Solved: the torch test
steps.body: Shine a torch through (a) salt solution — no visible path; (b) milk-water — path visible (colloid); (c) chalk-water — path visible, and particles settle later (suspension).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling milk a solution.
- Thinking colloids settle on standing.
- Mixing up dispersed phase and dispersion medium.

activity.prompt: Match the colloid to its type

quiz.why: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by particles in a colloid or suspension, making the path visible.
Milk is a colloid, so its particles are large enough to scatter light and show the Tyndall effect. True solutions like salt or sugar solution do not.
The particles of a suspension are large, so they settle when left standing. They are visible and do not pass through filter paper.
Colloid particles pass through filter paper, so filtration does not work. Centrifugation spins them out, as in separating cream from milk.

quiz.q: In fog, the dispersion medium is
quiz.why: In fog, tiny water droplets are spread in air, so the air (gas) is the dispersion medium and water is the dispersed phase.

lessons.title: Physical and chemical changes; elements and compounds

scenes.text: Ravi mixes iron filings with sulphur powder; a magnet pulls the iron out easily.
He heats another sample strongly — now the magnet does nothing. A new substance, iron sulphide, has formed.

steps.title: Physical vs chemical change
steps.body:
- **Physical change**: no new substance; usually reversible; e.g. melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting wood, boiling water. Physical properties: colour, hardness, melting/boiling point, density.
- **Chemical change**: a new substance with new properties forms; e.g. burning candle wax (the burning part), rusting, cooking food, digestion, curdling of milk. Chemical properties are seen in such changes (e.g. flammability).

steps.title: Elements
steps.body:
**Element**: basic form of matter that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions (Antoine Laurent Lavoisier's definition).
- **Metals**: lustre, conduct heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, sonorous (gold, iron, copper; mercury is a liquid metal).
- **Non-metals**: various colours, poor conductors, not lustrous/sonorous/malleable (oxygen, carbon, sulphur; bromine is a liquid non-metal).
- **Metalloids**: intermediate (boron, silicon, germanium).
About 118 elements are known; most are solids at room temperature, 11 are gases, 2 are liquids (mercury, bromine), while gallium and caesium melt just above room temperature.

steps.title: Compounds vs mixtures
steps.body:
**Compound**: two or more elements **chemically combined in a fixed proportion**; properties differ from those of the constituents; components separated only by chemical/electrochemical means; energy usually changes during formation.
Iron + sulphur **mixture**: magnet separates iron; with dilute acid gives H₂.
Iron sulphide **compound** (FeS): not magnetic; with dilute acid gives **hydrogen sulphide** (rotten-egg smell).

steps.title: Solved: classify the changes
steps.body: Growth of a plant — chemical. Rusting of iron — chemical. Mixing iron filings and sand — physical. Cooking food — chemical. Freezing water — physical. Burning paper — chemical.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a candle burning is only a physical change (melting wax is physical; burning wax is chemical — both happen).
- Saying compounds have the properties of their elements (sodium is a reactive metal, chlorine a poisonous gas, yet NaCl is table salt).

activity.prompt: Physical or chemical change?

quiz.why: Rusting forms a new substance, iron oxide, so it is a chemical change. Melting wax, breaking glass and dissolving salt are physical changes.

quiz.q: Elements were defined as substances that cannot be broken down chemically by
quiz.why: Antoine Lavoisier was the first scientist to define an element as a basic substance that cannot be broken down into simpler ones by chemical reactions.

quiz.q: A liquid non-metal at room temperature is
quiz.why: Bromine is the non-metal that is liquid at room temperature. Mercury is a liquid, but it is a metal.

quiz.q: Iron sulphide reacting with dilute acid gives
quiz.why: Iron sulphide reacts with dilute acid to give hydrogen sulphide gas, which smells like rotten eggs. This differs from the properties of the iron and sulphur mixture.
A compound has a fixed composition, with elements combined in a definite ratio by mass. It does not depend on the method of preparation.
Silicon has properties of both metals and non-metals, so it is a metalloid. Other metalloids are boron and germanium.

lessons.title: Separating the components of a mixture (extension)

scenes.text: Seema accidentally pours sand into the salt jar.
She dissolves the mix in water, filters out the sand, and evaporates the water to get her salt back.

steps.title: Choosing the method
steps.body:
- **Evaporation**: volatile solvent from non-volatile solute (salt from sea water, dye from ink).
- **Centrifugation**: spin to separate fine suspended particles (cream from milk; blood tests; washing-machine spin dryer).
- **Separating funnel**: immiscible liquids (oil and water; kerosene and water).
- **Sublimation**: a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable one (ammonium chloride/camphor/naphthalene from salt).
- **Chromatography**: components that dissolve in the same solvent but travel at different speeds (colours in ink, pigments, drugs in blood).
- **Distillation**: miscible liquids with large difference in boiling points (> 25 K) or a solvent from solution; **fractional distillation** when the difference is < 25 K (petroleum, gases of air).
- **Crystallisation**: pure solid crystals from solution (better than evaporation — impurities remain in solution; alum, copper sulphate, salt purification).
- Others: filtration, magnet, sieving, decantation.

steps.title: Solved: air separation
steps.body: Air is compressed and cooled to liquid, then warmed slowly in a fractionating column: **nitrogen** (b.p. −196 °C) boils off first, then **argon** (−186 °C), then **oxygen** (−183 °C).

steps.title: Solved: pick a method
steps.body: Butter from curd → centrifugation (churning). Camphor from salt → sublimation. Acetone (b.p. 329 K) from water (373 K) → distillation (difference 44 K). Pigments from a leaf extract → chromatography. Iron pins from sand → magnet.

steps.title: Solved: drinking water at a city plant
steps.body: River water → sedimentation tank → loading tank (alum, to help fine particles settle) → filtration tank → chlorination tank → water tank → houses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using evaporation when the solid decomposes or impurities must be removed — use crystallisation.
- Using simple distillation for close boiling points.

activity.prompt: Match the mixture to the separation method

quiz.q: Two miscible liquids with boiling points 20 K apart are separated by
quiz.why: For miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K, simple distillation is not enough. Fractional distillation is used.

quiz.q: Crystallisation is better than evaporation because
quiz.why: In crystallisation, soluble impurities stay in the solution while pure crystals form. Evaporation to dryness leaves the impurities with the solid.

quiz.q: Which gas boils off first from liquid air?
quiz.why: Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point of the gases in liquid air (−196 °C), so it boils off first.

options: move at different speeds with the solvent
quiz.why: In chromatography, the components of a mixture move at different speeds with the solvent, so they separate.

quiz.q: Kerosene and water are separated with
quiz.why: Kerosene and water do not mix, so they form two layers. A separating funnel lets us run off the lower layer.

questions.q: Which is a pure substance?
questions.why: Distilled water contains only water, so it is a pure substance. Brass, air and sea water are mixtures.

questions.q: Milk is an example of
questions.why: Milk is an emulsion, a colloid of liquid droplets (fat) in a liquid (water). It is neither a true solution nor an element.

questions.q: Rusting of iron is a
questions.why: Rusting makes a new substance, iron oxide, so it is a chemical change. It cannot be reversed by simple means.

questions.q: Mercury is a
questions.why: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. It is not a non-metal or a metalloid.

questions.q: Which shows the Tyndall effect?
questions.why: A starch solution is a colloid, so its particles scatter light and show the Tyndall effect. Sugar, vinegar and salt solutions are true solutions.

questions.q: Mass % of 25 g solute in 100 g solution
Assertion (A): A solution of salt in water does not scatter light. Reason (R): Particles of a true solution are smaller than 1 nm.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The particles of a true solution are smaller than 1 nm, so they cannot scatter light.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Brass is a compound. Reason (R): Brass contains zinc and copper in variable proportions.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: brass is an alloy, a mixture. The reason is true, as zinc and copper are in variable proportions, which shows it is not a compound.

questions.q: Concentration of 50 g sugar in 450 g water
Iron + sulphur heated forms FeS. Which property of FeS is correct?
options: can be separated by a magnet
questions.why: Iron sulphide, a compound, gives hydrogen sulphide when treated with dilute acid. It is not attracted by a magnet and has a fixed composition.

questions.q: Smoke is an example of a colloid with dispersed phase and medium
questions.why: In smoke, tiny solid particles are scattered in air, so the dispersed phase is a solid and the medium is a gas.

questions.q: Case: A student shines a laser through four beakers: A (salt water), B (milk + water), C (chalk + water, freshly stirred), D (copper sulphate). Beam visible in
questions.why: A laser beam is visible in milk (colloid) and chalk water (suspension), as their particles scatter light. In salt water and copper sulphate solution, it passes unseen.

questions.q: How much salt is needed to make 250 mL of a 4% (mass by volume) solution?
questions.why: A 4% mass by volume solution has 4 g in 100 mL. For 250 mL: 4/100 × 250 = 10 g.

questions.q: Case: Liquid air is warmed in a column. Boiling points: N₂ −196 °C, Ar −186 °C, O₂ −183 °C. The order in which they are collected as gases
questions.why: On warming, the gas with the lowest boiling point boils off first. So N₂ (−196 °C) comes first, then Ar (−186 °C), then O₂ (−183 °C).

questions.q: Which pair would you separate by fractional distillation?
questions.why: Fractional distillation is used for miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K. Ethanol (351 K) and water (373 K) differ by 22 K.

questions.q: A solution has 30% (mass by mass) sugar. Mass of water in 200 g of it
questions.why: Sugar in 200 g = 30% of 200 = 60 g. So the water = 200 − 60 = 140 g.

questions.q: Which statement about a colloid is FALSE?
questions.why: The statement that colloid particles settle quickly is false, as colloids are stable and their particles do not settle on standing. They are heterogeneous, show the Tyndall effect and pass through filter paper.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Atoms and Molecules
courses.summary: Laws of chemical combination, Dalton's atomic theory, symbols and atomic mass, molecules and ions, writing chemical formulae with valency, and calculating molecular and formula unit masses.
outcomes: State and apply the law of conservation of mass and the law of constant proportions
List the postulates of Dalton's atomic theory
Use symbols and atomic mass units correctly
Write formulae of compounds using valencies and polyatomic ions
Calculate molecular mass and formula unit mass
courses.note: mole concept may be trimmed in rationalised editions

lessons.title: Laws of chemical combination and Dalton's theory

scenes.text: Kavi burns a candle on a balance; the reading drops. 'Mass is destroyed!' he says.
His teacher repeats it in a sealed jar: the mass stays the same. The gases simply escaped in the open.

steps.title: Law of conservation of mass
steps.body:
**Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.** (Antoine L. Lavoisier.) Total mass of reactants = total mass of products, when nothing escapes.
Activity: mix copper sulphate solution and sodium carbonate solution in a closed flask (or barium chloride and sodium sulphate) — the mass before and after is the same.

steps.title: Law of constant (definite) proportions
steps.body: **In a chemical substance the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.** (Joseph L. Proust.) Water always has hydrogen : oxygen = **1 : 8** by mass, whatever its source; ammonia has N : H = 14 : 3.

steps.title: Dalton's atomic theory (John Dalton)
steps.body:
1. All matter is made of very tiny particles called **atoms**.
2. Atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
3. Atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties.
4. Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.
5. Atoms combine in ratios of small whole numbers to form compounds.
6. The relative number and kinds of atoms in a given compound are constant.
(Postulate 2 explains conservation of mass; postulate 6 explains constant proportions. Later discoveries showed atoms *can* be divided into subatomic particles.)

steps.title: Solved: conservation of mass
steps.body: 5.3 g sodium carbonate reacts with 6 g ethanoic acid giving 2.2 g CO₂, 0.9 g water and sodium ethanoate. Mass of sodium ethanoate = (5.3 + 6) − (2.2 + 0.9) = **8.2 g**.

steps.title: Solved: constant proportions
steps.body: Hydrogen and oxygen combine in 1 : 8 by mass. Oxygen needed for 3 g hydrogen = 3 × 8 = **24 g**.

steps.title: Solved: carbon dioxide
steps.body: If 3 g carbon burns in 8 g oxygen to give 11 g CO₂, then 3 g carbon in 50 g oxygen still gives only **11 g CO₂** (42 g oxygen left unused) — fixed proportions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting gases produced or used when checking mass.
- Thinking constant proportions means equal masses (it means a fixed ratio).

activity.prompt: Hydrogen : oxygen in water is 1 : 8 by mass. How many grams of water form from 2 g hydrogen?

quiz.q: Law of conservation of mass was given by
quiz.why: Antoine Lavoisier gave the law of conservation of mass, that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

quiz.q: In water, H : O by mass is
quiz.why: Water is always H₂O: 2 g of hydrogen combine with 16 g of oxygen, so the mass ratio H : O = 2 : 16 = 1 : 8.

quiz.q: Which Dalton postulate explains conservation of mass?
options: Atoms of an element are identical
Atoms combine in small whole numbers
Atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed
quiz.why: Dalton said atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a reaction. This explains why the total mass stays the same.

quiz.q: Law of constant proportions was given by
quiz.why: Joseph Proust gave the law of constant proportions: a compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio.

quiz.q: 12 g carbon + 32 g oxygen → CO₂ of mass
quiz.why: By conservation of mass, the product has the total mass of the reactants: 12 + 32 = 44 g.

quiz.q: Which Dalton postulate is no longer fully correct?
quiz.why: Dalton thought atoms were indivisible, but we now know that they contain electrons, protons and neutrons. The other postulates still largely hold.

scenes.text: If you lined up hydrogen atoms side by side, about 10 crore of them would fit across 1 cm.
Yet everything — mountains, rivers, you — is built from these bricks.

steps.title: How big is an atom?
steps.body: Atomic radius is measured in **nanometres** (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m). Hydrogen atom radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m. Modern techniques (e.g. scanning tunnelling microscopes) can image surfaces atom by atom.

steps.title: Symbols
steps.body: Dalton used circles with marks; **Berzelius** suggested letters. Today **IUPAC** approves names and symbols. A symbol is the first letter (capital) or first + another letter (second small): H, O, N, C, Al, Co, Cl, Ca. Some come from Latin: **Na** (natrium, sodium), **K** (kalium, potassium), **Fe** (ferrum, iron), **Cu** (cuprum, copper), **Ag** (argentum, silver), **Au** (aurum, gold), Hg (mercury), Pb (lead).

steps.title: Atomic mass
steps.body: The **atomic mass unit (u)** is exactly **1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12**. Relative atomic mass compares an atom's average mass with this. Common values: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.

steps.title: Solved: writing symbols
steps.body: Cobalt → **Co** (not CO, which is carbon monoxide!). Chlorine → Cl. Calcium → Ca. Potassium → K. Silver → Ag.

steps.title: Solved: how many times heavier
steps.body: A magnesium atom (24 u) is 24/12 = **2 times** as heavy as a carbon-12 atom, and 24/1 = 24 times a hydrogen atom.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the second letter of a symbol as a capital (CL ✗, Cl ✓).
- Confusing Co (cobalt) with CO (carbon monoxide).

activity.prompt: Match the element with its symbol

quiz.q: 1 u is defined as 1/12 the mass of
quiz.why: One atomic mass unit (u) is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The symbol for potassium is K, from its Latin name kalium. P is phosphorus.
Atoms are extremely small, so their radius is measured in nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m).
The atomic mass of sulphur is 32 u. 16 u is oxygen and 35.5 u chlorine.

quiz.q: Who suggested using letters for symbols?
quiz.why: Berzelius suggested using one or two letters of an element's name as its symbol. This was later adopted by IUPAC.

story.title: Oxygen you breathe, ozone that protects

scenes.text: The air you breathe contains O₂; high above, the ozone layer contains O₃.
Same element, different numbers of atoms per molecule — very different substances.

steps.title: Molecules
steps.body:
A **molecule** is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently and shows all its properties. It is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded.
- Molecules of elements: same type of atoms (O₂, N₂, O₃, P₄, S₈). Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) exist as single atoms.
- Molecules of compounds: different atoms in a fixed ratio (H₂O, NH₃, CO₂).
- **Atomicity**: number of atoms in a molecule — monoatomic (Ar), diatomic (O₂, H₂, Cl₂), triatomic (O₃), tetra-atomic (P₄), polyatomic (S₈).

steps.title: Ions
steps.body: Charged species are **ions**: **cations** (positive, e.g. Na⁺, Mg²⁺) and **anions** (negative, e.g. Cl⁻, O²⁻). Compounds of metals with non-metals are usually ionic, e.g. NaCl contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not molecules. A group of atoms carrying a charge is a **polyatomic ion**: NH₄⁺ (ammonium), OH⁻ (hydroxide), NO₃⁻ (nitrate), HCO₃⁻ (hydrogen carbonate), CO₃²⁻ (carbonate), SO₃²⁻ (sulphite), SO₄²⁻ (sulphate), PO₄³⁻ (phosphate).

steps.title: Solved: atomicity
steps.body: H₂SO₄: 2 + 1 + 4 = **7 atoms**. P₄: 4. Ar: 1. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (sucrose): 45.

steps.title: Solved: ratio by mass
steps.body: In NH₃, N : H by mass = 14 : 3. In CO₂, C : O = 12 : 32 = 3 : 8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling NaCl a molecule (it is a formula unit of ions).
- Forgetting that polyatomic ions stay together as one unit.

activity.prompt: Classify by atomicity

quiz.why: Atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule. Ozone is O₃, so its atomicity is 3.

quiz.q: A positively charged ion is a
quiz.why: A positively charged ion, formed by losing electrons, is a cation. An anion is negative.
The sulphate ion is SO₄²⁻. SO₃²⁻ is sulphite and S²⁻ is sulphide.
Noble gases like helium and neon are very stable and exist as single atoms (monatomic).
H₂SO₄ has 2 H + 1 S + 4 O = 7 atoms.
The ammonium ion is NH₄⁺, a positive ion. NO₃⁻ is nitrate.

scenes.text: Ms Iyer explains valency as 'hands' an atom offers for combining.
Aluminium has 3 hands, oxygen 2 — cross them and you get Al₂O₃.

steps.title: Valency and the criss-cross method
steps.body:
**Valency** is the combining capacity of an atom or ion. Rules:
1. Valencies (charges) must balance.
2. In a metal–non-metal compound, write the metal first (NaCl, CaO).
3. For a polyatomic ion, put it in **brackets** if more than one is needed: Ca(OH)₂, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Method: write symbols with valencies below, **criss-cross** the numbers, and simplify the ratio.

steps.title: Common valencies
steps.body:
1: H, Na, K, Ag, Cl, Br, NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻
2: Mg, Ca, Zn, Cu(II), Fe(II), O, S, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, SO₃²⁻
3: Al, Fe(III), N, PO₄³⁻
4: C

steps.title: Solved: formulae
steps.body:
Aluminium oxide: Al(3), O(2) → **Al₂O₃**.
Magnesium chloride: Mg(2), Cl(1) → **MgCl₂**.
Calcium oxide: Ca(2), O(2) → Ca₂O₂ → simplify **CaO**.
Calcium hydroxide: Ca(2), OH(1) → **Ca(OH)₂**.
Ammonium sulphate: NH₄(1), SO₄(2) → **(NH₄)₂SO₄**.
Sodium carbonate: Na(1), CO₃(2) → **Na₂CO₃**.
Aluminium sulphate: Al(3), SO₄(2) → **Al₂(SO₄)₃**.

steps.title: Solved: name from formula
steps.body: K₂SO₄ potassium sulphate; CaCO₃ calcium carbonate; NH₄Cl ammonium chloride; Al₂(SO₄)₃ aluminium sulphate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing CaOH₂ instead of Ca(OH)₂ (that would mean 2 hydrogens only).
- Not simplifying (Mg₂O₂ → MgO).
- Using the brackets when only one polyatomic ion is present (NaOH, not Na(OH)).

activity.prompt: Match compound to formula

quiz.why: Calcium has valency 2 and chlorine 1, so crossing over gives CaCl₂.
Magnesium has valency 2 and oxygen 2, so they combine 1 : 1, giving MgO.
Aluminium has 3 valence electrons that it loses, so its valency is 3.
Sodium has valency 1 and the nitrate ion NO₃⁻ has valency 1, so the formula is NaNO₃.
Aluminium has valency 3 and chlorine has valency 1, so cross-multiplying gives AlCl₃.
CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate, as it has calcium and the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻. Calcium oxide is CaO.

lessons.title: Molecular mass and formula unit mass

scenes.text: Pharmacist Anil needs to know how heavy one 'unit' of a medicine molecule is compared with others.
He simply adds the atomic masses of all atoms in the formula.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Molecular mass**: sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule (in u).
- **Formula unit mass**: same idea for ionic compounds (whose constituent particles are ions), e.g. NaCl.
Atomic masses: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Zn 65.

steps.title: Looking ahead
steps.body: The **mole** (6.022 × 10²³ particles) links these masses to grams; it is studied in Class 11 (and in some editions/boards at this stage).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting subscripts outside brackets: Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = 74 u, not 57.
- Using 35 instead of 35.5 for chlorine.

activity.prompt: Molecular mass of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)

quiz.why: Molecular mass of NH₃ = 14 + 3(1) = 17 u.
Formula unit mass of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 u.
Molecular mass of C₂H₆ = 2(12) + 6(1) = 30 u.
Molecular mass of O₂ = 2 × 16 = 32 u.

quiz.q: Formula unit mass is used for
quiz.why: Formula unit mass is used for ionic compounds, which do not form discrete molecules. Covalent compounds have a molecular mass.

questions.q: The law of conservation of mass says mass is
questions.why: The law of conservation of mass says mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of reactants equals that of products.

questions.q: Symbol of iron
questions.why: The symbol of iron is Fe, from the Latin ferrum. Ir is iridium.

questions.q: Atomicity of phosphorus (P₄)
questions.why: Atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule. P₄ has 4 atoms.

questions.q: Valency of carbon
questions.why: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, so its valency is 4. It can form four bonds.

questions.q: Molecular mass of H₂O
questions.why: Molecular mass of H₂O = 2(1) + 16 = 18 u.

questions.q: Formula of aluminium oxide
questions.why: Aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2, so crossing over gives Al₂O₃.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Water from any source has H : O = 1 : 8 by mass. Reason (R): Law of constant proportions.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. By the law of constant proportions, water from any source always has H : O = 1 : 8 by mass.

questions.q: Assertion (A): NaCl exists as molecules. Reason (R): NaCl is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: NaCl is made of a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not separate molecules. The reason is true, and it is why we use the formula unit.

questions.q: Formula unit mass of K₂CO₃ (K = 39)
Formula of ammonium phosphate
questions.why: NH₄⁺ has valency 1 and PO₄³⁻ has valency 3, so three ammonium ions are needed: (NH₄)₃PO₄.

questions.q: Molecular mass of HNO₃
Case: In an experiment 6.3 g of reactants in a sealed flask gave products. Some CO₂ formed. The sealed flask's total mass after the reaction is
questions.why: In a sealed flask nothing can escape, so by the law of conservation of mass the total mass stays 6.3 g.

questions.q: Carbon and oxygen combine in a 3 : 8 mass ratio in CO₂. Oxygen needed to react fully with 9 g carbon
questions.why: In CO₂, C : O = 3 : 8 by mass. For 9 g of carbon, oxygen = 9 × 8/3 = 24 g.

questions.q: Formula unit mass of Al₂(SO₄)₃ (Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16)
A compound has formula X₂O₃ and molecular mass 160 u (O = 16). Atomic mass of X
Which ratio of atoms is consistent with Dalton's postulate 5?
questions.why: Dalton's fifth postulate says atoms combine in small whole-number ratios. 2 : 3 is such a ratio, while 0.5 : 1.25, 1 : 1.5 and 1 : π are not.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Structure of the Atom
courses.summary: Discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons; Thomson's, Rutherford's and Bohr's models; distribution of electrons in shells; valency; atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars.
outcomes: Describe the discovery and properties of electrons, protons and neutrons
Compare the Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models and their limitations
Write electronic configurations of the first 20 elements using the 2n² rule
Find valency from electronic configuration
Use atomic number and mass number; define isotopes and isobars with uses

scenes.text: Neel runs a dry comb through his hair; it picks up bits of paper.
Rubbing transfers tiny charged particles. Atoms must contain charges after all — they are not indivisible.

steps.title: Subatomic particles
steps.body:
- **Electron** (e⁻): negative charge (−1), mass about 1/2000 of a hydrogen atom (negligible). Identified by **J.J. Thomson** (1897) using cathode rays.
- **Proton** (p⁺): positive charge (+1), mass ≈ 1 u. **E. Goldstein** (1886) discovered **canal rays** (positively charged radiations) in a gas discharge, which led to the proton.
- **Neutron** (n): no charge, mass ≈ 1 u. Discovered by **J. Chadwick (1932)**. Present in all atoms except ordinary hydrogen (protium).

steps.title: Solved: net charge
steps.body: An atom with 11 protons and 11 electrons has net charge 0. If it loses one electron it becomes Na⁺ (charge +1).

steps.title: Solved: mass of an atom
steps.body: Since electrons have negligible mass, mass of an atom ≈ (number of protons + number of neutrons) × 1 u. Carbon with 6 p and 6 n ≈ 12 u.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying neutrons are positively charged.
- Thinking electrons contribute much to atomic mass.
- Attributing protons to Thomson (he worked with electrons).

activity.prompt: Match the particle with its discoverer and charge

quiz.why: A neutron has no charge, so its charge is 0. It is found in the nucleus along with protons.
Canal rays discovered by Goldstein are positively charged. They are made of positive ions.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. The electron was found in 1897.
The electron's mass is about 1/1837 of a proton's, so it is almost negligible. Protons and neutrons are much heavier.
Protium, the common isotope of hydrogen, has 1 proton and no neutron. Deuterium has one neutron.

lessons.title: Models of the atom: Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr

scenes.text: Rutherford's team fired fast alpha particles at gold foil about 1000 atoms thick.
Most passed straight through, a few bounced back. 'It was as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back and hit you!'

steps.title: Thomson's model (plum pudding / watermelon)
steps.body: The atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon. Positive and negative charges are equal, so the atom is neutral. It could not explain Rutherford's results.

steps.title: Rutherford's α-scattering experiment (1911)
steps.body:
Observations → conclusions:
- **Most α-particles passed straight through** → most of the atom is **empty space**.
- **Some were deflected by small angles** → positive charge occupies very little space.
- **Very few (about 1 in 12000) bounced back** → all positive charge and most mass are in a tiny **nucleus** at the centre.
The nucleus radius is about 10⁵ times smaller than the atom's.
**Model**: positive nucleus; electrons revolve around it in circular paths.
**Drawback**: a revolving charged particle should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus — the atom would be unstable. But atoms are stable.

steps.title: Bohr's model
steps.body: Neils Bohr: electrons revolve only in certain special **discrete orbits** (energy levels) and **do not radiate energy** while in them. Orbits/shells are named **K, L, M, N…** or numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4…

steps.title: Solved: interpret an observation
steps.body: If an α-particle bounces straight back, it must have hit something small, heavy and positively charged — the nucleus.

steps.title: Solved: what would change with lighter foil?
steps.body: If the gold foil were replaced by a foil of a lighter element of the same thickness, there would be **fewer large deflections**, since the nuclei are less massive and carry less positive charge — but most particles would still pass through.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Rutherford's model was stable.
- Saying the nucleus is large.
- Mixing up which model had electrons 'embedded' (Thomson).

activity.prompt: Order the history of atomic models
items: Thomson: electrons in a sphere of positive charge
Rutherford: tiny nucleus with revolving electrons
Bohr: electrons in fixed energy shells

quiz.q: Most α-particles passing straight through shows that
options: most of the atom is empty space
quiz.why: Most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil, which showed that most of the atom is empty space.

quiz.q: Thomson's model is compared to a
quiz.why: Thomson's model resembles a watermelon (plum pudding): electrons embedded in a positive sphere. A solar system is Rutherford's model.

quiz.q: The drawback of Rutherford's model is
options: it cannot explain stability of the atom
quiz.why: Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom, as a revolving electron would radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.

quiz.q: In Bohr's model electrons in discrete orbits
quiz.why: In Bohr's model, electrons in discrete orbits do not radiate energy, which keeps the atom stable.
Rutherford bombarded gold foil with α-particles, which are helium nuclei. They are fast and positively charged.
The K shell is the first shell, closest to the nucleus, with n = 1.

scenes.text: The innermost ring of a stadium holds 2 seats, the next 8, and so on.
Electrons fill shells the same way — inner ones first, each with a maximum capacity.

steps.title: Bohr–Bury rules
steps.body:
1. Maximum electrons in a shell = **2n²**: K (n = 1) 2, L 8, M 18, N 32.
2. The **outermost** shell can hold at most **8** electrons.
3. Shells fill step-wise: a shell is occupied only after the inner shells are filled (true for the first 18 elements).

steps.title: Valency
Solved: sulphur
steps.body: Z = 16 → **2, 8, 6**. Valence electrons 6 → valency 8 − 6 = **2**.

steps.title: Solved: identify the element
steps.body: Configuration 2, 8, 3 → Z = 13 → **aluminium**, valency 3. An element with 2, 8, 8 is argon, valency 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing K as 2, 8, 9 (outer shell cannot exceed 8; it is 2, 8, 8, 1).
- Taking valency of oxygen as 6 (it is 8 − 6 = 2).

activity.prompt: Electronic configurations

quiz.q: Maximum electrons in the M shell
quiz.why: The maximum electrons in a shell is 2n². For the M shell (n = 3), it is 2 × 9 = 18.
Sodium has 11 electrons, arranged 2, 8, 1. The first shell takes 2, the second 8, and 1 remains.
Nitrogen has configuration 2, 5, so it needs 3 more electrons to complete 8. So its valency is 8 − 5 = 3.
Magnesium has configuration 2, 8, 2 and loses its 2 outer electrons, so its valency is 2.
The configuration 2, 8, 8 has 18 electrons, which is argon (Z = 18). Neon is 2, 8.
Silicon (Z = 14) has configuration 2, 8, 4, so it has 4 valence electrons.

lessons.title: Atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars

scenes.text: Two chlorine atoms behave identically in reactions, yet one is heavier.
They have the same protons but different neutrons — isotopes.

steps.title: Atomic and mass numbers
steps.body:
- **Atomic number Z** = number of protons (defines the element; equals electrons in a neutral atom).
- **Mass number A** = protons + neutrons (**nucleons**).
- Neutrons = A − Z. Notation: mass number on top-left, atomic number bottom-left, e.g. ¹⁴₇N has 7 p, 7 n, 7 e.

steps.title: Isotopes
steps.body:
Atoms of the **same element** (same Z) with **different mass numbers**. Same chemical properties, different physical properties. Examples: hydrogen ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium, D), ³H (tritium, T); carbon ¹²C and ¹⁴C; chlorine ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
**Average atomic mass** accounts for natural abundance: Cl = 35 × 0.75 + 37 × 0.25 = **35.5 u**.
Uses: **uranium-235** as nuclear-reactor fuel; **cobalt-60** in cancer treatment; **iodine-131** in the treatment of goitre.

steps.title: Isobars
steps.body: Atoms of **different elements** with the **same mass number** but different atomic numbers: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca and ⁴⁰₁₈Ar.

steps.title: Solved: particles
steps.body:
³⁹₁₉K: protons 19, electrons 19, neutrons 39 − 19 = **20**.
²⁷₁₃Al³⁺: protons 13, neutrons 14, electrons 13 − 3 = **10**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying isotopes have different chemical properties.
- Confusing isotopes (same Z) with isobars (same A).
- Taking mass number as neutrons only.

activity.prompt: Chlorine: ³⁵Cl 75% and ³⁷Cl 25%. Average atomic mass?

quiz.q: Atomic number is the number of
quiz.why: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so they have the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers.
⁴⁰Ca and ⁴⁰Ar have the same mass number (40) but different atomic numbers, so they are isobars.
Cobalt-60 is a radioactive isotope that gives gamma rays used in cancer treatment. Iodine-131 is used for thyroid problems, and uranium-235 is a nuclear fuel.
Deuterium is an isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton and 1 neutron. Protium has no neutron and tritium has two.

questions.q: Electron was identified by
questions.why: J.J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897. Chadwick found the neutron and Rutherford the nucleus.

questions.q: The nucleus contains
questions.why: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Electrons move around the nucleus.

questions.q: Maximum electrons in the L shell
questions.why: The maximum electrons in the L shell is 2n² = 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.q: Mass number =
questions.why: Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons, also called nucleons.

questions.q: Configuration of chlorine
questions.why: Chlorine has 17 electrons: 2, 8, 7. The configurations 2, 8, 8 belongs to argon.

questions.q: Valency of fluorine (2, 7)
questions.why: Fluorine (2, 7) needs 1 more electron to complete its octet, so its valency is 1.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Very few α-particles bounce back from gold foil. Reason (R): The positive charge and mass of an atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Only a few α-particles hit the tiny, dense, positive nucleus and bounce back, as most of the atom is empty space.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties. Reason (R): Isotopes have the same electronic configuration.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Chemical properties depend on the electronic configuration, which is the same for all isotopes of an element.

questions.q: Number of electrons in Mg²⁺ (Z = 12)
questions.why: Mg has 12 electrons. Mg²⁺ has lost 2, so it has 10 electrons.

questions.q: An atom has 2, 8, 6 electrons. It is
questions.why: An atom with 2, 8, 6 has 16 electrons, so Z = 16, which is sulphur. Oxygen is 2, 6.

questions.q: Neutrons in ³¹₁₅P
questions.why: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 31 − 15 = 16.

questions.q: Case: An element Z has 3 shells with 3 electrons in the outermost shell. Its atomic number and valency
questions.why: An element with 3 shells and 3 outer electrons has configuration 2, 8, 3, which is 13 electrons, atomic number 13. Its valency is 3.

questions.q: Case: Element Y has isotopes ⁷⁹Y (50%) and ⁸¹Y (50%). Its average atomic mass
questions.why: With equal amounts of ⁷⁹Y and ⁸¹Y, the average is (79 + 81) ÷ 2 = 80 u.

questions.q: Which pair are isobars?
questions.why: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. ⁴⁰Ca and ⁴⁰Ar fit, while the other pairs are isotopes.

questions.q: The main drawback of Rutherford's model that Bohr addressed was
options: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus
questions.why: Correct answer: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.

questions.q: An element has average atomic mass 10.8 u with isotopes ¹⁰X and ¹¹X. Percentage of ¹⁰X
Which is the correct electronic configuration of potassium (Z = 19) and why?
options: 2, 8, 8, 1 — outermost shell cannot have more than 8
questions.why: Potassium (Z = 19) is 2, 8, 8, 1, as the outermost shell can hold no more than 8 electrons. So the 19th electron goes into a new shell.

courses.title: Ch 5 · The Fundamental Unit of Life
courses.summary: Discovery of the cell and cell theory, the plasma membrane and transport (diffusion, osmosis, endocytosis), cell wall, nucleus, prokaryotes vs eukaryotes, the cell organelles, and cell division.
outcomes: Trace the discovery of cells and state the cell theory
Explain diffusion, osmosis and the effect of hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and plant and animal cells
Describe the structure and function of each organelle
Distinguish mitosis and meiosis

lessons.title: Discovery of the cell and the cell theory

scenes.text: In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his self-made microscope.
He saw tiny compartments like a honeycomb and called them 'cells' — Latin for 'little rooms'.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body:
- **1665 Robert Hooke**: cells in cork (actually dead cell walls).
- **1674 Leeuwenhoek**: first saw free-living cells in pond water with improved lenses.
- **1831 Robert Brown**: discovered the nucleus.
- **1839 Purkinje**: coined 'protoplasm'.
- **1838–39 Schleiden and Schwann**: **cell theory** — all plants and animals are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life.
- **1855 Virchow**: all cells arise from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula e cellula*).
- **1940 electron microscope**: revealed fine structure of organelles.

steps.title: Unicellular and multicellular
steps.body:
- **Unicellular**: a single cell does everything (Amoeba, Chlamydomonas, Paramecium, bacteria).
- **Multicellular**: many cells with **division of labour** (fungi, plants, animals). Cells vary in shape and size according to function: nerve cells long and branched; red blood cells disc-shaped; Amoeba changes shape.

steps.title: Solved: onion peel activity
steps.body: Peel the thin skin from an onion's inner layer, place in water on a slide, add a drop of **safranin** (or iodine/methylene blue), cover with a coverslip and observe: brick-like cells with a clear boundary (cell wall), a dark nucleus and cytoplasm.

steps.title: Solved: why is the cell called the structural and functional unit?
steps.body: Structural — every living thing is built of cells. Functional — every activity of life (nutrition, respiration, excretion, reproduction) happens in cells, each organelle doing its job.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Hooke saw living cells (cork cells are dead).
- Saying the cell theory was given by Hooke.
- Saying Virchow discovered the nucleus (Robert Brown did).

activity.prompt: Order the discoveries

events.text: Purkinje coins 'protoplasm'; Schwann completes cell theory
Virchow: all cells arise from pre-existing cells

quiz.q: Cells were first observed in cork by
quiz.why: Robert Hooke first saw cells in a thin slice of cork in 1665. He used a primitive microscope.
Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in the cell in 1831.

quiz.q: 'All cells arise from pre-existing cells' was stated by
quiz.why: Rudolf Virchow stated that all cells arise from pre-existing cells, which extended the cell theory.
Amoeba is a single-celled organism, so it is unicellular. A fish, mango tree and mushroom are multicellular.

quiz.q: The term protoplasm was coined by
quiz.why: Purkinje coined the term protoplasm in 1839 for the fluid substance of the cell.

scenes.text: Dadi soaks dry raisins in water overnight; by morning they are plump.
Grapes kept in thick sugar syrup shrink instead. Water moves across membranes — osmosis.

steps.title: Plasma membrane
steps.body: The outermost covering of a cell, separating it from its surroundings. It is **selectively permeable** — allows some substances in and out and prevents others. It is flexible and made of **lipids and proteins** (seen only under the electron microscope). Flexibility lets cells engulf food: **endocytosis** (e.g. Amoeba).

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.body: Movement of a substance from a region of **high concentration to low concentration** — CO₂ (waste) diffuses out of the cell; O₂ diffuses in. Gases exchange this way.

steps.title: Osmosis
steps.body:
Movement of **water** through a **selectively permeable membrane** from a region of **higher water concentration** (dilute solution) to **lower water concentration** (concentrated solution).
- **Hypotonic** outside solution (more dilute): water enters → cell **swells** (may burst in animal cells).
- **Isotonic**: no net movement → cell size unchanged.
- **Hypertonic** outside (more concentrated): water leaves → cell **shrinks**.
Unicellular freshwater organisms and plant root cells take in water by osmosis.

steps.title: Solved: the egg experiment
steps.body: Remove the shell of an egg with dilute HCl (the membrane remains). In pure water it **swells** (hypotonic outside). In concentrated salt solution it **shrinks** (hypertonic outside).

steps.title: Solved: potato osmometer
steps.body: A hollow potato cup with sugar solution placed in water: water moves **into** the cup by osmosis, so the level rises. A boiled potato does not work — its cells are dead and the membranes no longer function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying osmosis moves solute (it moves water).
- Mixing up hypotonic and hypertonic: 'hyper' outside = more solute outside ⇒ cell loses water.

activity.prompt: What happens to an animal cell in each solution?

quiz.why: The plasma membrane is selectively permeable, which lets some substances through but not others. It is not fully permeable.

options: water across a selectively permeable membrane
quiz.why: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of high water concentration to a lower one.

quiz.q: A cell in a hypertonic solution will
quiz.why: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the cell, so the cell shrinks. In a hypotonic solution it swells.
CO₂ is produced in the cell and moves out along its concentration gradient by diffusion. It does not need energy.
Amoeba engulfs food with its flexible membrane, a process called endocytosis. It does not need a mouth.
Dry raisins placed in water absorb it by osmosis and swell. The water enters the cells.

lessons.title: Cell wall, nucleus and the two kinds of cells

scenes.text: Plants are watered daily, yet their cells don't burst like an egg in pure water.
A tough cell wall pushes back — a feature animal cells do not have.

steps.title: Cell wall
steps.body:
Plant cells have a rigid **cell wall** outside the plasma membrane, made mainly of **cellulose**; fungi and bacteria also have walls. It gives strength and lets plant cells survive in hypotonic surroundings without bursting.
**Plasmolysis**: in a hypertonic solution, the living plant cell loses water, and its contents shrink away from the cell wall (seen in Rhoeo leaf peel in salt solution). Dead cells do not plasmolyse.

steps.title: Nucleus
steps.body: A double-layered **nuclear membrane** with pores encloses the nucleus. It contains **chromosomes** (visible as rod-shaped structures only during cell division), made of **DNA** and protein. DNA carries information for making and organising cells; functional segments of DNA are **genes**. When not dividing, the material is a tangled network called **chromatin**. The nucleus controls the cell's activities and plays a central role in reproduction.

steps.title: Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes
steps.body:
- **Prokaryotes** (bacteria): no nuclear membrane — the poorly defined nuclear region is the **nucleoid**; most membrane-bound organelles absent; size generally small (1–10 µm); single chromosome.
- **Eukaryotes**: well-defined nucleus with membrane; membrane-bound organelles; generally larger (5–100 µm); more than one chromosome.

steps.title: Solved: plant vs animal cell
steps.body: Plant: cell wall, large central vacuole, plastids (chloroplasts). Animal: no cell wall, small vacuoles, centrosome present, no plastids. Both: membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling bacteria eukaryotes.
- Thinking the cell wall is selectively permeable (it is freely permeable; the membrane is selective).

activity.prompt: Sort the features

quiz.q: Cell wall of plants is mainly
quiz.why: The plant cell wall is mainly cellulose. Fungi have chitin in their walls.

quiz.q: Shrinking of protoplasm away from the wall in hypertonic solution is
quiz.why: The shrinkage of the protoplasm away from the cell wall in a hypertonic solution is plasmolysis, caused by water loss.

quiz.q: The undefined nuclear region of bacteria is the
quiz.why: Bacteria lack a true nucleus. The region with the genetic material is the nucleoid, with no nuclear membrane.
Genes are functional segments of DNA that carry the instructions for making proteins. Chromatin is the DNA-protein material.
Bacteria are prokaryotes, as they have no nuclear membrane. Amoeba, yeast and the onion cell are eukaryotes.

scenes.text: Picture a busy factory: a head office, power plant, packing unit, roads and waste-disposal team.
A cell has all of these — organelles each doing one job.

steps.title: Membrane-bound organelles
steps.body:
- **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)**: network of membrane tubes. **RER** has ribosomes — makes proteins. **SER** makes lipids (fats); helps detoxify poisons and drugs in liver cells. ER forms channels for transport and makes membranes (membrane biogenesis).
- **Golgi apparatus** (Camillo Golgi, 1898): stacks of flattened sacs (cisterns); **stores, modifies, packages and dispatches** materials; forms lysosomes; makes complex sugars.
- **Lysosomes**: membrane sacs of **digestive enzymes**; clean the cell of worn-out organelles and foreign material; when a cell is damaged they may burst and digest it — '**suicide bags**'.
- **Mitochondria**: '**powerhouse**' — release energy as **ATP** (energy currency); double membrane, inner one folded. They have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins.
- **Plastids** (plants only): **chloroplasts** (green, chlorophyll, photosynthesis) and **leucoplasts** (colourless, store starch, oils, proteins); also have their own DNA and ribosomes.
- **Vacuoles**: storage sacs; large central vacuole in plants (up to 50–90% of cell volume) gives turgidity; contractile vacuole in Amoeba expels water; food vacuoles.

steps.title: Ribosomes
steps.body: Tiny particles (not membrane-bound) where **proteins are made**; found free in the cytoplasm and on RER.

steps.title: Solved: identify the organelle
steps.body: 1) Detoxifies drugs in liver → SER. 2) Packs and dispatches → Golgi. 3) ATP → mitochondria. 4) Digests worn-out parts → lysosome. 5) Stores starch in potato → leucoplast.

steps.title: Solved: what if…?
steps.body: If the Golgi apparatus were removed, the cell could not package and dispatch proteins to their destinations; secretions like enzymes would not be released properly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ribosomes are membrane-bound.
- Saying animal cells have chloroplasts.
- Calling lysosomes the powerhouse.

activity.prompt: Match organelle to function

quiz.why: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell. It stores and supplies energy for cell activities.
Mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins. Other organelles lack their own DNA.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that may digest the cell itself if it is damaged, so they are called suicide bags.
Camillo Golgi first described the Golgi apparatus in 1898, and it is named after him.
Proteins are made on ribosomes, which are sometimes called protein factories. They may be attached to the rough ER.

quiz.q: A large central vacuole is typical of
quiz.why: Plant cells typically have a large central vacuole that stores water and nutrients. Animal cells have small ones, if any.

scenes.text: Ishita falls and scrapes her knee. Within two weeks new skin covers the wound.
Her skin cells divided again and again — by mitosis — to replace the damaged ones.

steps.title: Why cells divide
steps.body:
Growth, repair of damaged tissues and reproduction. Two main types:
- **Mitosis**: one mother cell → **two identical daughter cells** with the **same chromosome number** as the mother. For growth and repair.
- **Meiosis**: in reproductive organs/tissues; one cell → **four** cells with **half** the chromosome number. Forms **gametes** (sperm, egg) so the chromosome number stays constant across generations after fertilisation.

steps.title: Solved: chromosome numbers
steps.body: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. After mitosis each daughter cell has **46**; each gamete formed by meiosis has **23**; after fertilisation the zygote has 23 + 23 = **46**.

steps.title: Solved: which division?
steps.body: Root tip growth → mitosis. Pollen grain formation → meiosis. Healing a cut → mitosis. Sperm formation → meiosis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying mitosis halves the chromosome number.
- Saying meiosis occurs in skin cells.

activity.prompt: Mitosis or meiosis?

quiz.why: Mitosis produces two identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. It is used for growth and repair.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes have half the chromosomes of the parent cell. Fertilisation then restores the full number.
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, so a gamete has half, 23.
Repair of tissue needs new identical cells, which are made by mitosis. Meiosis makes gametes.
Meiosis occurs in the reproductive organs, where gametes are formed. Skin, blood and bone cells divide by mitosis.

questions.q: The basic structural and functional unit of life is the
questions.why: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Tissues and organs are made up of cells.

questions.q: Powerhouse of the cell
questions.why: Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP, so they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

questions.q: Which is found only in plant cells?
questions.why: Plastids are found only in plant cells. Nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are in both plant and animal cells.

questions.q: Cell theory was proposed by
questions.why: The cell theory was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann. Virchow later added that cells come from earlier cells.

questions.q: Osmosis involves movement of
questions.why: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. It is not for gases, proteins or solutes.

questions.q: Bacteria lack
questions.why: Bacteria lack a nuclear membrane, so they have no true nucleus. They do have DNA, ribosomes and a cell membrane.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A red blood cell placed in distilled water bursts. Reason (R): Water enters the cell by osmosis from a hypotonic solution.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cell, so water enters by osmosis and the red blood cell swells and bursts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Lysosomes are called suicide bags. Reason (R): Their enzymes can digest the cell's own components when it is damaged.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Lysosomes can digest the cell's own parts if it is damaged, so they are called suicide bags.

questions.q: Which organelle helps detoxify drugs in liver cells?
questions.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) helps in detoxifying poisons and drugs, especially in liver cells.

questions.q: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in
questions.why: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, as water leaves the cell and the protoplasm shrinks.

questions.q: Number of daughter cells after one meiosis
questions.why: One meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosomes. Mitosis produces two.

questions.q: Case: A student puts one deshelled egg in pure water and another in concentrated salt solution. After 5 hours
questions.why: The egg in pure water gains water by osmosis and swells, while the egg in concentrated salt solution loses water and shrinks.

questions.q: Case: A boiled potato cup with sugar solution in water shows no rise in level. Reason
options: cells are dead, membranes no longer selectively permeable
questions.why: A boiled potato has dead cells, whose membranes are no longer selectively permeable, so osmosis does not occur. So there is no rise in level.

questions.q: Which pair both contain their own DNA and ribosomes?
questions.why: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and ribosomes. The other organelles do not have DNA of their own.

questions.q: If a cell's Golgi apparatus stopped working, the first function to fail would be
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus packages and dispatches proteins and other substances made in the cell. If it failed, this would stop first.

questions.q: A plant cell does not burst in pure water but an animal cell may. The best explanation
options: Plant cell wall resists excess turgor pressure
questions.why: A plant cell has a cell wall that resists the excess pressure (turgor pressure) from water entering. An animal cell has no wall, so it may burst.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Tissues
courses.summary: Why multicellular organisms need tissues, plant meristematic and permanent tissues (simple and complex), and animal epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.
outcomes: Define tissue and explain why plants and animals have different tissues
Classify meristematic tissues by position and describe their role
Compare parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem
Describe the types and functions of epithelial and connective tissues
Compare striated, smooth and cardiac muscle and describe a neuron

scenes.text: Arnav marks a seedling's root tip and the middle of the root with ink dots.
After a few days only the region near the tip has grown longer — that is where dividing tissue lives.

steps.title: What is a tissue?
steps.body: A **tissue** is a group of cells similar in structure and/or working together to perform a particular function (e.g. blood, muscle, xylem). Plants are mostly stationary and need lots of supportive (dead) tissue; growth is limited to certain regions. Animals move, use more energy, and most of their tissues are living; growth is more uniform.

steps.title: Meristematic tissue (plants)
steps.body:
Tissue of actively **dividing cells**, found in growing regions:
- **Apical meristem**: tips of stems and roots — increases **length**.
- **Lateral meristem (cambium)**: increases **girth** (thickness) of stem/root.
- **Intercalary meristem**: at the base of leaves or internodes (on twigs), e.g. in grasses.
Cells: very active, dense cytoplasm, thin cellulose walls, prominent nuclei, **lack vacuoles**.

steps.title: Solved: the onion root experiment
steps.body: Two jars of onions; roots of jar 2 are cut by 1 cm after 2 days. Jar 1 roots keep growing; jar 2 roots stop growing in length, because the **apical meristem** at the tip has been removed.

steps.title: Solved: grass after mowing
steps.body: Grass regrows after mowing because the **intercalary meristem** at the base of leaves keeps dividing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying meristematic cells have big vacuoles (they lack them — vacuoles would slow division).
- Mixing up apical (length) and lateral (girth).

activity.prompt: Match the meristem with its position/role

quiz.why: Meristematic cells are dividing cells with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, but have few or no vacuoles. Vacuoles appear in mature cells.

quiz.q: Girth of a stem increases due to
quiz.why: The lateral meristem (cambium) increases the girth (thickness) of stems and roots. The apical meristem increases length.

options: a group of similar cells doing a function
quiz.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells that together perform a specific function. Many tissues make an organ.

quiz.q: Roots stop growing in length if we cut
quiz.why: The root tip contains the apical meristem, where cells divide to lengthen the root. If cut, the root stops growing in length.

quiz.q: Most plant tissues that support are
quiz.why: Most supportive plant tissues, like sclerenchyma, are dead, since they only give strength. This is why plants can stand up without much energy.

story.title: The coconut husk and the lotus stem

scenes.text: The coconut's husk is tough and fibrous; the lotus stem is full of air spaces and floats.
Both are plant tissues — sclerenchyma for strength, aerenchyma for buoyancy.

steps.title: Simple permanent tissues
steps.body:
Formed when meristematic cells lose the ability to divide (**differentiation**).
- **Parenchyma**: living, thin-walled, loosely packed with intercellular spaces; supports and **stores food**. Variants: **chlorenchyma** (with chlorophyll — photosynthesis), **aerenchyma** (large air cavities — buoyancy in aquatic plants).
- **Collenchyma**: living, elongated, cells irregularly thickened at the corners, little intercellular space; gives **flexibility** (leaf stalks, below the epidermis; lets stems bend without breaking).
- **Sclerenchyma**: **dead**, long and narrow, walls thickened by **lignin**, often no internal space; makes the plant hard and stiff (coconut husk, seed coats, nut shells, veins of leaves, around vascular bundles).

steps.title: Protective tissues
steps.body:
- **Epidermis**: single outer layer; often covered with waxy **cutin** to prevent water loss; in desert plants it is thick. Has **stomata** (pores enclosed by two kidney-shaped **guard cells**) for gas exchange and transpiration. Root epidermis has root hairs for absorption.
- **Cork** (bark of older trees): dead, compactly arranged cells with **suberin** in their walls — impervious to gases and water. Cork from the cork oak is used for bottle stoppers and insulation.

steps.title: Solved: identify the tissue
steps.body: Husk of coconut → sclerenchyma. Leaf stalk bends in the wind → collenchyma. Lotus stem floats → aerenchyma. Green leaf mesophyll → chlorenchyma. Potato stores starch → parenchyma.

steps.title: Solved: functions of stomata
steps.body: Exchange of gases with the atmosphere (CO₂ in, O₂ out in photosynthesis) and **transpiration** — loss of water as vapour, which helps pull water up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling sclerenchyma living.
- Mixing up cutin (epidermis) and suberin (cork).

activity.prompt: Living or dead at maturity?

quiz.q: Tissue with lignin, dead, giving hardness
quiz.why: Sclerenchyma has thick lignified walls and dead cells, giving hardness and strength. It is found in husk and seed coats.
Aerenchyma has large air spaces that help aquatic plants to float. It is a type of parenchyma.

quiz.q: Flexibility to leaf stalks is due to
quiz.why: Collenchyma gives flexibility, which lets leaves and stems bend without breaking. It is found in leaf stalks.
Cork cells have a chemical called suberin in their walls, which makes them impermeable to gases and water.
Each stoma is enclosed by two guard cells that open and close it. They control gas exchange and water loss.

quiz.q: Food storage in plants is mainly by
quiz.why: Parenchyma cells are thin-walled and living, and they store food. Sclerenchyma and cork are dead.

scenes.text: A tall coconut tree lifts water up from its roots 20 m to its leaves, and sends sugar from leaves down to the roots.
Two separate 'pipes' — xylem and phloem — run side by side as vascular bundles.

steps.title: Xylem
steps.body: Conducts **water and minerals upward** from roots. Elements: **tracheids** and **vessels** (tubular, dead, thick-walled — transport water vertically), **xylem parenchyma** (living — stores food, helps sideways conduction), **xylem fibres** (supportive).

steps.title: Phloem
steps.body: Conducts **food (sugars)** from leaves to other parts — in **both directions**. Elements: **sieve tubes** (tubular cells with perforated walls), **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**. All phloem cells are **living except phloem fibres**.

steps.title: Solved: xylem vs phloem
steps.body: Direction: xylem one-way (up); phloem both ways. Material: water + minerals vs food. Living cells: xylem mainly dead (only parenchyma living); phloem mainly living (only fibres dead).

steps.title: Solved: girdling
steps.body: If a ring of bark (including phloem) is removed from a tree trunk, food cannot move down to the roots; the roots eventually starve while water still rises through xylem for a while.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying phloem moves food only downward.
- Saying xylem vessels are living.

activity.prompt: Xylem or phloem?

quiz.why: Water moves up from the roots to the leaves through the xylem. Phloem carries food.

quiz.q: The only dead element of phloem
quiz.why: Of phloem's elements, only phloem fibres are dead. Sieve tubes, companion cells and parenchyma are living.

quiz.q: The only living element of xylem
quiz.why: Xylem parenchyma is the only living element of xylem. Tracheids, vessels and fibres are dead.
Food moves in the phloem in both directions, up and down, according to the plant's needs. Water in the xylem moves only upwards.
Xylem and phloem are made of more than one kind of cell working together, so they are complex tissues.

scenes.text: Dhruv fractures his arm; the doctor talks about bone, ligaments, cartilage and blood.
All are connective tissues — different jobs, one family. His skin covering is epithelium.

steps.title: Epithelial tissue
steps.body:
Covering/protective tissue: cells tightly packed in a continuous sheet with little intercellular space, separated from underlying tissue by a **basement membrane**. Controls exchange of materials.
- **Simple squamous**: thin, flat — lining of blood vessels, lung alveoli, mouth/oesophagus lining (thin delicate lining).
- **Stratified squamous**: layers — skin (prevents wear and tear).
- **Columnar** (tall, pillar-like): inner lining of intestine (absorption, secretion); with **cilia** in the respiratory tract (ciliated columnar, moves mucus).
- **Cuboidal**: kidney tubules, ducts of salivary glands (mechanical support).
- **Glandular**: folds inward to form glands that secrete.

steps.title: Connective tissue
steps.body:
Cells loosely spaced in an intercellular **matrix**.
- **Blood**: fluid matrix **plasma** with RBCs, WBCs and platelets; transports gases, food, hormones, wastes.
- **Bone**: hard, strong matrix of **calcium and phosphorus** compounds; framework and support.
- **Ligament**: bone to **bone**; elastic, strong.
- **Tendon**: muscle to **bone**; fibrous, great strength, limited flexibility.
- **Cartilage**: widely spaced cells in a matrix of proteins and sugars; smoothens bone surfaces at joints; in nose, ear, trachea, larynx.
- **Areolar**: between skin and muscles, around blood vessels and nerves, in bone marrow; fills spaces, supports, repairs.
- **Adipose**: below skin and between organs; stores fat, insulates.

steps.title: Solved: identify
steps.body: Lining of kidney tubules → cuboidal epithelium. Muscle attached to bone → tendon. External ear flexibility → cartilage. Fat below skin → adipose. Lining of alveoli → simple squamous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping ligament (bone–bone) and tendon (muscle–bone).
- Calling blood a 'liquid organ' rather than a connective tissue.

activity.prompt: Match the tissue with where it is found

quiz.q: Muscle is attached to bone by
quiz.why: A tendon joins muscle to bone and is strong and flexible. A ligament connects bone to bone.

quiz.q: The fluid matrix of blood is
quiz.why: The fluid matrix of blood is plasma. It carries cells, nutrients and hormones.
Skin is made of stratified squamous epithelium, with layers of flat cells to protect against wear. A single layer would wear out.
Bone's matrix is hard because it is rich in calcium and phosphorus compounds. Bone is strong and supports the body.
Adipose tissue stores fat, which serves as an energy reserve and insulation. It is found below the skin.
The intestine lining has columnar epithelium, with tall cells that help in absorption and secretion.

scenes.text: Your heart beats about 70 times a minute, every minute of your life, without tiring.
Cardiac muscle works rhythmically; your arm muscles obey your wishes; nerves carry the messages.

steps.title: Muscular tissue
steps.body:
Elongated **muscle fibres** with **contractile proteins** that contract and relax to cause movement.
- **Striated (skeletal, voluntary)**: long, cylindrical, unbranched, **multinucleate**, light and dark bands (striations); attached to bones; move limbs at will.
- **Smooth (unstriated, involuntary)**: long, spindle-shaped, **uninucleate**; in alimentary canal, iris of eye, ureters, bronchi of lungs; movement of food, etc.
- **Cardiac (involuntary)**: in the heart; cylindrical, **branched**, uninucleate; rhythmic contraction and relaxation throughout life.

steps.title: Nervous tissue
steps.body: Cells of brain, spinal cord and nerves are **neurons**. A neuron has a **cell body** with a nucleus and cytoplasm, short branched **dendrites** (receive messages) and a long **axon** (carries messages; can be up to a metre long). Many nerve fibres bound by connective tissue make a **nerve**. Signals are electrical impulses; nerve and muscle together let us respond quickly.

steps.title: Solved: identify the muscle
